#5639. As Hearings Begin, Sierra Club Virginia Calls for the SCC to Stop the Dominion NextEra Merger

Richmond, Virginia — Tomorrow, November 17, the Virginia State Corporation Commission (SCC) will begin the evidentiary hearing for NextEra Energy and Dominion Energy’s merger proposal, which would create the nation’s largest ever utility. Sierra Club filed expert testimony last month urging the SCC to reject the merger given the way it threatens the Virginia’s Clean Economy Act (VCEA) and violates the Utility Transfers Act, posing a significant risk to energy affordability for Virginia families.

Dominion and NextEra have failed to show that customer benefits, not shareholders profits, were a motivating factor for the merger. The utilities have offered a temporary $10 per month bill credit to Virginia customers for four years to help cover any additional costs. However, the credit does not so much as cover the $30 per month Virginia families expect to pay in anticipated bill increases to maintain fossil fuel plants and meet AI data centers demand in 2027 alone.

If approved, the new utility would service 10 million customers across the Southeastern United States. Allied groups will rally outside the SCC tomorrow for the Stop the NextEra Takeover: Final Rally at the SCC.

Ahead of tomorrow’s hearing, Connor Kish, Director of the Sierra Club Virginia Chapter, issued the following statement:

“Throughout November, Virginians have shown up in droves at public hearings to oppose Dominion and NextEra’s proposed merger. Utility customers, independent policy experts, and local leaders have cited sky-high energy bills, AI data center demand, and abandoned climate goals as reasons to be wary of Dominion and NextEra’s bid to become the country’s largest ever utility.

“Meanwhile, the utilities have yet to prove the merger will result in any tangible benefits for customers. Their offer of a temporary $10 monthly bill credit for customers is nothing in comparison to the $10 billion in profits shareholders are anticipated to receive should the SCC approve the merger. Virginia deserves utilities that prioritize families, not shareholders out for bonuses. To keep the lights on and make bills affordable, it’s critical that SCC fulfill its duty to the public and reject the merger.”

#5638. Here's How Much It Can Cost To Refuel These 5 Vehicles Due To High Diesel Prices

With the national average cost of a gallon of diesel fuel having been over six dollars for several months now, as a direct result of the Trump administration's war with Iran shutting off much of the world's oil supply, it's been an expensive time to own a diesel-powered vehicle. Add to that the inflation-and-tariff-driven ballooning cost of insurance, car payments, parts, and maintenance, and you've got a perfect storm of anti-consumer policies playing out in real time. As an owner and semi-regular driver of a 2013 Porsche Cayenne diesel, these policies have hit me directly in the pocketbook. I'm managing to weather the storm well enough, but many of America's working class families have been devastated by this blow to the affordability of daily life.

Recent reports from Fortune Magazine indicate that the war has cost the average American household nearly $2,000 since it began in February, with the lion's share of that cost coming as a result of increased energy costs. We're all getting hit pretty hard right now at the pump. I wanted to take a look at just how hard us diesel drivers are getting crunched, and provide a bit of context for the people who might not fully understand the numbers.

Let's take a look together at the increase in costs to fill a tank of diesel in a handful of diesel-powered machines. We'll also look at historical diesel cost trends, what some non-Americans are paying, and how this price increase impacts other segments of the global economy.

Here's a fun one to kick off this exercise. Between 2002 and 2008, Volkswagen stuffed a giant ten-cylinder turbocharged diesel V10 into its flagship SUV, the Touareg. It was a torque powerhouse with 553 pound-feet on tap. A product of the engineering excess Volkswagen Group committed to during Ferdinand Piech's tenure as Chairman, this engine was completely unnecessary, but in hindsight, pretty frickin' cool. One major downside, however, was that it was rated at just 17 mpg combined.

The fuel tank in a V10 TDI Touareg holds 100 liters, or 26.41 gallons. With the current national average price of diesel sitting at $6.17 per gallon, if you rolled in with a completely empty tank (not recommended, by the way), it would cost a staggering $162.95 to fill it back up to the tippy top. Do you think that's expensive? Let's look at what our friends to the north are paying in Canada. The current Canadian average for diesel fuel is about 2.60 CAD per liter. That equates to about $1.84 per liter, or $184 to fill that same tank. Europe is the home of expensive fuel, right? Over in the European Union, they're paying €2.15 per liter on average. At current exchange rates, that's $2.41 per liter ($9.12 per gallon), or $241 for a diesel Touareg fill-up.

On average, Americans drive around 13,660 miles per year. If they happened to be one of the few people in the country daily-driving a twenty-year old German SUV with a Volkswagen V10 TDI under the hood, at current diesel rates they're going to pay around $4,957.78 for fuel this year. If I owned one, I think I'd be looking for something a little more efficient.

The Volkswagen XL1 wasn't sold in the U.S. market, but it's another product of the Piech era of over-engineering at VW. The goal here was to build the world's most efficient vehicle, using an offset two-seat configuration, a tiny carbon fiber monocoque, extreme lightweighting and aerodynamic advancements, and a two-cylinder 48-horsepower diesel engine mated to a plug-in hybrid electric motor. While the car was absurdly expensive and not really very good at anything but looking cool and sipping fuel — it managed to do over 100 kilometers on just 0.9 liters of diesel. That's the equivalent of about 261 mpg. It's basically the philosophical opposite of the Touareg V10 TDI.

With just enough battery capacity to travel about 31 miles on a charge, plus a tiny 10-liter fuel tank, the XL1 is hardly a long-legged touring machine. That said, topped up on both, it's efficient enough to travel around 500 miles at a go. Only 250 of these machines were built, so it's unlikely you will have a practical use for this information, but maybe you can trot it out at a party or something. Let's compare the XL1 to the Touareg.

Obviously, since the tank is one-tenth the size of the Touaregs, a fill up in the XL1 will be one-tenth the cost. I certainly wouldn't mind spending $16.29 for a full tank of diesel. That same fill-up would be $18.40 if you're Canadian, or $24.10 for our European friends. The same 13,660 miles that cost almost five grand in a Touareg would be just $322.92 (plus a few extra bucks on your electricity bill to charge the hybrid gubbins) in the XL1. It just goes to show how important fuel efficiency is for your annual running costs.

It's been a handful of years since Ford offered a diesel option for its basic F-150 pickup, but the F-series Super Duty lineup still offers the massive 6.7-liter Power Stroke turbo diesel V8 as a $12,495 option. This is one of the most popular diesel vehicles in the U.S. today.

If you opt for the long-wheelbase 8-foot bed Crew Cab configuration, the truck is delivered with a gigantic 48-gallon fuel tank. Now that's an incredibly expensive fill-up. At the $6.17 average we mentioned earlier, that's $296.16 per tank. If you happen to drive a Power Stroke Super Duty in California, where a gallon of diesel is $8.14, you're looking at nearly $400 in diesel. And don't even get me started on the cost of DEF.

Because the F-250 doesn't have to report fuel economy numbers and isn't subject to EPA reporting, it's hard to get an exact number, but Power Stroke Super Duty owners report real-world fuel economy on Fuelly around 14 mpg. At that rate over the same 13,660 miles per year, a diesel F-250 owner is paying $6,020.15 for a year of fuel. If they're Californian, you can pump that number up to $7,942. Add with the cost of a monthly truck payment and decent car insurance, and you're going to see a really high cost of ownership here.

Have you noticed that the produce in your local grocery store is getting more expensive? According to the Department of Agriculture, U.S. fruit and vegetable prices have risen nearly 5% and 3%, respectively, with further increases expected through 2027. At least some of that increase can be attributed to the increase in diesel prices, as basically every farm implement on the planet is run by diesel fuel. The Farm Bureau reports that U.S. farmers spent a combined $2.4 billion more on diesel fuel during the 2026 planting season compared to 2025.

Let's take a look at the best-selling combine harvester in the market for the purposes of this exercise, John Deere's S780. This giant machine chews up, separates, and spits out most field-grown grains, corn, soybeans, rice, and even sunflower. It also burns quite a lot of diesel.

The S780 has an absolutely massive fuel tank, taking on a full 330 gallons from dry to full up. Obviously, farmers don't pay the same price as standard road diesel, as "red dye" off-road diesel is exempt from road excise taxes. Federal taxes are levied on diesel at a rate of about 25 cents per gallon, while state diesel taxes average around 35 cents per gallon. It's hard to say exactly what farmers will pay because there are delivery fees and bulk purchase discounts to take into consideration, but for the sake of simplicity, let's just take that 60 cents from the $6.17 national average road diesel price and say farmers pay $5.57. That means filling up this John Deere will still be an impressive $1,838 bill. Back in January, when road diesel was about $3.47, a fill-up would have been just $947.10, about half as much.

If you thought farm equipment was expensive to fill up, just wait until you hear about the incredible costs of fueling a semi. And we'll use the current market leader, the Freightliner Cascadia, as our benchmark.

The Cascadia is available in a bunch of different configurations, and each configuration has its own separate fuel tank capacity, depending on engine size, sleeper length, and axle count. Each truck carries one large aluminum tank on either side of the cab, ranging from 80 gallons to 150 gallons of capacity each. For maximum effect, let's look at the largest 300-gallon long-haul trucker configuration. At today's prices, it would cost a whopping $1,851 to cram both tanks full of diesel. That really puts things into perspective, doesn't it?

The Department of Energy says semi-trucks on the road in the U.S. travel an average of 58,890 miles per year. Considering there are around 2.9 million active registered semi trucks on the road today, that's a whole lot of miles travelled and a whole lot of diesel burned. At the current average price of diesel, and with the Cascadia achieving an astonishing industry-best 10 mpg, each one of these monsters costs $36,335.13 per year to feed. If you've been wondering why prices are going up at the grocery store lately, this is a pretty big part of it. Transporting goods from manufacturer to retailer is expensive.

#5636. Scientists Are Using Your Unhinged Driving Behaviors In Grand Theft Auto To Make Roads Safer

As you're preparing to explore all of 212 GB's worth of "Grand Theft Auto VI" and go on the ultimate chaotic crime driving spree in the game's Florida-like state of Leonida, scientists are gearing up for their own run through the new game. GTA's years of detailed city streets, paired with drivers' unhinged behaviors behind the wheel have unintentionally created a solid test bed for a variety of scientific studies aimed at making real-life driving and travel safer, according to the BBC.

If scientists want to look at how humans react to dangerous situations on the road, what game has better scenarios than GTA? The game's detailed city maps and roads also help make the science cheaper.

Pavlo Bazilinskyy, a human factors engineer at Eindhoven University of Technology in the Netherlands, told the BBC that a video game with such a massive budget is "miles ahead of the average simulator setup." GTA provides a realistic environment for Bazilinskyy and his fellow researchers. It's an ideal space for them to use technology like eye-tracking, or more specifically, cyclist behavior as they head towards hazardous situations.

Intel Labs and Darmstadt University in Germany shared a paper in 2016 on how the two used Grand Theft Auto's road scenes and objects to teach AI how to detect both. MIT Technology Review wrote that using the video game's already categorized imagery and streets would help researchers save thousands upon thousands of hours trying to collect and label that street imagery. The game's addition of changes in time and weather, which can both influence the road conditions, helps models experience realities that are difficult and expensive for researchers to recreate digitally.

Institutions like the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology conduct similar research today, using GTA to help train its AI driving software to avoid dangers on the road. In the U.S., at Eastern Michigan University, researchers have used GTA to train an AI's ethical decision-making. EMU's work found that the tests helped reduce fatal accidents by 24%.

There are devices currently in development that could alert cyclists and pedestrians of upcoming hazards on busy roads, acting like a sixth sense for detecting traffic behind them. To test one of these devices, researchers at the Osnabrück University of Applied Sciences in Germany placed participants on a stationary bike with screens showing GTA V in front of and behind them. The devices successfully spotted traffic as it headed towards the cyclists, but without the inherent danger that would be a part of testing the device on a real road.

Science and road safety may be the two furthest things from the average GTA player's mind come Friday, when the sixth installment is available for gameplay. However, scientists and researchers will likely be thrilled to have a newer, even more realistic setting to play with.

#5635. Obesity-Related Cancer Deaths Doubled Over the Past 30 Years

— Liver, pancreatic, and uterine cancer deaths drove the surge

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. -- Deaths attributable to cancers related to high body mass index (BMI) have more than doubled over the past three decades, according to U.S. data.

Using estimates from the Global Burden of Disease 2023 study, cancer deaths linked to a BMI of 25 or higher increased 104.2%, from 23,236 in 1990 to 47,450 in 2023, reported Digantkumar Patel, MD, of the Springfield Clinic in Illinois.

During this period, the age-standardized death rate increased by 8.1%, from 7.28 to 7.87 per 100,000 people. That uptick indicates that the rise in obesity-related cancer deaths "cannot be explained by population growth and aging alone," Patel said at the ObesityWeek annual meeting.

"We all know about the association between obesity and cancer, but we have less information about how much the burden of these cancers has changed over time," he noted, suggesting that pinpointing the fastest-growing malignancies can help target screening and prevention.

"Our findings reinforce the importance of obesity prevention and treatment as a part of cancer prevention," Patel added.

Among the 12 high BMI-related cancers, deaths from liver, pancreatic, and uterine cancers grew the fastest between 1990 and 2023, with increases of 566% (from 913 to 6,081 deaths), 487% (from 414 to 2,432 deaths), and 193% (from 1,935 to 5,677 deaths).

Despite those sharp increases, colorectal cancer accounted for the highest total number of high BMI-related cancer deaths in 2023, at 11,161, reflecting a 53% increase in deaths since 1990.

Total deaths also rose for the remaining eight cancers -- thyroid (+145%), multiple myeloma (+121%), kidney (+104%), leukemia (+73%), ovarian (+69%), gallbladder/biliary tract (+61%), non-Hodgkin lymphoma (+60%), and breast (+50%) -- though age-standardized mortality rates actually declined over time by average annual percent change for breast (-0.91%), non-Hodgkin lymphoma (-0.82%), colorectal (-0.57%), ovarian (-0.33%), gallbladder/biliary tract (-0.26%), and leukemia (-0.17%).

These shifts rearranged the mortality rankings among high BMI-related cancers during this time period. Liver cancer jumped from eighth to second place, uterine cancer climbed from fifth to third, and pancreatic cancer moved from 11th to seventh. Meanwhile, breast cancer dropped from second to fourth place, kidney cancer fell from third to fifth, and leukemia dipped from fourth to sixth. Thyroid cancer remained in 12th place throughout the study period.

Disability burden climbed alongside mortality. Since 1990, disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) nearly doubled, rising 97.4% from 560,000 to 1.11 million, while years lived with disability spiked 129.5%, from 36,997 to 84,892.

Adults ages 55 to 79 bore the brunt of the burden, accounting for 71.3% of all high BMI-related cancer DALYs in 2023, with the heaviest concentration among those ages 65 to 69. In adults 70 and older, DALYs surged by 615% for liver cancer and 655% for pancreatic cancer.

However, among females ages 15 to 39, uterine cancer DALYs rose 220%. "This is particularly concerning because it suggests that the growing burden is not limited only to older adults," Patel said.

The burden also varied by geography. Age-standardized death rates increased in 37 states, led by those in the South. West Virginia, Kentucky, and Mississippi recorded the highest death rates in 2023, while the steepest increases since 1990 occurred in Oklahoma (+43%), West Virginia (+39%), New Mexico (+36%), and Tennessee (+36%). Conversely, the largest declines were seen in Washington, D.C. (-26%), New Jersey (-18%), and New York (-17%).

After colorectal cancer, uterine or liver cancer ranked second for high BMI-related cancer deaths in nearly every state, except in Mississippi and Alabama, where breast cancer held the second spot.

"It suggests that cancer prevention strategies should be catered to different regions rather than using the same approach in all states," Patel said. "From a public health perspective, we need to focus resources in states where the burden is highest and the fastest-rising."

Moving forward, he noted that research should examine disparities by sex and race and model projections through 2060 to account for the expanding use of modern obesity treatments, including GLP-1 medications.

#5634. The Smallest V10 To Ever Power A Car Was The Size Of Most 4-Cylinders

V10 engines are the ultimate metaphors for what gearheads love about performance cars — relics of a bygone era where noise, power and absolute combustion were the go-to recipes of kings. The Lexus LFA and Porsche Carrera GT – arguably two of the greatest road-going supercars ever – used them. So too did the Sesto Elemento, which was Lamborghini's answer to the very essence of track-day hoonery. They even featured in the E60-generation BMW M5 – a perhaps ugly but elegant grand tourer that made a mockery of purpose-built, seven-figure unobtanium thanks to an unrestricted 200-mph-plus top speed.

But aside from the actual cylinder count, what these cars all have in common is big displacements. The LFA's V10 is the smallest of the bunch, and even that measures in at 4.8 liters. You'd think, then, that all V10s must surely have to be meaty by nature to work, but you'd be wrong. Say hello to the Connaught Type D concept: a sports car conceived in 2004 and equipped with a pipsqueak 2.0-liter V10. Yes, two liters.

For some perspective, many passenger cars these days use 2.0-liter four-cylinder engines, including the Honda Civic hatchback, which is the platonic ideal of economy cars. Now imagine constraining yourself to such a small surface area, with the added complication of having to manage an extra six cylinders. The result would be ... amazing, actually.

The standard Connaught used a naturally aspirated V10 and a Lynch electric motor for 162 hp. Yes, hybrid technology was being tested as far back as 2004 with this car, long before the hypercar Holy Trinity was formed and crowned. However, in the top-spec "Syracuse GT" version, the Type D's V10 engine was instead paired with a supercharger for a healthy 300 hp. The Connaught Type D Syracuse GT's 0 to 60 mph was projected to be in the low-four-second range, and popular publications cited a top speed of roughly 171 mph. This thing also tipped the scales at just 1,874 pounds.

Those are some serious numbers and would be enough to trouble many four-cylinder sports cars that, dare we say, could be called super. Even today's fleet of racey four-banger metal wouldn't be safe. The Honda Civic Type R, which is a rowdy teenage dirtbag, takes about a second longer to get to 60 mph, while the 2026 Ford Mustang RTR (with its 2.3-liter engine) only just edges it by two-tenths of a second (via Car and Driver). Unfortunately, the Type D never made it past the concept stage and into production due to funding issues.

The brand was acquired in 2016 by a British automotive design company called Bevan Davidson International (BDI), and in 2021, it came up with a wild idea to revive Connaught with a 20-cylinder supercar called the X20. We'll give you a moment to rub your eyes and re-read the final part of that sentence.

That 20-cylinder engine would be made up of two horizontally opposed and mid-mounted 2.0-liter V10s. It would also blow its waste gases out of no fewer than 20 exhaust pipes, rev all the way up to 10,000 rpm, and, as far as the company's calculations go, produce more than 500 hp. That sounds less like a car, and more like a miniature steam train from the 17th century, but no word on whether any have been produced yet.

Whether BDI chooses to also bring the original Type D back to life remains to be seen, but just think about it for a second: A tiny-displacement, supercharged V10-powered sports car built to comply with the ever-growing regulations posed on the industry by lawmakers. Wouldn't that be just marvelous?

#5632. Next-Generation Oral SERD Approved for Breast Cancer

— Combination of giredestrant plus everolimus reduced risk of progression or death by 62%

The FDA approved the next-generation oral selective estrogen receptor degrader (SERD) giredestrant (Wilserdly) in combination with everolimus for previously treated estrogen receptor (ER)-positive, HER2-negative, ESR1-mutated breast cancer.

The all-oral combination is indicated for patients with locally advanced or metastatic cancer whose disease recurred during or after completion of endocrine-based adjuvant therapy or progressed on at least one endocrine-based regimen in the metastatic setting.

"As oncologists we are always looking for better and more effective treatments for patients with metastatic breast cancer, particularly when their disease progresses on endocrine therapies and CDK4/6 inhibitors," said Erica Mayer, MD, MPH, of the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston, in a press release. "Today's FDA approval of giredestrant gives patients an important new therapeutic option, which substantially improves disease control while also providing the convenience of an all-oral regimen."

Approval was based on results from the global phase III evERA study, which evaluated giredestrant plus everolimus versus standard endocrine therapy plus everolimus in patients with ER-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer, more than half of whom had ESR1 mutations.

The study showed that among those with ESR1-mutated cancer, median progression-free survival (PFS) nearly doubled from 5.5 months with standard endocrine therapy to 10.0 months with giredestrant and everolimus (HR 0.38, 95% CI 0.27-0.54, P<0.001).

In the overall study population, median PFS was 8.8 months for patients receiving giredestrant plus everolimus (HR 0.56, 95% CI 0.44-0.71, P<0.001).

The most common adverse reactions in patients receiving giredestrant plus everolimus were stomatitis, rash, fatigue, diarrhea, musculoskeletal pain, pneumonitis, and nausea, while the most common laboratory abnormalities were decreased hemoglobin, lymphocytes, white blood cell count, neutrophils, platelets, calcium, potassium, and sodium, and increased aspartate transaminase, alanine transaminase, and creatinine.

Prescribing information includes warnings and precautions for bradycardia and embryo-fetal toxicity.

The FDA also authorized the FoundationOne Liquid CDx assay as a companion diagnostic device to identify patients with breast cancer with ESR1 mutations.

#5631. 2027 Toyota GRMN Corolla Cranks The GR's Fun Factor Up To 11

Toyota shook up the compact performance car space when it introduced the GR Corolla back in 2022, and perhaps even more remarkably, it has continuously improved the car each year since. I had the distinct pleasure of hucking the 2026 GR Corolla around Sonoma Raceway last year at the press launch, and in a rare turn of events, I actually got to compare its driving dynamics to a 2025 car as well as a 2024 model.

That comparison showed me how the GR team's gradual tweaks positively impacted the experience of driving a GR Corolla, and last week I got the chance to try out their latest creation. Toyota let me loose the limited-production 2027 GRMN Corolla around Eagles Canyon Raceway in Texas to experience what is the ultimate Corolla — for now, at least. Again, the changes are small, but the resulting improvements are immediately palpable.

Full disclosure: Toyota wanted me to sample an array of its new offerings for 2027 so badly that it flew me out to Texas, put me up in a hotel for a few nights, and kept me fed so I could drive its cars. I only got to drive the GRMN Corolla on the track, so I cannot offer on-road impressions.

The GRMN Corolla earned those last two letters while lapping arguably the most iconic race track on the planet, the Nürburgring. The MN in GRMN represents the fact that this version of the GR Corolla was tuned by the "Meisters of the Nürburgring," and that's not just marketing jargon. The GR team made suspension, aerodynamic, cooling, and drivetrain tweaks. They also swapped some metal body panels for carbon-fiber ones, all with the goal of making the GRMN Corolla the most track-focused GR Corolla yet.

Suspension-wise, Toyota changed the bump stops because it found the GR Corolla's standard suspension would hit the bump stops on certain corners of the Nürburgring, causing sudden understeer. Aerodynamically, Toyota added a larger hood duct, bumper side splitters, fender ducts from the Super Taikyu hydrogen-engine GR Corolla development car to reduce front-end lift, and that adjustable rear spoiler for increased stability. The entire hood, both front fenders, and the rear spoiler are made from carbon fiber, and the rear seat was removed in order to save weight, making the GRMN weigh 66 pounds less than a standard GR Corolla.

Moving to the drivetrain, Toyota added a supplemental AWD transfer case oil cooler that will also be available for other GR Corollas but comes as standard on the GRMN, which keeps the system cool even after repeated laps in high temperatures. There's also a standard intercooler sprayer to keep it and the turbo working hard in high temperatures, too.

Engineers retuned Track Mode in the GRMN's GR-Four all-wheel-drive system to make it more rear-biased, and they managed to increase the turbocharged 1.6-liter three-cylinder engine's torque output by 7 pound-feet while also making maximum torque available at lower engine speeds, so it now produces 300 horsepower and 302 lb-ft. The changes are definitely palpable on the track, with my favorite upgrades being the GRMN's sticky Pilot Sport Cup 2 tires, the retuned steering rack with increased feedback, and the close-ratio transmission from the Morizo Edition, all of which heightened the GRMN Corolla's dynamics.

Toyota so graciously let the media go hog wild on Eagles Canyon Raceway before, which I had never seen or driven before, and luckily I was in the perfect car to attempt to learn the 2.7-mile "Italian Canyon" course's 15 corners, 20 apexes, and 150 feet of elevation change. We weren't allowed to do any consecutive laps — we had to enter the pits on each lap — but we were allowed to do as many laps as we pleased. I drove both the GRMN Corolla and a 2026 GR Corolla to see if I could tell the difference, and the answer was a resounding "hell yeah!"

Taking off from the pits, the GRMN Corolla's inputs immediately felt more taut and communicative, from the snickety shifter to the talkative steering. Once I left pit lane and got to wring out the powertrain, the GRMN's extra mid-range torque and lighter weight made it feel like it had noticeably more shove than the standard GR. Cornering is where the GRMN really shined, though.

When I first entered a corner, the GRMN's reworked steering felt sharper and more direct, and the more rear-biased all-wheel-drive tune in Track Mode made its nose feel like it could change direction like a greyhound weaving through the slalom at the AKC National Agility Championship. Compared to the GR, the GRMN felt markedly more agile and more eager to rotate rather than understeer.

The GRMN's retuned engine pulled its lighter weight out of corners stronger than the GR, and its Cup 2 tires made it cling to the road with what felt like merciless ferocity. Naturally, since this was my first time on this track I made my fair share of corner misjudgments, but even when I overcooked a decreasing radius turn, a dab of brakes made the GRMN dive toward the apex, expertly turning "oh crap" moments into drama-free learning experiences. Chief Engineer for the GR Corolla Naoyuki Sakamoto called the GRMN, "a car you can confidently push the limits in," and Sakamoto-san was absolutely correct.

The GRMN Corolla is an extremely limited-production vehicle, with just 730 units planned globally, so the U.S. market will get even fewer than that. Exclusivity paired with the GRMN Corolla's other driving experience enhancements and proven track-oriented capabilities make it a rare special edition that truly feels special. That said, it's set to cost $65,665, so it had better be pretty damn special to make you pay $65k for a freakin' Corolla.

The interior is all Corolla, but at least it has more aggressive bucket seats and a flocked instrument panel and A-pillars. You also forgo the opportunity to bring more than one passenger along for the ride, since the GRMN has what looks like a lap bar from a roller coaster rather than a back seat. Perhaps the biggest issue I had with the GRMN Corolla was that its rear windows do not roll down. The driver's window control panel has just two switches, one for the driver's side front door and one for the passenger side window, which I can imagine will cause horrendous wind buffeting for anyone who enjoys driving with the windows down.

In case you couldn't tell, I was totally taken by the GRMN Corolla. I already loved driving the GR Corolla, but the GRMN Corolla's sharpened inputs, hardcore style, and delightful driving dynamics take that love even further. I truly hope this was not the last time I can drive one.

#5629. BMW In South Carolina: A Free Trade Success Story

I recently attended BMW’s “Beyond The Machine” event in South Carolina. The largest facility of the German company globally is Plant Spartanburg in Greer, South Carolina. As part of the event, I saw the opening of BMW’s new battery plant in nearby Woodruff. We stayed in the nearby city of Greenville, which was transformed by BMW and the businesses that followed.

Beyond the vehicles and manufacturing, which I plan to cover in more detail in future articles, one of the most striking aspects was the human impact. From the “Woodruffian” Mayor fighting back tears at the opening of the battery plant to the plant employees to the people I met exploring the town, they clearly appreciate what BMW has done for the community. Throughout the presentations and discussions, there was support for free trade along with the local benefits. People in the area pride themselves in their resilience. They have reason to be proud. And they were optimistic about the growth of the increasingly clean manufacturing and electrified products from this global company.

The area around Greenville, South Carolina the rose to prominence in the 1870s on the textile industry. Cotton from throughout the South that had previously been shipped to other areas for processing was processed in Greenville and Spartanburg counties. However, as global competition increased in the 20th century, the mills became less competitive. The last textile mill closed in Greenville in 1977, although a few textile operations continued in the region into the 1980’s. As that industry left, the local economy declined. If the story ended there, many might use it as an argument against free trade.

When BMW came to South Carolina in 1992, they saw a lot of potential. Michelin had already started making tires there in 1978. Local leaders were enthusiastic to work with BMW. The people were also enthusiastic to receive training for the new jobs. The deep-water port of Charleston on the other side of the state facilitated shipping, while nearby rail links connected to much of the US.

Since 1992, BMW has invested over $15.8 Billion. The new Woodruff battery plant is their most recent major investment. In the process, an area that could have been considered a casualty of global trade became one of its greatest beneficiaries.

The first model, an E36 3 series, rolled off the line in 1994. BMW also produced the Z3 in the plant, including the first “German” car driven by James Bond on camera. However, the big breakthrough came with the introduction of the X5 in 1999. At the time, relatively few SUVs were being sold in Europe. BMW Spartanburg as the center of SUV production was intending to largely for the US. However, global markets shifted.

Now, Spartanburg is the “Home of X.” It currently produces the X3, X5, X6, X7 and XM, including electrified versions. It is the sole manufacturing plant for a number of those SUV models globally. A little over half of their production is exported, which also makes it consistently the top US overseas automotive exporter. Export volume topped $9 Billion in 2025 over roughly 200,000 X vehicles.

BMW designed those vehicles to be able to use ICE, PHEV and BEV powertrains. While some may want them to make just pure BEV, the approach gives BMW the ability to shift rapidly with the market. The different models also give the plant a level of market resilience. However, to fuel that resilience they need a very flexible supply chain that can respond quickly. Suppliers being close to the plant creates greater resilience.

BMW is designing its vehicles to be globally competitive. While 400+ miles of EPA range and charging speeds approaching 500 kW may be at the top of the US market, they are also competitive in global markets. While BMW developed the cells and packs, they use multiple suppliers to manufacture the cylindrical cells to their specifications. Packs at the plant currently use AESC cells, but they will shift to LG in the future and use other suppliers in other markets.

BMW also worked with the state of South Carolina to develop people. Nearby Clemson University provides a source of engineering talent, and BMW partners with the university on the Clemson University International Center for Automotive Research, where both students and BMW benefit from the development of new innovations. They are also developing potential future suppliers with the BMW Venture funds. One such company will be supplying flax-based composites to future M models.

A heavy emphasis is placed on technical training at the factory. In addition, they collaborated with community colleges to provide technical training. But the development programs start much earlier, with a heavy emphasis in middle school and sponsoring the First Robotics Competition for elementary school students.

BMW also worked with the South Carolina Department of Transportation to build infrastructure to support the plant and its suppliers. Moving forward, that infrastructure will increasingly include electrification and EV charging. BMW also worked with the SC Ports Authority to develop an “inland port,” which is essentially a direct rail link to the Port of Charleston. By moving freight by rail, emissions are greatly reduced. In addition, a lot of emphasis is going into transferring freight quickly, as every minute a truck sits idling is also wasted emissions.

While BMW employs 11,000 workers, over four times as many jobs are supported by the plant, according to a Clemson economist. That multiplier is much higher than most companies due to how BMW operates. Part of the impact on the local economy beyond employee count comes from the strategy behind the manufacturing. Overall, more than 70% of the value of the vehicles comes from outside suppliers.

Plant Spartanburg receives 3.3 million parts per day delivered by 1200 truckloads and 50 sea containers, 6 days per week. All those parts then go into over 1500 vehicles produced per day. The plant is laid out a bit different than some other manufacturing plants to facilitate the supply chain. Multiple fingers go up off the main line, along which parts are delivered to be assembled nearby. There isn’t much in the way of warehousing. Trucks come to the plant each day and the parts can end up on vehicles driving off the line the same day.

In the initial stages of manufacturing, more of the supply base came from overseas. However, as the plant established itself, more suppliers localized. That growing supply chain then attracted additional companies to the region, like Mercedes, Volvo and Scout. Those companies then create greater scale for the suppliers, who can reduce costs and expand operations.

Overall, for heavy, bulky components, localization will tend to  happen naturally. For a company that relies on suppliers to consistently and almost constantly deliver parts, that localization tends to increase. The more localized the supply chain, the more capable it becomes to respond to market dynamics. Once scale is attained for heavy, bulky components like batteries, that production will naturally become more localized.

BMW has a growing supply chain footprint across the Americas and especially across the Southeastern US. There will be over 850 Tier 1 supplier locations in the Americas by 2027, with multiple times as many Tier 2 and Tier 3 suppliers providing materials, parts and components. BMW focuses on value creation, competitiveness and collaboration in their supply chain. In addition, while they are bringing economic benefit, they are also focused on decarbonization.

Of course, all this economic activity has brought “green” in terms of money to the local communities. As I was stranded in Greenville due to flight interruptions, I had time to walk around the town and speak to some of the locals. Streets that were once desolate and unsafe are now vibrant with shops and restaurants. An area that people once wanted to leave is now growing rapidly and attracting people from around the world. I started conversations  with several friendly people in town about trade. I heard stories of transformation from past struggles to current successes.

Even though it was clear that they were benefitting from the economic impact, I was still surprised how strongly and openly they supported free trade and realized the benefits. A local guide pointed out major buildings and businesses that were new. Downtown is now pleasant and walkable. Part of that is due to the restoration of a river that runs through the city, surrounded by shops and artwork, where I saw some locals fishing in the clear water. This gets to the other kind of “green.”

While there are a lot of trucks transporting materials and components, shortened travel distances and efforts to streamline intermodal transfers reduce emissions. The proximity enables packaging to typically be sent back to the supplier to be reused. BMW is also putting a lot of effort into reduced CO2 emissions steel produced locally, which I plan to follow up on. Over half the steel in their vehicles is reduced CO2. Solar panels and landfill gas provide power for their facilities.

As the company relies heavily on its supply chain, the supply chain is a major focus of its decarbonization strategy. While EVs reduce emissions overall, the proportion of emissions from the manufacturing phase tends to be higher than for ICE vehicles, adding emphasis to decarbonization of manufacturing. At the same time, they strive to create regional strength, resilience and value creation while reducing emissions. Close collaboration is the key to meeting these goals. BMW plans to have net zero CO2 emissions throughout their supply chain by 2050 at the latest.

The new Woodruff plant will produce their sixth-generation battery. BMW develops the batteries first and then outsources the cell manufacturing, but they will now be manufacturing the packs locally. Initially, this will be for the iX5, to be delivered domestically and to global markets. However, additional EV models may benefit in the future.

Overall, politicians in the 1970’s could have tried to block global competition to protect the textile mills. That might have extended the life of those plants for a few years. However, in the process, those plants would become less globally competitive and less globally relevant. Protectionism would have only extended a slow, painful decline.

However, by keeping the market open and staying open to new business opportunities, Greenville, Greer, Spartanburg and Woodruff created the circumstances for their current success. People were open to new companies from other countries. They were open to industries that were new to the area. And they were open to investing in retraining to better take advantage of the new opportunities.

In the initial site selection, South Carolina could have imposed strict regulations and tried to force localization before the factory was built, production was ramped up and scale was attained to support that localization. If that happened, the plant would have undoubtedly been built elsewhere, and the economic benefits would have gone to someone else. By taking a more collaborative approach, rather than being confrontational, both BMW and local suppliers benefitted greatly. Building on that approach, more companies came to the region, building scale and amplifying the benefits.

BMW is not being hypocritical in their support of free trade. They are not promoting free trade just when it benefits them and then putting up barriers for other competitors. They are not shying away from global competition. They are seeking to make globally competitive vehicles for global markets. While global competition is fierce, by facing that competition, rather than hiding from it, their products become more competitive.

In the process, one of the brightest spots in US automotive trade globally, as well as one of the leaders in electrified product and supply chain decarbonization, comes from a German company.

Change and globalization can be scary things. Especially in the short term. The transition to EVs can also be scary, especially for those tied to the past. However, hiding behind political and trade walls rarely works out in the long run. A willingness to be open and collaborative with people who might come from within different lines on a map or sound different than you can have long term benefits. And the courage to engage with the technology transition and compete globally can put you ahead of many established competitors. That cannot only transform how we power our vehicles, but also transform the lives of people in communities for generations to come. As Woodruff Mayor Kenneth Gist put it at the battery plant opening:

BMW and the City of Woodruff wanted the same thing. Success in business, success in our community, and success in building the next generation of BMW electric vehicles to be the best in the world…

…When I think about this plant, I think about our children, our grandchildren. Educational partnership that will open the doors for them, the career that will be waiting for them, and a Woodruff they would be proud to call home for decades to come. BMW, you have been a true partner to me personally, to every person in this community.

#5628. Bird Flu Cases May Be Underreported in Washington Outbreak

— Farm workers union says official numbers are a "vast undercount"

Human cases of H5N1 avian influenza are likely going unreported amid an ongoing bird flu outbreak in Washington state, experts said.

There have been 3 avian flu cases and one death in a patient with underlying health issues, according to Yakima County health officials. But a union representing farm workers said it believes the "official case numbers are a vast undercount."

"We have now connected with a number of workers and have confirmed that more workers are sick with avian flu symptoms who have not been tested," United Farm Workers said in a post on Bluesky. "Their symptoms range from very mild to very severe."

Amesh Adalja, MD, senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security in Baltimore, told MedPage Today that if workers with symptoms aren't getting tested, mild infections are likely going unreported.

"The case count is a floor," Adalja said, adding that the recent death "is a reason to look harder."

He noted that farm workers "have every reason not to come forward," as many have "no paid sick leave, and some fear immigration consequences."

"Given the current and ongoing ICE [U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement] surge in the Yakima Valley, many or most of the workers are understandably reluctant to proactively engage with public agencies," the union posted on Bluesky.

The union also raised concerns that workers may not be receiving adequate training on how to safely handle infected cattle or milk. Adalja said that simply handing out personal protective equipment (PPE) without adequate training on handling infected milk and animals does little to help stop disease spread.

A spokesperson for the Washington State Department of Health told MedPage Today that the agency is doing site visits and educating both owners and workers on how to use PPE.

The agency also is "reaching out to producers and workers to encourage them to report symptoms and to get tested," the spokesperson added.

"We are emphasizing in our messaging that health information is private, and that we are not sharing identifying information with federal agencies," the spokesperson said.

Yakima Health District said it is running radio advertisements in Spanish encouraging dairy workers to protect themselves and to visit a clinic if they develop symptoms. It is also distributing printed materials in English and Spanish on how to prevent avian influenza and where to seek care and vaccines.

The state health department said it's also working with Yakima health officials and local clinics to provide dairy workers with vaccines and antiviral medications.

Since the outbreak began in October, the only cases in humans have been among those exposed to infected dairy cattle, officials said, and the general public remains at low risk for developing avian influenza. Currently, 43 dairy herds have cases of H5N1, and they are concentrated in Yakima and Benton counties.

Adalja noted that what's particularly concerning about the timing is the intersection with seasonal influenza. If a patient was infected with both seasonal flu and H5N1 at the same time, that would be a "real concern," he said.

Such a case would call for aggressive case-finding among workers and their households, rapid sequencing every positive, giving oseltamivir to exposed or symptomatic workers, and seasonal flu shots for dairy workers, Adalja said.

He added that every human infection gives bird flu another chance to adapt and potentially become more transmissible to and between people.

#5627. Driving The Scion By Toyota KEI-01 Will Make You Giggle And Jiggle In Places You Didn't Know Could Jiggle

I was just as shocked as you all were last week when Toyota announced the launch of the Scion by Toyota brand in the United States with a right-hand-drive kei truck. The KEI-01 is limited to 25 mph in order to conform to low-speed vehicle (LSV) regulations, and as of now it's exclusively limited to fleet buyers. Though final details about the dinky little hauler remain slim, I did get a briefer-than-brief chance to whip around a prototype KEI-01 while attending the press event in Texas at which the truck was revealed, and the experience left me exceedingly tickled and slightly baffled.

I was baffled by Toyota's choice to bring such a niche product in the United States, its choice to do so under the name "Scion by Toyota," and by its choice to make it available to fleets only. I was tickled by the opportunity to contort my comically long limbs in order to squeeze my 6-foot-8-inch tall body behind its wheel and take it for a spin. The result? A truly unique automotive experience that is all but guaranteed to make you giggle.

Full disclosure: Toyota wanted me to sample a smattering of its new and updated models, so it flew me out to scenic Frisco, Texas, kept me fed and housed in a hotel for a few days. I got to witness the announcement of the Scion by Toyota brand there, and drive the KEI-01 a few hundred feet.

The KEI-01 is not a brand new vehicle — in fact, it's based on the Toyota Pixis Truck, which is a rebadged 10th-generation Daihatsu HiJet Truck that itself was introduced 12 years ago now. We are only getting the "extended cab" version of the kei truck, generously called the Jumbo on the Daihatsu HiJet, which adds a taller roof and about an iPhone's length of room behind the two seats for storage — I used that space to store my shoes, since I couldn't fit behind the wheel while wearing them.

In its U.S. specification, the dinky KEI-01 will only be offered with a mid-mounted 660cc three-cylinder engine that sends its power to all four wheels via a CVT automatic transmission. Toyota didn't make power figures public, but it's almost certainly the same 660cc three-cylinder used in the other kei trucks that share the platform, which produces about 50 horsepower and 47 lb-ft of torque. The standard four-wheel-drive system features a lock mode that should make this little pickup rather capable on unpaved roads, but that's only if your spine is up to the task.

They will all come standard with a weird mix of modern and throwback features, like dual front airbags, automatic emergency braking, push-button start, traction control, parking sensors, and an engine start/stop system. The standard climate controls are operated using horizontal levers like the ones in my grandfather's 1991 F-150, and the overall appearance of the interior looks like it belongs in a car that's being shown at Radwood, minus the big tacked-on infotainment screen. I didn't get to experience any of these technology features on my abridged drive, except the start/stop system that I instantly turned off because it cut the AC and was unsurprisingly annoying.

This was my first time driving a kei car, and I solely got to drive the KEI-01 on a short gravel loop, but the instant I started moving I was aware that it was not a refined vehicle. The suspension that gives it a 600-pound payload capacity also felt like it faultlessly transmitted even the smallest surface detail of every single piece of gravel I drove over directly to my butt. It jiggled parts of me that I didn't know could jiggle, and sounded very crashy going through dips and bumps. I wouldn't want to ride in one if I had a bad back. Though Toyota didn't release a spec sheet for the KEI-01, the Daihatsu Hijet has a truly puny wheelbase of 74.8 inches and laughably small tires, so no one should expect it to ride like a limousine.

As for its powertrain, the three-cylinder engine and CVT combination were more than enough to get the KEI-01 to its top speed of 25 mph, but the truck I drove did not have the limiter yet, so I saw as high as 40 mph. The CVT created a typical momentary lag between throttle pedal inputs and actual engine response, but discussing powertrain responsiveness in a kei truck that'll be limited to 25 mph is about as useful as discussing a new hyperpop album with an octogenarian.

If you didn't catch it upon first mention, I'm 6-foot-8, so I drew a bit of a crowd when I first tried inserting myself into the KEI-01. I'm all legs with a 40-inch inseam, and my first entry attempt was foiled by the immovable steering wheel. Once I took my shoes off and swung my left knee under the wheel first, I was able to finagle myself into a comfortable driving position, with about an inch left between my right knee and the hard plastic cupholder.

Headroom in the KEI-01 was downright impressive, though. Using the automotive industry's standardized headroom measurement, I had room to put one, maybe even two magician's hats on top of my head and still fit comfortably in the KEI-01. The cargo bed strangely protrudes a bit into the cab space, so the floor of the extended cab's rear storage area sits at about the same spot where the rear side window ends. It's a diminutive and awkwardly shaped and accessed space, but it allows for a bit of seat recline and is better than nothing.

Annoyingly, Toyota hasn't released pricing for the KEI-01 as of yet, but as we already know it will be limited to fleet buyers initially anyway, so it's not like anyone can go to a Toyota dealer and buy one off the lot. Car and Driver estimates that the KEI-01 will cost around $28,000, though, which would be a really tough sell. I love that American fleet buyers are getting access to a brand new genuine kei truck — especially one that's built in the U.S. — but I am left to grapple with the point of it, especially considering that anyone can go out and find a derestricted imported kei truck for a rather low price.

The so-cute-it-hurts Fiat Topolino is another recently announced U.S.-bound LSV, and I think it makes more sense than the KEI-01 since it will mainly be a cheeky electric neighborhood runabout for rich people. Its only competition are golf carts, where the KEI-01 will compete with a sea of UTVs that have served U.S. campuses, ranches, and other all-terrain hauling needs for ages. Who knows, maybe the fleet market will fall in love with the KEI-01, jiggles and all.

#5626. The BLUETTI Apex 200 Expandable Portable Power Station — CleanTechnica Tested

BLUETTI continues to innovate, finding new ways to move its portable power station technology into meaningful new formats that provide owners with additional capability, portability, and utility.

They recently reached out about a new stackable portable power station format based around the Apex 200 power station. It packs in a meaningful 2.5 kilowatt-hours (kWh) of storage capacity by itself, but the real magic is that it was built to be modular and can be linked up with additional storage modules to be stacked underneath, connecting directly to the main unit.

Disclaimer: BLUETTI provided the Apex 200, B300K, and a pair of solar panels to the author for the purposes of this review.

This modular format is a game changer because it means you don’t need an installer to bolt 300 pounds of batteries to the wall of your house. Instead, you can order them in manageable formats and add more as you need them. Among other things, this capability allows the owner to assemble and disassemble the battery pack that meets their needs when they need it.

If you’re heading out to camp for a week in your RV, you can grab an Apex 200 and one of BLUETTI’s B300K expansion batteries and bring 5.5 kWh of capacity with you on the road. When you get home from the trip, you can put them back into the garage and add that back into the battery capacity for your home.

The BLUETTI Apex 200 serves as a head unit or master controller for the battery stack, while the other battery modules are effectively servants to it. For example, when you’re setting the unit up to charge from a wall outlet or from a set of BLUETTI’s solar panels, which can wire directly into the Apex 200 with MC4 connectors, you simply plug one set of connectors or one AC charging cable into the Apex 200 and it automatically balances the energy storage across however many additional battery packs are plugged into the unit.

That really simplifies the charging structure and allows you to use the battery exactly how you want to. If you want to just head to the park with two solar panels that are portable, you can do that and have a much more manageable power system, effectively bringing a mini-grid with you on the go.

We tested the BLUETTI Apex 200 out on a wall charger and, much like most of the other portable power stations on the market, it effectively maxes out the capacity you can actually draw from a wall outlet, which is around 1,600 watts continuous. Even with the best charging cables, you’re going to notice some heat building up in the cable, and BLUETTI has made some concessions for this. The Apex 200 has a switch that allows you to select from different charging modes:

When it comes to solar, the BLUETTI Apex 200 can plug in to solar arrays through either an XT60 connector or the MC4 connectors that wire directly into the unit on the side. Between the MC4 connectors and the XT60 solar input, the unit can pull down 3,000 watts of solar, though you will need to make sure the voltage on your panels lines up with what each of the ports on the unit can handle. When we initially wired our two Bluetti 100-watt solar panels into the unit, we had them wired in parallel, which resulted in just 40 volts being pushed into the unit.

Stacking them in series gave us 80 volts, which pushed it over the minimum 60 volts for the MC4 connectors and allowed the BLUETTI Apex 200 to start charging from the panels. Pushing 2,000 watts maximum of solar power into a 5.5 kWh battery stack is going to take some time to get it charged up, but it’s easy to manage scaling the input power system up to an impressive 2,000 watts to really deliver some meaningful power.

The flexibility is pretty impressive, because it means you can dial the system in to exactly what you need, whether that’s bolting an array to the top of your RV or installing solar panels on the side of your house and then wiring them in a way that’s the most convenient for you.

BLUETTI also makes a larger B500K battery, so you can really pick and choose exactly the right level of storage that you need for your house and the right size battery packs that you want to be able to move around.

The MC4 connectors for solar panels are a little bit troublesome on the BLUETTI Apex 200 because they require a special tool to release the locks that connect the male and female ends of MC4 connectors together. That means if you have your solar panels wired up and plugged into the unit, you’ll need an MC4 connector release tool to disconnect the solar panels from the Apex 200 before you move on. Alternately, you can wire the solar panels up through an XT60 connector, which is a simple plug-and-play adapter for lower voltage solar setups.

When it came time to use the stored power from the BLUETTI Apex 200 and the B300K battery pack, we had to pick up some more high-draw appliances to really put them the the test. We bought a 1,500-watt electric fireplace and 1,500-watt portable heater for a total draw of around 3,000 watts by. We also grabbed an an Instant Pot from the kitchen to pull a bit more juice from the battery stack.

The BLUETTI Apex 200 handled both of the heaters running full blast without a problem. It shared a continuous power output capacity of 3,200 watts. This gets bumped to 3,600 watts when you attach a B300K extension battery. Beyond that, you can even pull a little bit more power, pulling peak usage up to 4,800 watts for a few seconds, because of its peak power handling capacity.

Keeping the larger heater unit attached, we added an Instapot to the the mix, and again the unit had no issues no matter what power levels we used. It’s a solid stack with impressive stats that actually deliver when you need them to the most.

BLUETTI has really built an impressive system here with the Apex 200 and its different expansion battery options. A single BLUETTI Apex 200 can be expanded up to 33.3 kWh, and they can even go bigger than that if you need something with more storage.

BLUETTI allows you to link three Apex 200 battery stacks together through their Hub 1 accessory for a total of just under 100 kWh of storage capacity. That can be accomplished by stacking three Apex 200s with a bunch of BLUETTI’s 5kWh B500Ks and then linking them all together through the Hub 1.

It’s a massive system that shows BLUETTI isn’t just building products for a quick sale, but building a much more comprehensive, flexible storage system that you can build at home into the right configuration for your needs with components that act more like LEGO building blocks.

The ability to wire in solar via XT60 connectors and MC4 connectors is exciting, giving homeowners even more options to produce power from the sun for them to run their lives on. The BLUETTI Apex 200 retails for $1,399 USD.

For more information about the BLUETTI Apex 200, the B300K, B500K expansion packs, or their solar panels, head over to their official website.

#5625. Novel Epinephrine Devices Promising in Mid-Stage Trials

— Sublingual and dry powder intranasal formulations aim to offer options for severe allergies

Novel epinephrine formulations are advancing through mid-stage trials, with promising data presented at the American College of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology (ACAAI) annual meeting.

"For years, patients' families' voice has been, 'We would love a needle-free option,'" said Jay Lieberman, MD, of the University of Tennessee Health Science Center in Memphis. "All these devices being studied, whether it's the approved nasal spray [neffy] or the nasal powders, the sublingual film that I presented data for, and there's a few others being studied. ... All of this big picture is just to give our patients options, because everything is about if you have it, if it's easier to carry, and if you're more likely to use it, that's the outcome we want."

A double dose of a novel intranasal powder formulation of epinephrine (NS002) absorbed faster and to a greater degree than did a double dose from a standard epinephrine autoinjector (EpiPen) among patients with a stuffy nose from allergic rhinitis, simulating the severe nasal congestion that can occur with anaphylaxis.

Those were the findings from a phase II study comparing the bioavailability of the two during a nasal allergen challenge in 50 adults with allergic rhinitis. Plasma epinephrine level peaked at over 700 pg/mL at 20 minutes with the powder given twice in the same nostril compared with a still-rising level of around 500 pg/mL at that point with the EpiPen (P=0.039).

NS002 reached the T100 clinical threshold -- a surrogate for hemodynamic stabilization -- two to four times faster than the EpiPen, with a higher proportion of participants achieving that threshold in the first 5 minutes.

"The FDA wants to know, is there any effect on absorption when, in fact, you have severe nasal congestion? And so that's the purpose of the nasal allergen challenge," said presenter Michael S. Blaiss, MD, of the Medical College of Georgia at Augusta University. "And then the other thing the FDA wants is we know that maybe up to 28% of patients having an anaphylactic episode will require a second dose of epinephrine for their anaphylactic reaction. So that's why the study also looked at double doses."

NS002 raised systolic blood pressure more than EpiPen (mean increase 22 vs 6 mm Hg at 15-20 minutes) -- a desired effect, although diastolic and heart rate changes were small.

The researchers called NS002 well tolerated with transient mild symptoms but no serious or cardiovascular adverse events. While runny nose, administration site discomfort, nasal itching, and nasal congestion were common local side effects, the most common systemic adverse events were headache, nausea, shakiness, stomach discomfort, lightheadedness, and vomiting.

Blaiss said the next step is a pivotal phase III study looking at NS002 versus EpiPen and intramuscular epinephrine with similar pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic studies in a larger number of patients.

A novel dissolvable film for sublingual epinephrine administration showed that half of symptoms resolved within 5 minutes, climbing to 82.9% symptom resolution with 54.2% of patients asymptomatic at the 12-minute mark when maximal plasma concentration was reached, Lieberman reported at the same late-breaking oral abstract session.

The sublingual epinephrine film, dubbed dibutepinephrine, was studied in a phase II, two-part, open-label study with 110 healthy adults treated for induced oral allergy syndrome symptoms in an oral challenge model. Participants were randomized in a crossover design to a single dose of 12 mg dibutepinephrine alone or with manual intramuscular epinephrine injection without oral challenge.

Time to maximal epinephrine concentration in the blood was earlier with the sublingual film than among patients getting conventional autoinjector epinephrine or intramuscular epinephrine. The novel formulation also had higher maximal plasma epinephrine concentration and higher maximal changes in heart rate and systolic and diastolic blood pressure compared with epinephrine autoinjectors (EpiPen, AUVI-Q) and intramuscular epinephrine patients.

"The sublingual film across studies performed very similarly, whether it was in healthy subjects, whether it was in patients who were allergic and not having a reaction, or whether it was in patients having a localized allergic reaction in their mouth to kind of simulate what might happen during anaphylaxis," Lieberman said. "And the concentration curves in all the studies were very similar, reproducible. And the effects on heart rate, blood pressure, etc., are all very similar and reproducible. So it lends to the idea that this product has performed very similarly across multiple studies."

Another phase I study presented at the session reported on dibutepinephrine results when the film was placed on the top of the tongue rather than under it, as intended. Again, maximal concentration was numerically higher with the film when placed under the tongue by the patient or a physician compared with intramuscular epinephrine (391.7 and 344.5 vs 334.5 pg/mL). Time to maximal concentration was 12 minutes with the film versus 45 with intramuscular administration. But top of tongue placement of the film had a lower concentration peaking at 112.7 pg/mL at 35 minutes.

"Even if it's misplaced, such as put on the upper tongue, it doesn't get absorbed as well, but it does have some hemodynamic effects, even in the worst-case scenario. And that's very reassuring," Lieberman said.

#5624. HLTH 2026: Noom pushes deeper into connected health with new wearable, Noom Band

HLTH 2026: Noom pushes deeper into connected health with new wearable, Noom Band" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Noom launched its own wearable to enhance its metabolic health platform with activity, sleep and cardiovascular data insights.

The device, called Noom Band, will be bundled into Noom’s existing enterprise partnerships at no additional upfront cost starting in early 2027. The wearable is also free for Noom Health employer and health plan customers.

The introduction of a wearable is part of Noom’s broader push to build an integrated metabolic health platform combining behavior change, virtual care, diagnostics, medications and continuous health data.

Noom Band is a faceless wrist-worn wearable powered by Sensor Bio, and it will be fully integrated into the Noom app. The device will track heart rate, heart rate variability, SpO2, sleep and activity, with the data feeding directly into Noom’s behavior change platform, executives said.

Noom is providing the wearable to enterprise clients at no additional upfront cost as it sees opportunities to use continuous data on sleep, activity and other physiological signals to keep members engaged and drive better outcomes in the company's weight management and metabolic health programs, Noom CEO Geoff Cook told Fierce Healthcare.

"We are getting outcomes-based payments, so we believe we will have more people hitting their 5% weight loss goals or 10% weight loss goals, if they have the wearable, than if they don't," Cook said in an exclusive interview about the launch of Noom Band.

Integrating a wearable device into Noom’s metabolic health program fills a major data gap, Cook said.

Noom has evolved from a weight loss app into a broader preventive care and clinical health platform. The company's behavior change platform uses psychology, clinical support and structured habit design to help users build long-term lifestyle shifts. The company also offers integrated telehealth services through its Noom Med platform, combining remote clinical care and prescription weight loss medications with its core behavior change app. And the company has expanded into at-home diagnostics with its Biomarkers Test Kit.

But Noom lacked continuous physiological information, particularly around sleep and activity, Cook said. Less than 10% of members have devices such as the Oura Ring, Whoop, or newer Fitbits, he noted. Continuous physiological data enables Noom to be a more comprehensive healthcare platform.

"This is all about just boosting signal so that we can deliver the right insights, and to do that, we felt we needed to bring a wearable deeper into our program," he said.

Noom is starting with the Noom Band as a wrist-based wearable, and the company is at an “earlier stage exploring ring-based options,” Cook said. "We believe ultimately it’s important to meet people where they are, and both the wrist and the ring form factors have a role to play in generating signal to drive health outcomes, as people have different preferences," he added.

Cook sees chronic care, telehealth, diagnostics and wearable companies increasingly converging as they broaden their capabilities and move into adjacent areas of healthcare.

"Every player in preventive health, which is looking more and more like healthcare generally, is chasing this same holy grail of determining what is going on in a patient or member’s body, and then suggesting a behavioral insight or a pharmaceutical intervention, or ordering a diagnostic test based on that signal," he said.

Noom is making strategic moves to cover all of those capabilities itself.

The company focuses on whole person health that goes beyond nutrition, Cook said, with extensive data and interventions around food and activity but comparatively little insight into sleep. Sleep is an important factor for metabolic health, and the Noom Band gives the company a way to incorporate sleep alongside nutrition, activity and mindset, executives said.

Noom is betting that wearables can improve outcomes for members in its weight loss programs. An analysis of 144,000 Noom Med members taking a GLP-1 medication found that those who used a connected wearable were 34% more likely to lose 20 pounds by the fourth month in the program, according to the company. A separate sleep analysis found that, on average, members on a GLP-1 weight loss drug who used Noom Band slept 90 minutes more per week after only two months, and members who started with a sleep deficit added 150 minutes of sleep per week, the company's data shows.

Studies have shown that chronic sleep restriction or poor quality sleep significantly increases the risk of insulin resistance, obesity and type 2 diabetes.

"Bringing that dimension of health into the program, we felt, was just critically important," Cook said.

The company built a device from the ground up rather than partner with an existing wearable player, so it could own the user experience. "We didn't want to pick a partner where essentially that partner’s app would be competing essentially with the Noom application for this signal interpretation," Cook noted.

Many existing wearables focus on optimizing health and athletic performance, Cody Fair, Noom Health’s chief commercial officer, told Fierce Healthcare. Noom developed Noom Band to capture measurements related to weight management and metabolic health, he noted.

Through the partnership with Sensor Bio, the wearable platform provides the validated sensors and underlying physiological data, while Noom controls how those signals are interpreted and incorporated into the interventions. Cook cited Sensor Bio's research, validation work and focus on device accuracy as key reasons Noom selected Sensor Bio as its partner to develop Noom Band.

By investing in a wearable, Noom also aims to improve member engagement to ultimately drive better outcomes for the members as well as payers and employers, Fair noted.

Members can lose motivation when the number on the scale stops moving. Giving them other measures of progress, including sleep, steps and recovery, provides additional "wins" that could keep them engaged, he said.

Noom also plans to offer the wearable as something that members can "unlock" when they hit early milestones in the program, turning the hardware into an engagement incentive, executives said.

"We didn’t set out to build another wearable—we set out to build the ultimate metabolic health program that drives better health outcomes for members, leading to increased ROI for clients," Fair said.

"For employers and health plans, that’s the difference between a fitness perk that gets left in a drawer and a tool built to deliver health outcomes they’re already paying for and that is available to their population at no additional cost, he said.

Expensive wearables can undermine the ROI payers are looking for, Cook noted. "I essentially believe that the devices are a commodity and should effectively be given away. That’s why we're including the wearable at no additional cost to the payer," he said.

Payers and employers also want to see ROI on health programs within a shorter time frame, within 12 to 24 months, Fair added. Providing employers with a program that combines behavior change, wearables and biomarker testing also reduces the number of vendors they have to work with, he added.

Health plans want evidence that daily behavior changes translate into measurable clinical and financial outcomes, such as improvements in blood pressure and A1C, and Noom plans to study whether its wearable can help deliver that ROI over the next year, Fair said.

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services’ ACCESS Model could serve as a proving ground for Noom to demonstrate how the combination of its behavior change program with wearables such as the Noom Band can affect cardiometabolic health.

Noom plans to participate in CMS’ Advancing Chronic Care with Effective Scalable Solutions model under the cardio-kidney-metabolic clinical track, focusing on conditions like obesity, prediabetes and diabetes improvement. ACCESS is a 10-year initiative to integrate tech-enabled care into Medicare.

"That model is an outcomes-aligned payment model. We're excited to bundle the blood pressure cuff, the wearable, along with the Noom program, to have the absolute maximum effect on the outcomes that are being measured, outcomes like A1C, blood pressure and weight," Cook said.

Cook is bullish that wearables will play a bigger role in chronic condition management as sensors are able to generate more sophisticated physiological data and AI gets better at interpreting the data.

"It should be possible, in my view, within years and maybe quicker than that to have the wearable signal itself provide a blood pressure signal that is validated, which would certainly simplify models like the CMS ACCESS model, if you didn't also have to ship a blood pressure cuff," he said. "These less invasive wearables, as they get more powerful, I think, can be transformative to healthcare generally, and I think the CMS ACCESS model is pointing the way to how they would democratize that, and at a relatively low cost to the ultimate payer."
