#5623. Groups Decry Trump EPA’s Decision to Grant Louisiana Oversight of Toxic Coal Ash

Testing at all Louisiana coal plants found unsafe groundwater contamination.

BATON ROUGE, La. — The Sierra Club, Earthjustice, and the Alliance for Affordable Energy Louisiana decried the Trump administration’s final decision today to put the State of Louisiana in charge of oversight of toxic coal ash waste. The Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality (LDEQ) has repeatedly allowed coal plants to violate federal coal ash protections.

Coal ash is generated when coal is burned, and massive quantities are stored at coal-burning power plants near Baton Rouge, Alexandria, and Shreveport.

At all three active Louisiana coal plants (Big Cajun 2, Brame Energy Center, R S Nelson), and the state’s one retired plant (Dolet Hills), monitoring data shows that coal ash is contaminating groundwater at levels above federal safe drinking water standards. These toxic chemicals include arsenic, boron, cobalt, lead, lithium, radium, sulfate, and thallium. More than 61% of Louisiana’s population relies on groundwater for all or part of their drinking water supply.

“Louisianans know all too well that we can’t trust our state regulators to hold polluters accountable, so it’s nonsensical that the Trump Administration just gave LDEQ even more authority to handle something as dangerous as coal ash,” said Darryl Malek-Wiley, a Sierra Club senior field representative in Louisiana. “It’s clear this decision is meant to favor wealthy coal-owning utilities at the expense of our health.”

“The Trump administration chose polluters over the people of Louisiana,” said Earthjustice senior attorney Mychal Ozaeta. “An alphabet soup of toxic chemicals from burning coal is contaminating groundwater in locations across the state. The right thing to do is make the polluters clean up their toxic mess, and protect sources of drinking water. Instead, the Trump administration is handing over authority to Louisiana’s state government which won’t lift a finger to clamp down on the concerning levels of contaminants poisoning the state’s groundwater.”

“Our state regulators are dangerously inadequate in their oversight and enforcement of polluting industries, which has already cost Louisiana our safe air and water. We simply don’t think LDEQ can handle even more responsibilities they won’t take seriously,” said Logan Burke, Executive Director of the Alliance for Affordable Energy.

Public interest groups submitted formal comments to EPA urging the administration to reject Louisiana’s request to handle coal ash oversight in the state.

Coal ash contains arsenic, mercury, chromium, lead, lithium, radium, and other heavy metals, which have been linked to numerous types of cancer, heart and thyroid disease, respiratory illness, reproductive failure, and neurological harm.

As an example of the state’s abysmal track record on coal ash, LDEQ has allowed power plants to close coal ash dumps with ash in groundwater, ensuring that the dumps will contaminate groundwater with toxic chemicals indefinitely. LDEQ should not be in charge of issuing permits that let coal plants continue to violate the law. These permits will shield power plants from federal enforcement and prevent Louisiana residents from stopping coal ash pollution.

LDEQ is a severely understaffed and extremely lenient environmental regulator. In addition to its coal ash failures, its air monitors are far away from Louisiana’s heaviest air-polluting facilities, and the agency has for years been criticized for approving permits for wealthy polluters, including LNG terminals and a massive Formosa plastics factory. Louisianans know all too well that LDEQ does not protect low-income communities of color, and creates a lax regulatory environment that has enabled disasters like the recent Smitty’s Supply explosion and spill.

Please see the Earthjustice Louisiana coal ash page.

#5622. At $27,000, Is This 1974 Lotus Europa JPS A Smokin'-Hot Deal?

According to the ad, the first owner of today's Nice Price or No Dice Europa owned the car for more than 51 years. That's some dedication, and the car shows the love they obviously had for it. We'll have to decide if we love the price the current owner has set for its sale.

At some point in one's life, it's best to take the road less traveled. The well-beaten path may be the safest, but the less popular way might just offer unexpected, memorable adventures. The 2004 Nissan 350Z we looked at on Monday is probably not everyone's first choice when it comes to used sports cars with a semblance of panache. The easy answer is Porsche's Boxster or a Mazda Miata, but that's part of what makes the 350Z such a rogue option.

Capable and seemingly in as-new condition, our 350Z came with a six-speed stick, a top that drops, and a $12,500 asking price. That's plumb right in the middle of 986 Boxster territory, but offering more power and potentially cheaper running costs. That concept didn't escape you all. Comments on the car ranged from "not for me, but a good deal for someone," to "if it were closer to me..." In the end, the vote went the Nissan seller's way, too, earning the Z a solid 76% 'Nice Price' win.

Nissan has never offered a mid-engine car for sale here in the States. In fact, of the major Japanese manufacturers, only Toyota and Honda (through Acura) have gone the (rear) mid-engine route here.

In the early 1960s, mid-engine layouts were all the rage in racing, with F1, Indy, and GT classes moving to place the driver ahead of the drivetrain. Britain's Lotus was at the forefront of this movement, debuting the mid-engine Type 18 Formula 1 racer in 1960. That car brought Lotus its first F1 checkered flag and World Champion title.

Lotus also dallied with mid-engine GT racers, designing a chassis and body that the company hoped would be bought by the Ford Motor Company (Lotus had a close relationship with Ford at the time) for the Americans' assault on Le Mans. Ford chose the already race-tested Lola Mk 6 chassis for its GT40 racing program, leaving Lotus with significant engineering expense and little to show for it. Instead of initially building a race car from the proposed chassis, Lotus took the more lucrative route and built a road car: Hethel's first mid-engined model.

The resulting Europa leveraged a design first used on the Elan: a stiff, folded and welded center backbone with the drivetrain and suspension bolted in place, and a fiberglass body mounted atop that in saddlebag fashion. The earliest cars had Renault engines and transmissions, while later cars, like this 1973 Europa Special, used the Ford Kent-based Lotus Twin Cam engine.

Not only does this Europa have the most powerful engine offered in Federalized form, but that 115-horsepower 1,557cc four-cylinder is backed by a standard five-speed manual, still sourced from Renault, originally designed for the French company's 16 model.

This isn't just a "Big Valve" (denoting a reworked twin-cam head) Europa; it's also one of 100 John Player Specials built to commemorate Lotus's 1972 F1 Championship win. The cars were wrapped in black paint with gold trim, emulating the cigarette pack design of the racer's sponsor, Nottingham, England's John Player & Sons. It's an iconic bit of 1970s chic, and very British. This car still wears its commemorative dashboard plaque, indicating it's number 90 of the 100 cars built.

While the basic Europa design is a bit odd with its bread van back end, this one appears to be in exceptional condition. Also, being a later edition (dubbed Type 47 by Lotus), it has a reworked engine cover and rear end providing better visibility out the back and slightly improved proportions.

Not only does this Europa appear to be in near-show car condition, but it comes with extensive documentation from the moment it was built (March 1973) to the present day. That paperwork details title transfers between all three owners (the second owner held on to the car for more than half a century), along with all the work that has gone into keeping it on the road and winning awards at car shows. As far as turnkey classics go, there's not much to complain about with this Lotus.

On the exterior, the black-and-gold color scheme still looks as elegant as ever, right down to the original gold anodized alloy wheels. All the badging, lights, and chrome are present and in excellent shape, which is a plus since parts are getting increasingly hard to find. The interior is just as nice, showing just some scuffing on the driver's seat side as evidence of the car's age.

According to the ad, the engine underwent an extensive rebuild and documentation just 2,000 miles ago, and now runs well when warm. Both the engine and gearbox are numbers-matching for the car. How cool is that after all these years?

The ad notes a clean title and mileage documented at 34,526. It also touts the car as a "once in a lifetime chance to own a fully documented Lotus." It should be noted that, while advertised in the Los Angeles Craigslist classifieds, the car is actually located a few hundred miles away on the California/Oregon border.

Some classic cars come with a story. Some come with a past veiled in mystery. This Europa comes with a dossier that would make a CIA agent proud. Not only that, but it's a prime example of a significant model in its final, some might argue, most desired form. What might something like that be worth?

The seller has set a price of $27,000, and since the ad for the car has been posted for almost a month, we now need to give that asking price some thought. What's your take on this original mid-engined marvel out of Hethel and the seller's cash-and-carry price? Is it really worth $27,000? Or is a fairer price yet to be documented in the car's records?

Los Angeles, California, Craigslist, or go here if the ad disappears.

#5620. Moving healthcare AI from pilot to practice

Moving healthcare AI from pilot to practice" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

There’s a growing tension between the urgency to innovate and the barriers to enterprise adoption in healthcare. Here's what it takes to move from promising pilots to enterprise-wide deployment.Whether we’re physicians, nurses, care managers, or the people who keep coverage and claims moving, most of us entered healthcare to help people. This responsibility gives us an extraordinary sense of purpose. Yet for the first time in my career, I see healthcare leaning in, because AI is exceptionally good at documentation and administrative work that sits between us and the patients we serve. Many of us have already experienced promising AI pilots. The question I hear the most now is how to move from small experiments to enterprise-wide deployment.As healthcare technologists, we’ve built healthcare technology one portal and system of record at a time. In a large health system, healthcare workers navigate at least 10 to 20 systems, each with its own login and dataset for each patient. For every hour physicians spend with patients, they spend nearly two more on EHR and desk work, plus one to two hours of “pajama time.” We're short on clinicians, and we keep asking them to do paperwork instead of practicing at the top of their license.When I grew up in India, the doctor near my home knew me personally from handwritten notes. Now, my information is in an EHR within a big provider system, yet no one knows me the way that doctor did. Healthcare today is data rich but intelligence poor. AI can help us put the right data in front of the right person, in the right context, at the right time.In my conversations about AI with providers and payers, I hear genuine excitement balanced by healthy pragmatism. None of us are ready for an AI doctor giving a diagnosis but documentation, phone calls, referrals, and back-office work? I see very little resistance to getting time back.

Gemini for healthcare is designed to address these core challenges and reduce operational pressures across the healthcare ecosystem. Built to wrap around existing systems of record, Gemini is the orchestration layer that coordinates work across the systems healthcare organizations already run on. By doing so, care teams can reclaim valuable time for patient care, member support, and core operations. Equipped with role-based access controls, audit logging, and verifiable citations, Gemini for healthcare is built to support HIPAA compliance and is delivered as a modular plugin within Gemini, combining specialized skills and healthcare connectors, along with the Gemini agent.

An open healthtech ecosystem provides access to an expanding network of specialized digital health ISVs and premier healthcare systems integrators building on Gemini for healthcare. Underpinning this is a secure and governable platform that unifies AI applications, skills, partner solutions, and healthtech connectors under a single framework, complete with built-in access controls, audit logging, and verifiable citations to give clinical, IT, and operational leaders full visibility and oversight.Organizations are using AI to provide more personalized patient care. Highmark, for example, is working with Google Cloud to connect fragmented information across care and coverage—helping teams create more coordinated member and patient experiences and surface timely, relevant context for clinicians. “Healthcare generates enormous amounts of information and data every day, yet patients often experience care as a series of separate interactions rather than one connected journey,” said Karen Hanlon, president of Highmark Health. “Through our work with Google Cloud, we're exploring how AI can help connect information across the healthcare experience, making it easier to support the whole person, create more personalized care experiences, and equip clinicians with meaningful insights at the right time.” Additional workflows Gemini for healthcare addresses includes medical records synthesis, pre-appointment preparation, coverage and policy review, and payer benefit determination. In the end, the real measure of healthcare AI is whether a clinician gets more time with a patient and whether a patient gets the right care sooner. After all those years of digitizing healthcare, we were building up to this moment. Gemini for healthcare is now available in preview.

I also hope he's a different type of Bond, campier and more fun than Craig got to be as 007. Most importantly, though, this casting brings us to the key question of the franchise: What car will this new Bond drive?

James Bond has driven all manner of cars in his years, from the Sunbeam Alpine of "Dr. No" to the various Aston Martins of "No Time to Die." He's usually driven British cars, particularly his Astons, but he's had his fair share of BMWs too — even Porsches if you dive into the video games. Bond had AMCs for a little bit! He drove a Ford Mondeo that one time! So, with the entire automotive world a possibility, what do you think Pattinson's Bond should drive?

Identity Confirmed pic.twitter.com/FCU5A9c1wk

This is maybe the hardest question I've had to answer for QOTD, because I'm so intent on getting it right. An Aston is the easy answer, maybe a new variant of the DB12, but I don't want this new Bond to just be more of the same. A Longbow Roadster would be sleek and techy, fitting Bond's love of gadgets, and an updated TVR Griffith would show a return to how things used to be for both brands. Maybe neither of those two cars ever actually come out, though. So, to settle things, I'm going to pick a car I think fits: The Morgan Supersport.

The Supersport is a British sports car, as befits an MI6 agent. It's a bit out of time, a bit of a modernized vintage design, as befits a Cold War-era spy whose box office draw has outlasted the Cold War and its espionage heyday. Most crucially, though, it's weird and impractical and fun — characteristics I hope befit Pattinson's Bond, who I hope will follow more in Pierce Brosnan's quippy brogue-prints than Daniel Craig's tactical bootsteps.

#5616. Tissue and Liquid Biopsies May Complement Each Other in Prostate Cancer

— Analysis found no significant differences in genomic alterations across ethnic groups

An analysis of patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) congress found no statistically significant differences in actionable genomic alterations, tumor mutational burden (TMB), or circulating tumor (ct)DNA fraction across ethnic groups. The findings also showed differences in mutation detection between tissue and liquid biopsies, suggesting the two testing methods may provide complementary information.

In this exclusive MedPage Today video, Virginia Yuk-Chun Lam, an MD candidate at King's College London, discusses the findings and their potential implications for identifying actionable mutations and guiding targeted treatment.

Following is a transcript of her remarks:

What we did this year is we looked at 350 patients with prostate cancer. They all have castration-resistant prostate cancer and had one line of ARPI [androgen receptor pathway inhibitor] and progressed.

So what we did is we looked at both the tissue and the ctDNA to check if they've got any actionable genomic mutations and looked at their tumor mutation burden and also their ctDNA fractions.

The reason we are particularly interested in this group of patients is we know that there are some ethnicity differences, and also where I'm based in Guy's Hospital, it is a very diverse population with a high number of Black [patients]. So we would like to see if there's any ethnicity differences in those kinds of actionable mutations, TMB, and also ctDNA fractions.

So what we found out is the actionable mutation BRAF is kind of numerically higher in Black patients. The highest numbers of mutations were TP53; however, there's no ethnicity differences in them. For the patients with aggressive mutations in TP53, RB1, and PTEN, there's no particular differences in the ethnicity either. But with all of these, there's no statistical differences in all of these patients, but BRAF is numerically higher.

The next thing we also looked at is the mutational burden to see if there's any ethnicity differences. And what we found out is that between the tissue and the ctDNA, they are higher in the ctDNA fractions, which we kind of expected because when we looked at the ctDNA, we know they pick up a little bit more and also when the ctDNA is taken, that is when they progress.

The last thing we looked at is to try to match the ctDNA fraction and the tissue concordances to see if we pick up higher concordances in certain kinds of mutations. In our 101 patients, they got paired samples. We found out there's high concordances in BRCA and also patients with aggressive mutations. However, in PTEN, there's low concordances, but mainly they're picked up by the ctDNA.

So that's kind of a top four of what we presented at ESMO this year. And from what we can make a conclusion of it, it is a single-center cohort, we would like to extend it to a multicenter cohort with a wider ethnicity as well. Statistically, there's no big differences amongst the actionable mutation, TMB, and also ctDNA fractions. However, numerically we know it is higher in BRCA1/2, and we also found out that PTEN, as I say, is better picked up in ctDNA.

So we hope that in the future these two modalities can help each other to pick up the most actionable mutations and can benefit to see if we can find targeted drugs for the patients who progress in this kind of cohort.

I know especially in the U.K. sometimes we don't do it together. A lot of time we do tissue at diagnosis and ctDNA when they progress. But I think we found that both modalities are important. So if we can, we can try to do both.

But I know probably in other countries, say in the U.S., you've got a little bit more resources and you might tend to do both, but in other settings, this is kind of an insight that we can consider both as a way to find the most targeted actionable mutations to targeted drugs.

#5615. When Less Is More: Rewilding as a Strategy for Nature Recovery

Can we bring nature back from the brink of collapse? That may sound melodramatic, but the evidence is sobering: the Planetary Health Check 2026 shows that we have crossed 7 of the 9 science-based planetary boundaries;[1] the Living Planet Report 2026 finds that wildlife populations have declined 73% on average since 1970;[2] and around 1 million animal and plant species are threatened with extinction, with 75% of the land surface having been significantly altered by human activity, according to the IPBES, the leading intergovernmental body for assessing the state of biodiversity.[3]

In fact, with vertebrate extinction rates up to 100 times the natural background rate, some scientists believe we are at the onset of a sixth mass extinction.[4] But perhaps we should not be surprised at this precipitous decline in the health of our living planet. After all, around $7.3 trillion is spent every year on activities that harm nature ($4.9 trillion by companies and $2.4 trillion in government subsidies), while only $220 billion goes towards protecting or restoring ecosystems (2023 figures).[5] In other words, for every $1 we spend on taking care of nature, $33 is spent on activities that degrade the environment.

The drivers of nature loss are many, including climate change, overexploitation of resources, pollution and invasive alien species, but the largest is land-use change, primarily for agriculture.[6] Research by UNEP and Chatham House goes so far as to identify agriculture as a threat to 86% of species at risk of extinction.[7] So, is regenerative agriculture the answer? That is certainly one approach that would help, as I explored in a previous CleanTechnica article. But there is another, more direct—and some would say more radical—solution that is gaining popularity: rewilding.

As with regenerative agriculture, rewilding is more a collection of ideas and practices than a well-defined science. Nevertheless, experts convened by the IUCN define rewilding as the process of rebuilding a natural ecosystem, following major human disturbance, by restoring natural processes and food webs.[8] The Global Rewilding Alliance puts it even more simply, as “helping nature heal”.[9] In practice, this can mean anything from leaving areas of nature undisturbed to actively introducing keystone species such as beavers, bison and wild boar.

Perhaps the most cited rewilding experiment is the reintroduction of wolves into Yellowstone National Park in 1995–96, after they had been eradicated there by 1926. This resulted in a so-called trophic cascade, whereby elk numbers fell, scavengers such as eagles, ravens and bears gained a year-round food supply, and willow and aspen began to recover in places.[10] The strength of that recovery, and the extent to which the wolves were the primary driver, has been contested,[11] but few dispute the overall positive effect on biodiversity and the ecosystem.

The Yellowstone case is rewilding on a large scale, but it is still dwarfed by the rewilding work of Tompkins Conservation, created by the late Doug Tompkins, co-founder of The North Face and Esprit, and his wife Kristine McDivitt Tompkins, former CEO of Patagonia. Working primarily in Chile and Argentina, they have helped create or expand 16 parks protecting over 45 million acres of land and sea, and reintroduced 14 species, including around 50 wild jaguars.[12] Besides the ecological benefits, ecotourism is boosting local economies.[13] In Chilean Patagonia, every dollar the state invested in the national parks along Chile’s Route of Parks in 2024 returned US$6 to local communities,[14] while visitors to Argentina’s Iberá Park, partly degraded by cattle ranching in the past, have doubled in a decade to 60,000 a year.[15]

At a more local scale, the Knepp Estate in the UK has become another well documented case of rewilding. In her book Wilding: The Return of Nature to a British Farm, Isabella Tree tells the story of how she and her husband, Charlie Burrell, converted their 1,400-hectare farm from intensive dairy and crop agriculture, which was losing money, into a thriving “wild farm,” with free-roaming herbivores such as cattle, ponies, pigs, and deer.[16] A 20-year review shows an incredible rejuvenation of biodiversity, including a 916% increase in breeding bird abundance in the southern block, a 132% rise in bird species richness, a near-ninefold increase in dragonflies and damselflies, and a doubling of butterfly species in some areas.[17] There are climate benefits too, with 5.2 tCO2e/ha/yr sequestration, comparable to new native woodland.[18]

Critics of rewilding often frame it as a trade-off: more nature means less food; more wildlife means fewer jobs; more biodiversity means lower economic growth. These arguments can (and should) be tested, for in many (but not all) cases they will prove to be a false choice. My view is that it should be about balance. I saw this pragmatic approach at a rewilding site in Norfolk, England, called Wild Ken Hill, where they have designated separate areas for regenerative farming, coastal conservation, and rewilding—including 30 or so wild Exmoor ponies, 6 very inquisitive and vocal Tamworth pigs, and a small herd of Red Poll cattle.

My conclusion on rewilding is that it can certainly help us to reach the global goal of reversing biodiversity loss and becoming nature positive. It is by no means the only strategy, but it is one of the most direct and impactful. As I noted in the chapter on nature restoration in my book Thriving: “We know that nature is on the ropes, bruised and battered by dumb agriculture and dumber economics. But another thing we know is that, given half a chance, nature bounces back. Ecosystems are resilient and designed to flourish. The most powerful and effective action we can take is to step back and give nature space and time to recover.”[19]

#5614. Engaging Medicaid’s Hardest-to-Reach Members Helps Plans Control Medical Spend

Engaging Medicaid’s Hardest-to-Reach Members Helps Plans Control Medical Spend" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Every Medicaid managed care plan has them.They’re the members who remain outside the reach of traditional outreach and care management after the calls, texts, letters and emails haven’t worked. Their phone numbers may be disconnected, their addresses outdated. They’ve been targeted with different outreach strategies, even assigned to outside vendors that specialize in finding hard-to-reach members—and still remain disconnected.And they’re often among the members plans most need to reach.They’re Medicaid’s hardest-to-find, hardest-to-engage members: people with complex medical and behavioral health needs, often compounded by unstable housing, food insecurity, transportation barriers and other circumstances that make navigating healthcare extraordinarily difficult. Many are also among a plan’s highest-cost members, cycling through emergency departments and hospitals while remaining disconnected from care that could help stabilize their health.Plans have struggled for years to reach this population. What makes the challenge more urgent today is growing financial pressure on Medicaid plans to manage costs and demonstrate that every public healthcare dollar is yielding measurable results — and the recognition that some of the greatest opportunities to reduce avoidable spending and improve quality lies with high-risk, high-cost members traditional approaches still aren’t reaching.An estimated 4–8% of a managed healthcare plan’s Medicaid membership may fall into this hardest-to-engage cohort, driving an estimated 35-50% of an MCO’s total medical spend. he opportunity is to reach members who have remained disconnected and reduce the costly utilization that can occur when successful engagement never happens.When Traditional Outreach Has Run Its CourseManaged healthcare plans have built sophisticated outreach and care-management capabilities across multiple channels, supported by digital tools, data analytics and centralized teams. Many have changed tactics and brought in outside vendors. Those approaches work for most members.But the hardest-to-reach members are still left behind.For this population, simply finding the member is often the biggest challenge. Someone moving between temporary housing, shelters, encampments or other locations may be impossible to locate using the information a plan has on file. Finding that person may require combining data and technology with local knowledge, community relationships and people on the ground.And finding the member is only the beginning.A member may not trust the person who finds them. Housing, food, transportation or an immediate behavioral health need may matter far more at that moment than making a primary care appointment. Language differences and difficult experiences with the healthcare system can create additional barriers.That’s why the distinction between contact and engagement matters. Contact means reaching someone. Engagement means listening, building trust, addressing barriers and helping the member take the next step.What It Takes to Truly Engage MembersTechnology can help determine where to look, prioritize the next best action and make field teams more efficient. But technology doesn’t create trust. This is ultimately a human effort—technology-enabled but led by people.

While finding members is often the hardest part, it’s only the beginning. What happens next is what can change outcomes.Experience with hardest-to-reach Medicaid populations has shown 25–40% reductions in ED utilization and 35–55% reductions in inpatient utilization after members were located and engaged, barriers addressed, and ongoing follow-through provided.*For plans, that’s where the financial opportunity lies. Reaching high-risk, high-cost members and helping them reconnect to care creates an opportunity to reduce avoidable ED visits and hospitalizations—and the costs that come with them.At a time when every avoidable ED visit and hospitalization matters, reaching and serving these members is more important than ever. It’s an opportunity to improve care while addressing a significant source of avoidable healthcare spending.

#5613. Bentley Torcal EV Is Already Sold Out Through 2027

Good morning! It's Tuesday, November 17, 2026, and this is The Morning Shift, your daily roundup of the top automotive headlines from around the world, in one place. This is where you'll find the most important stories that are shaping the way Americans drive and get around.

In this morning's edition, Bentley's Torcal EV is sold out all the way through 2027, Tesla is going to invest over $3.3 billion in expanding its German factory so it can build Cybercabs, General Motors wants to add a lot more robots and automation into its facilities and BMW wants the U.S. government to cut it some slack on tariffs.

If you'd like a recap of the latest auto news sent to your inbox each weekday, you can sign up for Jalopnik's free Morning Shift newsletter here.

Bentley's first all-electric vehicle might have a bit of a silly name and slightly polarizing styling, but it would seem that's not enough to keep buyers away. Initial demand for the Torcal is shockingly strong, with the electric crossover already sold out through 2027. Now, if you want one, Bentley is taking orders for 2028. You'll be lucky to get one before you vote for the next President.

One caveat to all of this is that Bentley hasn't said how many Torcal build slots were actually available for 2027, and it hasn't indicated any sales volumes, so theoretically, it could have sold like 5 of the Cayenne-sized EVs, but I sort of doubt that. A spokesperson for the British luxury automaker said it was "very pleased with the response and the position we're in" following the Torcal's reveal in September. From Automotive News:

Based on orders, the S variant has been the most popular Torcal so far, [Bentley CEO Frank-Steffen] Walliser said. In general, Bentley has seen the Torcal attract new and younger customers to the brand.

The Torcal, based on Volkswagen Group's Premium Platform Electric, is slotted beneath the Bentayga, Bentley's first crossover.

It will become Bentley's fourth nameplate alongside the Bentayga, Continental GT coupe and convertible, and Flying Spur sedan. The rest of the Bentley lineup is offered with gasoline and plug-in hybrid powertrains.

The Torcal has a range of up to 375 miles from a 113-kilowatt-hour battery and offers fast charging at 400 kilowatts. Power is rated at 810 hp and 881 pound-feet of torque for the Torcal and 876 hp and 996 pound-feet of torque for the Torcal S, making it the most powerful Bentley to date.

U.S. pricing starts at $222,495 for the Torcal, $262,695 for the high-performance Torcal S and $300,995 for the Torcal First Edition.

Bentayga pricing starts at $231,150, the Flying Spur starts at $254,850 and the Continental GT starts at $288,750. All prices include shipping.

The EV market is sort of an unknown in the ultra-luxury space. Sure, Rolls-Royce brought out the Spectre in 2023, and that has been a success; the Cadillac Celestiq is doing alright and the Ferrari Luce is selling well, despite its deeply polarizing design. However, Lamborghini killed its Lanzador EV earlier this year.

The Torcal's success is paramount for Bentley in the coming years. It invested $463 million to upgrade its factory in Crewe, England to build the EV, and it has spent even more than that on R&D and supply chain preparations. That's a lot of money to make back for a low-volume automaker like Bentley. It's doubly important because the automaker's global sales fell 17% through September, and the brand's profits dropped by over half to $54.1 million through the first nine months of 2026. This thing needs to be a sales success, and luckily for Bentley, it's looking that way.

Tesla is about to drop $3.31 billion to add a new facility at its Berlin-Brandenburg factory in Germany in an effort to boost production of CEO Elon Musk's latest pet project: the Cybercab. The news comes just days after Tesla opened direct sales to select customers. The plan is for production to officially begin in 2029, and it'll eventually ramp up to 1 million vehicles per year, according to factory lead Andrew Tierig. Construction is slated to begin in the first half of next year.

That's quite an expansion. The German factory, which first opened in March of 2022, makes hundreds of thousands of Model Ys and millions of battery cells, but it doesn't exactly produce a million vehicles per year. From The Wall Street Journal:

The group said on X Friday that "select customers are now being invited to purchase Cybercab for personal use" at an estimated purchase price of $29,990 and a $299-a-month subscription to Tesla's autonomy software.

Tesla started adding Cybercabs to its Austin fleet of robotaxis in September, and the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration opened an investigation to determine whether the steering-wheel-free vehicles comply with safety standards. Tesla told the regulator that the Cybercab meets all applicable standards, the NHTSA said in a filing.

Musk recently said the company would wind down production of the Cybertruck at its gigafactory in Texas next year to make room for increased production of the self-driving Cybercab. Adding a dedicated facility in Germany would allow Tesla to make the Cybercab on both sides of the Atlantic.

As Tesla's sales in Europe started regaining strength earlier this year after declining in 2025, the company has sought to boost output in Germany. In May, Thierig said the group would invest $250 million into its German factory to increase production of EV battery cells.

I'm skeptical of the scale of this project, but if it works, it would be good news for Germany's struggling automotive industry. Local automakers are having a tough time right now and cutting tens of thousands of jobs as they look for ways to remain competitive against Chinese rivals. Obviously, building out Tesla's factory and then staffing it would create a lot of theoretical jobs.

General Motors is looking to increase the use of robots and other automation by 20% at its factories in North America by 2028 as it looks for ways to deal with higher labor and onshoring costs.  The General is said to be developing its own robots and assembling them at its Kokomo, Indiana, plant, according to unnamed sources who spoke with Reuters. It's focused on using autonomous mobile robots to move parts around its plants. Unsurprisingly, the United Auto Workers union is rightfully worried about this plan.

Currently, GM is buying robotics equipment from outside suppliers while developing its own in-house, and it's asking parts suppliers bidding on new contracts to submit automation plans for their own operations. GM is using a scorecard to rate suppliers' automation efforts and even considering the scores in contract decisions. From Reuters:

GM said it uses automation to improve safety, quality and ​efficiency. "As competition intensifies globally, we continue to put these technologies to work in ways that support our manufacturing teams," its statement said.

US automakers have increased automation ​to contain manufacturing costs since the United Auto Workers won record contract gains in 2023 and President Donald Trump's drive to bring more factory work home put pressure on production costs.

The UAW, as you may have imagined, is not a fan of this.

The UAW won the contract gains from GM and its crosstown competitors Ford Motor and Jeep-parent Stellantis. GM said the contract would add about $575 ​in labor costs per vehicle; Ford pegged its added cost at $900 per vehicle.

At the time, analysts said the companies likely would increase automation as a ​way to defray the higher labor costs. GM last year said it had about 100 roboticists, AI engineers and hardware specialists working on advanced robotics systems.

US automakers have long ‌said their ⁠labor costs exceed those of foreign rivals and newer competitors such as Tesla, whose US factories are largely nonunion.

The companies face another round of potentially contentious negotiations in 2028, when the contracts are scheduled to expire. UAW President Shawn Fain already has warned that AI and increased automation pose a threat to workers.

"The fruits of our labor have multiplied like never before, but workers aren't reaping the harvest. That's theft," Fain said at a UAW convention in ​June. "And if AI continues to be used ​as an accessory to that ⁠crime, it has to be stopped."

Automation is nothing new at vehicle factories, but automakers are exploring more ways to integrate AI and robotics into their plants. At the end of the day, a robot is less expensive and less needy than a person, and if a company can save even a dime by using a robot versus a human, it's going to do it 10 times out of 10.

BMW is sick and tired of being sick and tired over these tariffs, and it wants some relief. It's the latest in a group of foreign automakers that are currently in talks with the Trump administration that are trying to catch a break on import duties by investing billions in new U.S. factories. Last year alone, BMW ate more than $1 billion in U.S. import tariffs, according to Robert Engelhorn, CEO of BMW Manufacturing.

The German automaker is pointing toward the $1.7 billion it spent on expanding its U.S. footprint for EV production at its plant in Spartanburg, South Carolina. The company produces more than 400,000 vehicles per year there, and ships about half of them to 120 countries. From Automotive News:

BMW's status as the largest auto exporter by value in the U.S., as well as its recent investments, are worthy of consideration for tariff relief, as company officials see it.

South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster said he would like to see lower tariffs for a company bringing outsized economic benefit to the state.

"Over time, I've had conversations with the people in Washington about that very thing," McMaster told Automotive News at a Nov. 13 event celebrating the opening of BMW's battery pack factory. "Nothing moves real fast sometimes, but it's all going to work out just fine, and this is more proof of it right here."

Last year, it imported about 215,000 vehicles to the U.S., most of which were sedans like the 3 Series and 4 Series. I'm not sure if it'll be enough to sway the Trump administration, but it's worth a shot. I'm sure having McMaster, a character we saw during Trump's first administration when he served as the National Security Advisor, in its corner is helpful, though.

The thing is, Rich, you were a bit of a crook in this one regard. Listen, I know everyone was out to get you, and you're one paranoid son of a gun, but I'm pretty sure you did that stuff, man. What gets lost in all of this is that Nixon made this proclamation at Disney World, and that really tickles me. Anyway, if you want to learn more about Crooked Rich, head over to History.com.

Fuel prices continue to tumble, as we hit another huge milestone when it comes to diesel. It's easy to see why, too. Both WTI Crude Oil futures and Brent Crude prices are down, sitting at $86 and $94, respectively, at the time of publication. We should enjoy these good times while we can, because who knows how long they're going to last.

Here's where national average prices stand right now, according to AAA:

This all shakes out to the average price of a gallon of gas dropping another 3 cents overnight to $3.78, according to AAA. Diesel is the big winner, though. Even though it only had a 1-cent drop overnight, it hit $5.99, which means it's under $6 a gallon for the first time in at least 5,000 years. That's a big win, if you ask me.

I know the Grammys are stupid and nonsensical junk every single year, but I still get sucked into the dumb crap they do without fail. How are you not going to nominate Getting Killed for Album of the Year? Ridiculous. On the same note, Charli xcx's Music, Fashion, Film should also have been nominated. A travesty. A disgrace. A farce.

#5612. China’s Electric Heavy Trucks Are Taking Sales from Diesel and LNG

In September 2026, battery-electric trucks captured 49.8% of China’s new domestic heavy-truck registrations. Of 65,800 trucks registered, 32,800 ran on batteries. Another 36 used hydrogen fuel cells. Battery electric accounted for more than 99% of the broader new-energy category. China’s freight operators are buying batteries at a scale that puts diesel and LNG suppliers under pressure.

The shift has gathered speed. Battery electric accounted for about 13% of domestic heavy-truck registrations in 2024, 28% in 2025 and nearly 38% in the first nine months of 2026. The figures come from compulsory-insurance registrations for trucks sold into the domestic market, excluding exports. China’s total domestic truck market remains below its pre-pandemic levels. Battery trucks are gaining share while the market for new heavy trucks remains constrained.

From May through September, new-energy heavy trucks exceeded 40% of new registrations for five straight months. The category reached approximately 226,400 vehicles in the first nine months, up 64% from the same period in 2025, and nearly 99% were battery electric. Tractor units that pull semi-trailers are leading the change. In September, 64.48% of new domestic tractor registrations belonged to the new-energy category. Electric trucks are moving freight on ordinary commercial routes, including work beyond ports and industrial yards.

My full TFIE Strategy Briefing traces China’s heavy-truck sales from 2015 through 2026, examines real freight costs and charging choices, and assesses the consequences for manufacturers, logistics companies and fuel demand.

The operating economics explain much of the appeal. Trucks earn money by carrying cargo, so annual kilometres, payload, electricity prices, charging stops and vehicle availability matter as much as the price on the invoice. High-mileage routes make electricity and maintenance savings more valuable. A costly grid connection or charging queue can eat into those savings. Fleet operators need to evaluate the truck and its route together.

Recent ICCT case studies document how those economics play out. A Guangdong warehouse fleet of 28 electric trucks had estimated five-year ownership costs 16% below comparable diesel trucks. In Yangtze River Delta express delivery, 50 electric tractor-trailers working routes of 300–500 km achieved a narrower 3% advantage over six years without purchase incentives. Another operation covering 900 km a day with strategically placed high-power charging showed estimated ownership costs 19% below diesel. The differences reflect route, utilization and charging arrangements.

Those three operations offer a more useful procurement lesson than a single quoted range figure. The operator starts with cargo, schedules and energy access, then selects equipment. The narrow 3% margin in express delivery also shows why financing and charging costs can determine whether a viable electric route makes money.

Battery swapping has carved out a sizable part of this market. In September, 20.09% of newly registered battery-electric heavy trucks were classified as swap-capable. That compares with 22.92% across January–September 2026 and 30.39% for all of 2025. The number of swap-classified trucks continued to rise, while conventional charging gained a larger share of the expanding electric market. China’s registration classification also includes some trucks with leased batteries that are recharged rather than exchanged.

Swapping fits dense, repeatable freight operations such as steelworks, ports and bulk-material haulage. Fleet operators and station owners can standardize vehicles and use stations often enough to pay for batteries held in inventory. Conventional charging serves a wider range of routes and can fit scheduled stops, overnight parking and depot operations. Both approaches depend on predictable truck traffic and reliable electricity connections.

China is building infrastructure around those freight patterns. Yunnan commissioned 3,350 km of heavy-truck charging corridors in 2025, with 113 stations and 869 connectors. Fujian opened a 649 km coastal corridor in October 2026, including 15 charging stations and eight swapping stations. The IEA’s 2026 charging review describes the concentration of heavy-vehicle charging around freight corridors and industrial centres. Long-haul coverage still has gaps, but the network is expanding where trucks already have work to do.

Hydrogen has found little traction alongside this expansion. China registered 689 fuel-cell heavy trucks in the first nine months of 2026, compared with more than 223,000 battery-electric trucks. LNG has a much larger installed customer base, although its advantage over diesel has narrowed as gas prices change. Battery trucks offer a different cost structure built around drivetrain efficiency and lower maintenance needs. That makes the competition increasingly difficult for equipment and fuel suppliers dependent on combustion engines.

Sales changes take years to work through the operating fleet. Kpler projects that new-energy trucks, predominantly battery electric, will account for about 8% of Chinese heavy trucks in service at the end of 2026. It also estimates they will displace about 230,000 barrels of diesel per day compared with moving the same freight using diesel trucks. Freight vehicles with high daily utilization can have a large effect on fuel demand before they become a majority of vehicles on the road.

China’s June 2026 heavy-truck programme joins purchasing incentives, grid access, charging corridors, financing and logistics planning. Its 2030 targets include a 40% share of new-energy heavy-truck sales, a 20% share of the operating fleet and 30,000 km of zero-carbon freight corridors. Monthly new sales have already surpassed the sales-share target. Building and replacing enough vehicles to reach the fleet target will take longer.

Other countries have different electricity tariffs, road networks and freight routes, but the procurement method travels. Start with the actual jobs trucks perform. Identify routes with strong electric economics, plan the charging and grid connections those routes require, and finance vehicles and infrastructure as one programme. Other drivetrains can compete where their operating costs or performance are better. The evidence from China’s largest commercial freight applications increasingly favours batteries.

The complete TFIE Strategy Briefing includes the historical registration series, the ICCT ownership-cost cases, charging and swapping corridors, and fleet-turnover analysis. TFIE Strategy works with fleets, utilities and policymakers on freight-electrification scenarios and investment decisions.

#5611. 'He Should Talk to His Primary Care Doctor About That'

— We should treat the patient in front of us whenever possible

One spring day during my neurology rotation, a man in his nineties came to our clinic. He was walking with a cane but otherwise remarkably independent, with the air of distinguished gentlemanliness a brown tweed jacket lends. We had an instant connection. Talking for just a few moments, we realized he hailed from my own family's ancestral town. As I spoke with him in his native language, he soon began calling me "pota" for "grandson." Quickly though, my resident and I also realized our patient was with us by mistake. Perhaps due to a miscommunication, or an administrative error, he thought he was at his primary care physician (PCP). He had been experiencing constipation.

After we clarified the confusion, my resident -- someone who taught me a great deal -- asked me to walk our patient out to the front desk and help him schedule a primary care appointment. The front desk said the next PCP appointment wouldn't be available for 7 weeks. I went to ask the resident if we could do something to help our patient; after all, while constipation may turn out to be a complex symptom either due to a serious condition (colorectal cancer, sigmoid volvulus) or as a precursor to downstream pathology (diverticulosis, fecal impaction), it is also quite common among older adults.

Both the resident and I had rotated on internal medicine and knew the questions to ask to identify any red flags and suggest a bowel regimen. And we had the time -- our patient didn't have a neurological concern, but he still had the appointment slot. Yet, when I returned to the clinic room to ask my resident if we could give our patient the relevant advice, he looked up from the queue of notes he was finishing and replied: "He should talk to his PCP about that."

Economics tell us that workforce efficiency is maximized when everyone spends time on what they are uniquely best at doing: labor arbitrage. As a management consultant prior to medical school, I spent years evangelizing this concept of "top of license work" to clients -- mostly large academic and nonprofit hospital systems. And I still believe in the principle broadly, albeit with perhaps a bit more reticence and understanding more nuance than before.

Top-of-license work in medicine doesn't only apply vertically across levels of training; it also operates horizontally, across fields. Patient outcomes are generally maximized when neurologists focus on diseases of the nervous system and gastroenterologists the digestive system because each specialty is doing work only they can do. Yet, that day in the neurology clinic taught me a nuance to this perspective.

At the end of the day, all physicians should consider themselves doctors first, and specialists second. Medical specialization shouldn't absolve specialists of the duty to help the patient before them -- especially when doing so requires minimal time and resources -- even if the patient's concern is not directly within their field.

Of course, there are challenges to this perspective. I can empathize with the medico-legal concerns of a neurologist who is served a subpoena and deposed by a lawyer: "Firstly, why did you manage this constipation? And why did you not order XYZ tests for this patient with constipation who turned out to have colorectal cancer?" And I recognize the confusion medical teams may feel when checking charts and seeing who prescribed certain medications: "Why is the prescribing doctor for this patient's cetirizine (Zyrtec) an orthopedic surgeon?"

These concerns are real. But primary care is a limited resource too. The dumping of basic tasks on primary care -- a field with its own specialized expertise that is often not recognized -- has been discussed ad nauseam; specialists should help relieve this burden when possible.

Labor arbitrage and top of license work still apply when specialists help patients with "primary care problems." However, because of the design of our healthcare system, there is little structural incentive for physicians to work outside of their typical scopes. If, for instance, we financially incentivized all of a patient's physicians by the same quality metrics, specialists would be incentivized not just in their field, but across the spectrum of the patient's health. Or even if we had less insurance churn, payers would perhaps better leverage incentives within their networks to promote overall health.

Responding to incentives does not mean physicians have moral failings. It shows they are human. But if we continue to depend on our system as currently designed, we will continue to have rampant "moral alibis" -- a term coined by Sachin Jain, MD, MBA, to highlight how physicians at times emphasize problems with the system to escape responsibility for personal decisions -- that limit the impact of our care.

The vast majority of physicians enter medicine to help patients. It is the design of our system that has forced practice to occur in unnatural ways. But perhaps while we solve these structural problems, we can start changing things by treating the patient in front of us -- one case of constipation at a time.

#5609. The Rising Tide Of Distributed Energy Resources

Centralized power plants can trip widespread brownouts or blackouts when under stress. They make fat targets for enemy weapons, too. In contrast, distributed energy resources (DERs for short) can improve overall resiliency in the face of both natural and human-made disasters, while also enabling ratepayers to take advantage of utility discounts, and even earn revenue from their personal energy assets. The DERs field includes — but is not limited to — rooftop solar, EV charging stations, and home batteries. And, we ain’t seen nothing yet. DERs stakeholders have also begun moving into the distributed computing field as well.

DERs first surfaced on the CleanTechnica radar in the early 2000’s during the Obama administration, when the US Department of Energy began promoting decentralized, home-and community-based energy resources as the leading characteristic of a modernized and more resilient electricity grid. Made possible by the falling cost of solar, wind, and energy storage, the agency’s embrace of small-scale, localized electricity generation was a sharp contrast with the traditional emphasis on large centralized power plants for energy security (see more DERs background here).

Nowadays the DERs field embraces practically any non-centralized power generation resource, regardless of size or type. The DERs field can include, for example, a new gas power plant commissioned to run an adjacent AI data center.

To get some perspective on the journey of DERs since the early 2000’s, consider the case of the leading rooftop solar installer Sunrun. After launching in 2007, Sunrun segued into energy storage and virtual power plants, with “virtual” referring to smart grid technology that coordinates thousands of far-flung energy producing (and consuming) devices to balance supply and demand at peak periods of consumption.

For the record, Sunrun now presents itself as a storage-first company. The company’s focus remains on renewable energy but the storage field is source-agnostic, embracing practically every energy resource on the planet.

Sunrun CEO Mary Powell also prefers to use “distributed” instead of “virtual” in reference to decentralized power systems, to emphasize that hardware is the foundational element. As of this month, Sunrun ranks as the biggest distributed power plant in the US, with solar and storage assets spread among 164,000 enrolled households.

Back in 2021, Sunrun entered into an installation partnership with the home energy management startup SPAN, known for its next-generation home electrical panels among other products, and that layed the ground work for a partnership on distributed computing systems. Earlier this year, SPAN introduced XFRA, a new product consisting of computer nodes to be staged at homes and smaller commercial spaces to form a distributed data center. The model is similar in concept to the familiar Internet-enabled citizen scientist platform, except that XFRA deploys its own nodes instead of using a participant’s personal computer.

This past September, Sunrun announced its selection as an authorized installation partner for XFRA with a focus on new home developments, aiming for gigawatt-scale distributed computing networks beginning in Texas and other selected markets. “Sunrun’s battery-plus-solar systems will maintain reliable electricity for both the homes and the XFRA compute nodes, while preventing the overloading of local distribution infrastructure—allowing SPAN to maximize node deployment.,” Sunrun explains.

“By pairing home energy generation and storage with XFRA compute nodes, we are unlocking new economic value for our customers and for Sunrun, while also solving certain speed-to-power constraints that would otherwise limit AI deployment,” Sunrun CEO Mary Powell elaborated in a press statement.

Arch Rao, founder and CEO of SPAN, also chipped in his two cents. “We can now drastically increase our penetration of XFRA compute nodes by pairing them with Sunrun energy systems to deliver cost-effective AI compute capacity at unprecedented speed while also reducing compute cost for certain AI applications,” Rao said.

Back when the Energy Department initially began promoting DERs as a function of the energy transition, the agency used the term “prosumer” to describe ratepayers who are empowered to engage with their local power grid as a renewable energy producer, not simply as a passive consumer. The distributed data center adds another layer of engagement to the prosumer mix.

At a personal appearance during Climate Week in New York City in September, Powell referenced distributed computing as the latest demonstration of the company’s ongoing dialog with its customers and other stakeholders, leading to innovative new products that put more power management tools in the hands of ratepayers.

Powell reiterated the point during an appearance at the 2026 “DERVOS” summit at the Brooklyn Navy Yard on November 5, and the DERVOS gathering itself provides further insights into the widening scope of DERs activity.

“DERVOS” is a play on Davos, which is shorthand for the annual meeting of the World Economic Forum. Like the World Economic Forum, DERs stakeholders have emerged in force upon the global economy as well as here in the US, stretching far from its do-it-yourself roots in the off-gridder movement of the 1970’s.

The event itself is the brainchild of the collaborative trade organization DER Task Force. The group formally launched in 2019 but it claims roots much earlier, in the 1970’s-era New York City activist organization Energy Task Force, whose activities were highlighted by the installation of a wind turbine in the city — illegally, of course.

By the time DERVOS 2026 rolled around, the DER Task Force had become an organization with a reach far beyond New York, and it has also embraced the size-doesn’t-matter ethos  under the slogan, “Everything is DER.”

“That’s what we mean by Everything is DER: not that everything is small, or even literally ‘distributed,’ but that the center of gravity is shifting toward energy resources that are closer to load and controlled by those who need the power,” the Task Force explains (emphasis theirs).

“Sometimes that shift is bottoms-up, sometimes it’s centrally planned, but either way, DERs aren’t the sideshow anymore. They’re the main event,” they add.

I’ll have much more to report from DERVOS 2026 in the coming days and weeks, but for the time being let’s go back to the foundational idea of improving grid resiliency and security. Climate change aside, in recent years Russia and the US have both provided textbook cases for transitioning out of energy systems that involve building fat, juicy infrastructure targets for attack, alongside precariously long energy transportation systems. If you have any thoughts about that, drop a note in the comment thread.

Image: The renewable energy “prosumer” envisioned by the US Department of Energy in the early 2000’s has become the sophisticated distributed energy resources manager of today (graphic by Sara Harman courtesy of US DOE).

Tina has been covering advanced energy technology, military sustainability, emerging materials, biofuels, ESG and related policy and political matters for CleanTechnica since 2009. Follow her @tinamcasey on LinkedIn, Mastodon or Bluesky.

#5608. Acura ZDX Recalled For Temporary Loss Of Braking Like Its GM Brethren

General Motors issued another recall intended to address temporary loss of braking in several of its Ultium-platform models late last month, and now we know the problem plagues 2024 Acura ZDXs, too. You're forgiven if you forgot about the brief existence of the Acura ZDX EV, so allow me to refresh your memory. The ZDX was Acura's first EV, and beneath its sharp and aggressive exterior it was based on the Chevrolet Blazer EV, sharing that crossover's powertrain and technology. According to the NHTSA Recall Report, 14,648 all-wheel-drive 2024 Acura ZDXs need a software update to correct the same temporary loss of braking issue plaguing GM's EVs. Rear-wheel-drive ZDXs are not affected by the recall.

The temporary loss of braking only arises under very specific conditions, and it corrects itself after the driver releases the brake pedal and presses it again, but any loss of braking is a scary and dangerous situation. In GM's recall of over 67,000 EVs, it was aware of 20 minor accidents due to the fault, two of which resulted in minor injuries; Honda is unaware of any warranty claims or injuries related to the recall.

As with the GM recall, the only time the Acura ZDX's temporary loss of braking occurs is under very specific circumstances. According to the recall report, "the software logic used to calculate vehicle reference speed (Vref) may become unstable when wheel slip associated with turning and light braking occurs together with travel over a road disturbance and release/reapplication of the brake pedal. On a high-friction surface, the unstable calculation may incorrectly determine that the wheels are in deep slip and command an inappropriate reduction in brake pressure."

To fix the condition, Honda will update the Electronic Brake Control Module software. Owners who have accepted the terms and conditions to accept over-the-air (OTA) software updates can download the updated software remotely, but all owners can take their ZDX to the Acura dealership to have the update installed, too.

I attended the first drive event of the Acura ZDX Type S back in 2024, and I wasn't the biggest fan of the car. It drove fine, but the interior didn't feel any more upscale than the much cheaper Blazer EV, and considering that Acura canceled the model after just one year on sale, I expected sales numbers to be much lower. Check out NHTSA's website for more recall information.

#5606. Chemicals in Many Everyday Items Pose a Growing Threat, U.N. Report Says

— Health-related costs from exposure is estimated to exceed $1.1 trillion annually worldwide

Chemicals in many everyday items that tinker with a body's hormones are a growing threat to human health and the environment, and science now better understands the harm they cause, a new United Nations report said Tuesday.

Endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) are found in many plastic items, personal care products, pharmaceuticals, toys, household goods, electronics, and pesticides. The new report, written by scientists, estimates the health-related costs from exposure to these chemicals exceed $1.1 trillion annually worldwide. It calls for urgent, coordinated international action to protect human health and the environment.

The policies and regulations to transform the products and sectors causing widespread exposure to these chemicals remain "fragmented and insufficient," it says.

The U.N. Environment Program (UNEP) and World Health Organization issued the report.

"This report is an important step towards a safer world, free from exposure to EDCs," the two U.N. bodies wrote in the foreword. "Solutions do exist. Some safer alternatives are available. The task for policymakers is to ensure that these solutions and alternatives are deployed -- to protect human, animal and planetary health, and save trillions of dollars each year."

The "state of the science" report describes what scientists have learned about exposure to EDCs and their effects since 2012. Previous reports assessed the science on EDCs in 2002 and 2012 to inform policymakers and guide action.

Jacqueline Alvarez, PhD, chief of the UNEP Chemicals and Health Branch, said the new report builds on those assessments, while reflecting a field that has advanced substantially in the breadth of health effects documented, in the sophistication of exposure science, in the development of testing and assessment methodologies, and in a growing understanding of the socioeconomic costs of regulatory inaction.

Report Says There's Strong Evidence These Chemicals Harm Health

Humans and wildlife are exposed to a wide range of these chemicals, and the evidence linking exposure to diseases and disorders "is strong and continues to grow," the report says. People can be exposed through ingestion, skin absorption, inhalation, and direct contact with medical devices during procedures. Children can also be exposed by putting toys containing these chemicals in their mouths and through skin contact with the toys.

Prenatal and early-life exposure to EDCs affects neurodevelopment, cognition, and behavior; EDCs are linked to cancer, cardiovascular disease, obesity, type 2 diabetes, and metabolic liver disease, according to the report. Reproductive organs, fertility, and thyroid functions are also disrupted.

When the 2012 report was published, there was a lot of evidence these chemicals harmed health, but it was not necessarily pointing in the same direction at the same kind of health effects, said Laura Vandenberg, PhD, one of the lead authors for Tuesday's report. Vandenberg also contributed to the 2012 report.

Now, there's "essentially a statement of irrefutable evidence linking EDCs to human health effects and also environmental damage," said Vandenberg, a professor of environmental health sciences at the University of Massachusetts Amherst.

People Are Exposed to These Chemicals Through Some Plastics

Some countries are pushing to regulate chemicals used to make plastics as part of the negotiations over a global treaty to end plastic pollution. This report empowers those countries that are pushing for controls, said Bjorn Beeler, international coordinator for the International Pollutants Elimination Network (IPEN).

Beeler said the amount of harm from these chemicals is only going to increase in future years as plastic and chemical production is projected to skyrocket -- a "toxic tidal wave" no one is prepared for. IPEN wants a treaty that places global controls on hazardous chemicals in plastics and ends the rapid growth of plastic production. Negotiations are set to resume early next year.

Chemical additives to plastics impart flexibility, rigidity, UV stabilization, durability, and other characteristics that help products perform as intended, said the American Chemistry Council (ACC), a trade group that represents the U.S. chemical industry. The industry considers the safe use of chemicals paramount, said Kimberly Wise White, PhD, ACC's vice president of regulatory and scientific affairs.

The plastics industry opposes efforts to impose new restrictions through the treaty, arguing that chemicals used in plastics are best regulated through existing international conventions and national laws that consider all of a chemical's uses. White said comprehensive frameworks, like the Toxic Substances Control Act in the U.S. and the European Union's Registration, Evaluation, Authorization, and Restriction of Chemicals regulation, that evaluate uses of a chemical to determine risk, are the most effective way to regulate plastic additives.

The International Council of Chemical Associations, which represents manufacturers and producers around the world, has contributed $1.65 million and provided technical expertise to help countries implement chemical management systems, as well as created a publicly accessible plastic additives database.

Few Chemicals Have Been Tested for Endocrine Disruption

More than 350,000 chemicals and chemical mixtures have been registered for production and use globally, but the vast majority have never been evaluated for endocrine-disrupting properties, the report says.

There has been more effort in recent years to develop testing programs, which were highlighted as a major need in the 2012 report. However, most of that testing has not led to action to regulate these chemicals and control exposure, Vandenberg said.

The take-home message from Tuesday's report, she said, is that "in many, many cases we know enough to act. Why haven't we acted?"

Chemicals have been removed from products when people become aware and stop buying products containing a certain chemical, like bisphenol A (BPA), which has been used to make plastic containers for storing food and beverages, Vandenberg said. But that can lead to a "whack-a-mole problem," where a substitution is created but it's structurally similar or insufficiently tested, she added.

To truly reduce people's exposures to these chemicals, it must be done at a policy level throughout society, Vandenberg said.

The report says regulators should aim to protect vulnerable populations from exposure, particularly during pregnancy, infancy, and childhood; improve monitoring and understanding of exposure to these chemicals; advance the identification and testing of them; account for the costs of exposure; and strengthen regulations, among other steps.

The estimate of the annual health-related costs is a conservative calculation that accounts for the cost of health treatment and lost productivity, the report says. The $1.1 trillion price tag doesn't account for the additional costs associated with contaminated drinking water, loss of biodiversity, impacts on food production, and even human rights.

Bethanie Carney Almroth, PhD, U.N. Special Rapporteur on toxics and human rights, said she hopes the report will spur action, though international cooperation is challenging.

"This report makes clear that new regulations are needed, new testing paradigms must be adopted," said Carney Almroth, an ecotoxicology professor at Sweden's University of Gothenburg. "We need to reverse responses from reactive to proactive. We need to prevent harm from occurring, rather than merely documenting and treating it after the fact."
