#5605. BYD E6Y Odyssey

A couple of friends embark on a road trip to pick their EV purchase, and it turns into an Odyssey.

The BYD E6 is a BEV classic. Globe-trotting friends have ridden in them as taxis in Singapore. Majella and I even took one for a test drive (it reminded me of a ’70s Chrysler Valiant). It was the best selling pure electric car in China in 2016, with about 600,000 sold globally, and it is viewed by many as ahead of its time. So, when one showed up at our coffee and cake morning tea, I had to interview the owner, Joanne, and her road trip friend, Meredith. What they shared with me was truly an odyssey of determination to get Jo’s car home. Please note: this story took place 6 years ago. Charging availability has improved and so has Joanne’s knowledge of living with an electric vehicle.

Joanne told me that she had been looking for an EV for two years when a search on carsales.com found an ad for an E6Y (the taxi version of the BYD E6). It was a pre-COVID import and had been mothballed at Sydney airport after the company importing the vehicles had decided not to go ahead with taxis. Photos of all the BYDs at the airport were widely circulated as evidence that no one wanted to buy an EV. The cars were being “sold by a mate out of the back of the factory.” At the low cost of AU$32,000, claiming a 400 km range from its 83-kWh battery and only 100 km on the odometer, Joanne saw it as a bargain.

There was some consideration of putting the car on a flatbed and having it shipped, but in the end, the two friends decided on a road trip.

Jo informs me that: “They only brought 120 of the BYD E6Y taxi versions into the country. BYD sold some GLX versions, which had more bells and whistles.”

She was soon to find out that all is not as it seems. Her lack of knowledge of EVs meant that her trip in the car from Sydney back to Brisbane would be an odyssey of Greek tragedy proportions. Jo reminisces: “Meredith reminded me our original plan had been to spend just two days driving back to Brisbane with the one overnight stay. I thought I could ‘fast charge’ the car and make it back to Brisvegas on the second day. Hahahaha. Lesson learned the hard way.” They expected it to be just a twelve-hour trip. Meredith adds, “I told her we would laugh about it one day.”

Joanne contacted the seller and planned her flight to Sydney. Meredith got excited and joined the “road trip” in Newcastle. Jo paid the money and took ownership of the car. “It took two hours to get out of Sydney.” To be fair, that wasn’t the car’s fault — just Sydney’s congested traffic. However, the fact that the previous owner had only charged the car to 50% didn’t help. She was able to charge the car to 80% on the outskirts of Sydney. “But I had no idea that I wouldn’t get the expected range at highway speeds.”

Another learning curve was the state of charging points — sure, there were plenty listed on PlugShare, but many were unavailable or broken. Again, dear reader, I must emphasize this was 6 years ago.

Her next planned stop was accommodation she had booked at Newcastle. She got to within 2 km when the battery readout said “zero.” She was unable to find a place to charge — the car had not come with a granny charger. Jo clarified her Newcastle experience by email: “the Uni in Newcastle was the first I tried to charge. My friend Meredith and I tried three other places to charge all with no luck. I found out later that the Newcastle chargers were notorious for not working.” She confided to me that she now knows that the car can go a little further even when it says zero battery. She also had to learn the difference between AC and DC charging. The BYD she had bought could only handle AC charging.

With the battery reading zero, she felt she had no choice but to leave the car at a nearby garage. The owner of the accommodation she had booked kindly came and picked her and her friend up. The next day, the BNB owner dropped them back to the garage and a tow truck was ordered. The tow truck took them and their car to a local winery where they trickle charged next to the golf carts. The winery also had a Tesla level 2 charger for customer use. It was charging when they arrived. “We left a note on the windscreen of the Tesla that was using the level 2. During breakfast the Tesla owner rang and said the charger was available. We left the winery fully charged and off up the highway.” Not a bad place to get stuck, methinks.

280 km up the road to Kempsie, there was access to free charging in the council carpark, but no available accommodation! That’s what happens when you travel on the Queen’s Birthday long weekend. “We were checking out the back seat of the car as a place to sleep when a friend of a friend told them he had a farm in area. ‘Have I got a place for you!’ he told them. After we finished charging, we had to drive down this dark farm track. We couldn’t plug the car in because we still didn’t have a granny charger!” They made themselves comfortable in the available beds in the barn. The next morning in the light of day they found they had driven alongside of a lagoon! “We could have easily driven into that!”

Meredith adds: “I didn’t think I’d be sleeping in a shed with a tractor and then I couldn’t sleep because of the smell of diesel.” The trip was not just a challenge, but torture.

Their next adventure was just a few kilometers up the road at Gladstone NSW. Low on juice, they contacted people through PlugShare and got a message from a local café owner. You can check out the café here. He already owned a Hyundai Ioniq, and so had a granny charger to lend. The café owner knew a fellow who was visiting his mum in town. This friend had ordered an Atto 3 from BYD and was waiting on this first shipment of BYDs to arrive. Jo took him for a ride around town in her car. “This was his first ride in a BYD.”

He arranged for them to leave their car at his mother’s home in the next town (Smithtown). Jo and her friend were now in a hurry, as both had to get back to Brisbane to go to work the next day. Leaving the car charging, “We belted back to Brisbane in this horrible little roller skate hire car.” Home in Brisbane, Jo had to plan how to retrieve her BYD purchase. Meredith did not want another “road trip.”

This time, Jo travelled south by train. Even this trip was not without drama. She missed her stop. Thankfully, she was able to get off at the next stop and change to the northbound train to make it back to where her car waited faithfully for her. She took a taxi to her car, returned the borrowed granny charger, and began her journey home. She was so keen that she ended up with a speeding ticket.

Joanne arrived at her motel in Balina with 10 km of range showing on the dashboard. But the available ocular charger soon filled up the car. By 9:00 pm, with a full battery, she couldn’t wait to go home. The fireworks display in town was a fitting sendoff for the final leg of her journey.

Jo would like to acknowledge all the good advice and offers of help she received from fellow users of PlugShare, as well as all those referred to above. She is now a confident and competent driver of her BYD E6Y and has made many trips back and forth to Sydney from Brisbane with less drama. The BYD E6Y Facebook group has been a great help. She says she would not part with her green E6Y Singapore taxi — “a comfortable and solid basic car.” Rumour has it that there are about 250 on Australian roads, with the record distance travelled over 1 million km.

Another owner commented: “This unstoppable tank will outlive me I’m sure, best of all its super basic … no internet, no lane assist, no self-driving and plenty of new and used cheap parts available. This is why it seems like there are so few … they are so good NO ONE who has one is selling them.”

Jo has even taken her car camping. “The camping trip was to Yandina up the coast. I did sleep in the back of the car on that trip very comfortably. But that time I had a mattress and bedding. I did take out the bottom half of the back seat from the car so I could get a completely flat rear area for the mattress. When I returned from the camping trip, I popped the rear seat bottom back in the car. It’s just two bolts and a couple of plastic clips that hold it in.”

And in the future, I asked? “It will be hard to part with my E6. I am waiting on the first solid state 1000km BEVs before I would consider parting with it. I just love the two-tone paint job.”

Jo is another happy battery electric vehicle owner, sharing her learning experience “odyssey” and having fun. “Thanks for the opportunity to immortalise the odyssey,” she told me in her latest email. The future is bright and electric as we learn to live with our new vehicles.

#5604. A Smaller Electric Land Rover Defender Is Coming In 2027

Rumors of a smaller, electric Land Rover Defender have been swirling for quite some time now — we first reported on it three years ago — and now we're finally getting some concrete information on when we'll be seeing the compact SUV. Jaguar Land Rover CEO PB Balaji says the battery-electric Defender is set to be sold alongside the existing combustion-engine model sometime in 2027, according to Automotive News.

From the spy shots we've seen, the so-called Defender Sport will be quite a bit smaller than the current five-door Defender. We know it'll be the second model underpinned by JLR's brand-new 800-volt Electrified Modular Architecture platform, the first being the Range Rover GT that should be revealed in just a couple months. When production spins up in Halewood, England, it will also mark the end of the Range Rover Evoque and Discovery Sport. The baby Defender will be powered by the same battery pack as the Range Rover GT, which JLR said will have up to 450 miles of range on the European cycle, but the boxier shape of the Defender will certainly cut down on that number.

Those who are into the idea of a smaller Defender but who aren't sold on an electric drivetrain needn't worry. Like the GT, the Defender EV is being developed with hybrid powertrain options as well. However, those buyer is going to have to wait a little while, because the hybrids aren't going to be on sale until 2028 at the earliest. Balaji told AutoNews that they are "fully underway" but "won't catch next year's timelines."

The Defender EV is set to be JLR's fifth electric vehicle, sitting alongside the aforementioned Range Rover GT, as well as the electric versions of the full-size Range Rover and Range Rover Sport, and the Jaguar Type 01. Yes, there was also the Jaguar I-Pace, but that's long dead. While pricing for the Defender EV hasn't been revealed or hinted at yet, AutoNews expects it to be fairly close to the current Defender 110. That means both will be priced significantly above the Evoque and Discovery Sport, a clear sign that JLR is continuing its move upmarket while leaving entry-level luxury behind.

The one caveat to all of this is that JLR's EV timelines have been a bit fugazi of late. The Range Rover Electric was only just officially revealed in September, two years after it was initially slated to go on sale. Keep in mind, the fifth-generation Range Rover was first revealed all the way back at the end of 2021.

This new model will be the first in a proposed series of vehicles meant to establish Defender as its own brand within Land Rover, according to Car and Driver. It's part of JLR's "House of Brands" strategy that we first told you about all the way back in 2023. I'm not sure if that's a play that'll work, but who am I to tell a brand how to run. You've got to think the Defender EV will be a solid off-roader. It has the Defender name to uphold after all. It really cannot get away with being mediocre when the going gets rough, can it?

If that nameplate sounds familiar, the Aston Martin Dreadnought was originally a digital-only vehicle exclusively designed for "Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4."

The two-time F1 world champion won't be heading out into the desert alone. He will reunite with his previous Dakar co-driver, Marc Coma. Few competitors are as accomplished and experienced as Coma. The 50-year-old won the Dakar five times with KTM and briefly served as the rally's race director between 2016 and 2018. As a pairing, Alonso and Coma finished 13th in the 2020 Dakar Rally with Toyota. Alonso said his return was driven by a desire to challenge himself. Honestly, F1 isn't much of a challenge at Aston Martin this season. The Spaniard is just trundling around, hoping to finish races. He said in a release:

"After deciding to continue racing in Formula One with the Aston Martin Aramco, I thought carefully about Dakar. In the end, the decision became simple. I wanted to embrace the challenge completely and take on both Formula One and the Dakar Rally in the same year."

The version of the Aston Martin Dreadnought won't feature a carbon-fiber chassis, military-grade armor plating or weapons storage like its Call of Duty counterpart. This Dreadnought is based on the Prodrive-designed Dacia Sandrider. The machine is fitted with the same three-liter, twin-turbocharged Nissan engine. The starkest difference is the bodywork, styled after the digital-only combat SUV, most evident in the square headlights and the louvered rear window.

The Prodrive-run effort will also include another usual suspect at the wheel of a Dreadnought: Nine-time World Rally Champion Sébastien Loeb. The living legend has never won the Dakar Rally, but has finished second on three occasions. The third Dreadnought will be driven by Lucas Moraes. The Brazilian joined the Dacia-Prodrive effort after winning the World Rally-Raid Championship with Toyota in 2025. The vehicle's origin may seem ridiculous, but Aston Martin has a legitimate chance of winning the Dakar in January. Prodrive is the returning winner after Nasser Al-Attiyah took the 2026 victory in a Dacia Sandrider.

#5602. FDA Wants Liquid Statin Off Shelves

— Missing annual reports put simvastatin oral suspension on thin ice

The FDA wants a liquid formulation of simvastatin (FloLipid) withdrawn from the market, though the agency is giving the drugmaker an opportunity for a hearing.

Approval of simvastatin oral suspension is at risk because Salerno Pharma "has repeatedly failed to file required annual reports" to the FDA, according to a notice in the Federal Register.

According to FDA policy, these annual reports are supposed to convey labeling information and technicalities, such as a current list of approved chemistry, manufacturing, and control information.

Initially approved in 2016 for a host of indications, simvastatin oral suspension is marketed as the first LDL cholesterol medication in liquid form for U.S. patients. The product was developed for patients who have difficulty swallowing pills, and the recommended usual starting dose is 10 mg or 20 mg once a day in the evening on an empty stomach.

Regarding safety, an increased risk of myopathy, including rhabdomyolysis, has been observed in patients taking an 80-mg dose of the oral suspension. Other patients unable to hit their LDL cholesterol goal taking the 40-mg dose are advised to initiate alternative LDL cholesterol-lowering treatments. In 2020, the drug label for the liquid simvastatin formulation was updated with a warning of rare reports of immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy associated with statin use.

According to the Federal Register notice -- which came from Michael Davis, MD, PhD, the FDA's top drug regulator -- Salerno is being given a shot at requesting a hearing if it wants to argue why the approval should not be withdrawn.

Salerno's simvastatin suspension was previously manufactured for Rosemont Pharmaceuticals, a Perrigo company.

Oral suspension atorvastatin (Atorvaliq) is an alternative liquid statin on the market.

#5601. HLTH 2026: Calibrate, Withings study finds wraparound care boosts GLP-1 weight loss by more than 60%

HLTH 2026: Calibrate, Withings study finds wraparound care boosts GLP-1 weight loss by more than 60%" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

As health plans and employers continue to evaluate the costs and outcomes associated with GLP-1 weight loss drugs, a new study found that wraparound clinical care and behavior change support can make expensive GLP-1 treatments more effective and durable.

A two-year real-world study from Withings Health Solutions and Calibrate Health suggests that pairing GLP-1 medications with Calibrate’s integrated obesity care program produced substantially greater weight loss than GLP-1 treatment alone, and Calibrate members sustained more of their weight loss.

The study followed 4,961 U.S. adults who began GLP-1s between 2022 and 2024, comparing 3,422 Calibrate members with 1,539 Withings users taking GLP-1s without the program. After adjustment for differences between the groups, Calibrate members lost 17.3% of their starting weight at two years versus 10.7% for the GLP-1-only group, a more than 60% relative difference.

The study was a real-world observational analysis, not a randomized controlled trial. Because Calibrate members chose to join the program, the two groups differed at the start. Before comparing, a statistical adjustment made them comparable on age, sex, race, BMI, health conditions and GLP-1 treatment, according to the study. Weight was followed for over 24 months.

The study findings, shared first with Fierce Healthcare, underscore that GLP-1 treatment may work better when medication is paired with personalized clinical management, behavioral coaching and continuous monitoring, rather than being treated primarily as a prescription benefit, according to Calibrate, a digitally integrated obesity management solution.

The study results also reinforce that obesity should be treated as a disease, another chronic metabolic condition requiring intensive, ongoing support, rather than a medication-only problem, Linda Anegawa, M.D., Calibrate Health’s chief medical advisor, told Fierce Healthcare.

“With any chronic disease, like hypertension for example, you won’t get as good outcomes if you just hand someone a medication and don’t support them across other pillars of health, like self-monitoring blood pressure, physical activity and stress reduction. Type 2 diabetes is another good example; you can give high doses of insulin, but medication can’t do the job alone without nutrition education and support,” she said.

“[The study results] make it very clear that treatment [for obesity] shouldn’t stop at just drug coverage,” she added. “As we envision the future, I’d like to see obesity care looking very similar to diabetes care, with insurance covering the full range of necessary services from medication treatment to nutrition education and overall lifestyle support. Obesity is a complex, chronic disease deserving of the same coverage parity as any other."

Treating obesity as such not only prevents health complications and improves quality of life, but it will also lower overall long-term health systems’ costs of care, Anegawa asserted.

The advantage of the integrated care program persisted despite weight regain, the study found. While both study groups regained some weight after reaching their lowest point, the Calibrate members remained about 16.6% below their starting weight, according to the study results. The GLP-1-only group reached a best point of 12.6% weight loss and was about 9.2% below baseline at the peak of its rebound.

There was a body-composition benefit as well. In a subgroup of 974 participants followed for body composition, the muscle-to-fat ratio improved 49.3% for Calibrate members versus 39.9% for GLP-1-only users at 18 months, roughly a 9-point difference.

The study data is based on two years of daily weigh-ins from Withings-connected scales, analyzed with causal-inference methods. Body composition was followed over 18 months in 520 Calibrate members and 454 Withings users.

The study reinforces the importance of evaluating body composition, rather than weight alone, in obesity treatment, Anegawa said.

“We know that abnormal visceral fat accumulation and dysfunction is what drives most of the metabolic conditions we treat, so if we aren’t equipping members to maximize visceral fat loss and preserve muscle, we can actually end up making people sicker. Losing muscle has severe consequences—it isn’t just scaffolding. Muscle is a critical metabolic organ that regulates energy balance, hormonal signaling and insulin sensitivity,” she said.

Adding the insights of body composition to Calibrate's clinical and metabolic data allows the company to better monitor trends and adapt care based on quality evidence, she noted.

There are several key factors that make an integrated obesity care program more effective than a medication-only program, Anegawa said.

"Physician-led personalized care that includes medication optimization for each member’s needs, tailored wraparound support, and features that drive continuous engagement—all of which are designed to maximize clinical outcomes," she said.

"Breaking this down, we start with a comprehensive clinical evaluation for each member, vs. other programs, which only require a questionnaire for a prescription. This helps us get to know each member’s medical and weight histories in detail. We analyze comprehensive lab data to understand their baseline metabolic profile. This information is then used by our expert clinicians to personalize clinical care from day one," Anegawa said.

Live one-to-one coaching support focuses on four pillars of healthy weight maintenance: nutrition, activity, sleep and mindset shift. Tailored education and anticipatory guidance help members manage side effects and stay on treatment, while connecting members to their personal motivations helps sustain engagement through challenges and supports lasting improvements in metabolic health, according to Calibrate.

Calibrate Health has been working with connected health device maker Withings for over five years. The company's members use Withings devices regularly as a required part of the program, according to Anegawa.

"We were already getting body composition data that gave us additional insights into individual members’ health. That data led to additional questions, such as are there significant differences that we can see in aggregate? If so, how large are the differences, and are they changing clinical outcomes? Can we use these data to inform and improve the evolution of our protocols and clinical care? So in asking these types of questions, it became clear to both the Calibrate and Withings teams that we should formalize this into a collaborative study," she noted.

The use of smart devices, specifically Wi-Fi or Bluetooth-connected scales, provides continuous data to help identify weight loss patterns that might not have been apparent through traditional clinical measures, noted Antoine Pivron, vice president of Withings Health Solutions.

"Today, most people on a GLP-1 are monitored through a keyhole. A patient whose primary care doctor prescribes the drug might be weighed a few times a year, and each reading reflects one day: what they ate, the time, the clothes they wore. Between visits, nobody knows whether they plateaued in month three, started regaining in month five, or stopped the drug altogether," he said.

"Specialty programs do better, but many rely on self-reported weights from whatever scale the patient owns. And people tend to stop reporting exactly when things go wrong, which is the moment the care team most needs to know," he added.

Body composition is the biggest blind spot, Pivron asserted. Withings' smart scales track weight and detailed body composition metrics to help identify whether the weight coming off during treatment is fat or muscle.

"In the study we did with Calibrate, two years of data let us see the full shape of the journey: the drop, the low point, and the partial regain that follows. We could also see the quality of the weight loss, not just the quantity. Program members improved their muscle-to-fat balance more, but part of their extra weight loss was muscle. That tells a program exactly where to focus next: protein and strength training," Pivron said.

Withings, a French consumer electronics company, launched its B2B health solutions division in 2019 to meet the growing market around virtual care and remote management in the U.S.

Pivron expects connected health devices like smart scales to play a growing role in GLP-1 treatment programs and broader chronic disease management.

"A GLP-1 prescription isn’t a care plan. The programs that work combine three things: the drug, the clinical and coaching support around it, and the data that shows whether it’s working. Miss one, and real-world results rarely match what we see in trials," he said.

Body composition will become standard in GLP-1 care, Pivron asserted: "That’s where the clinical definition of obesity is already heading."

Connected devices provide the data layer—continuously tracking weight and body composition, predicting when patients may be veering off course and identifying additional risks such as hypertension.

"But a risk score is not a diagnosis. A notification with no next step just creates anxiety. These signals belong inside a care program with a protocol: confirm with a cuff, see a clinician, treat if needed," he said. "Employers and payers are moving toward paying for outcomes. Connected devices are how a program proves it delivered them."

Employers face rising healthcare costs—projected to climb 9.5% next year—and GLP-1 treatments are a major contributor to that cost growth.

The study provides evidence of better outcomes with wraparound care, but it did not evaluate the impact on healthcare spending.

Anegawa contends that improvements in markers associated with high metabolic risk, like Hemoglobin A1c, the liver enzyme ALT and lipids, would point to meaningful cost savings.

Calibrate data from separate evaluations show substantial improvements in these markers among Calibrate members.

“Among Calibrate members who started the program with diabetes or prediabetes, 80% reached normoglycemic status at one year. Among those with abnormal ALT, 79% shifted to the normal range, and 68% of those with abnormal triglycerides were normal at year one," she said.

Withings' body composition data builds on Calibrate's prior data and gives the company another lens on the whole picture, "suggesting that lower healthcare spend is likely,” Anegawa said.

Greater treatment persistence could also ultimately reduce costs. An integrated approach helps keep members engaged so they stick with treatment and get the full benefit of therapy, she noted.

Along with weight loss and metabolic improvements, Calibrate members also report compelling health and productivity outcomes, Anegawa said. Among members with a high work-related burden at intake, 82% no longer reported it at one year.

“My favorite evidence of all is that 90% report that Calibrate improved their overall quality of life, and 94% say that their health is better than a year ago - the most clinically meaningful to me overall,” she said.

#5599. Peanut Peptide Injections Promising for Allergy Immunotherapy

— A novel route to immunotherapy for peanut allergy passes phase II test

A novel peptide-based immunotherapy for peanut allergy appeared safe and modestly efficacious for reducing children's symptoms over the first 12 months, a phase II trial showed.

For the primary efficacy endpoint, the higher of two monthly PVX108 shot dosages significantly boosted the maximum tolerated dose of peanut from baseline to month 12 by 2.4-fold, compared with a 1.2-fold change in the placebo group, reported Brian P. Vickery, MD, of Emory University and chief of the Division of Allergy/Immunology at Children's Healthcare of Atlanta, at the American College of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology annual meeting.

In terms of safety, there were no cases of anaphylaxis or other treatment-related allergic or severe adverse events with the shot. Only six of the 71 trial participants reported any adverse event (13% with the higher dose tested), largely local administration site reactions.

At an oral food challenge at 1 year, 39% of patients on the higher dose tolerated at least 300 mg of peanut protein compared with 17% in the placebo group (the equivalent of one peanut). "This is more than double, on average, what causes accidental reactions in the field when people are exposed accidentally while they're trying to avoid peanut. And it's been shown in previous work that ... is probably clinically meaningful for most patients with peanut allergy," Vickery said. But he acknowledged it "is probably less than what you'd expect in a study of oral immunotherapy, where the participants are swallowing about 300 mg of protein daily as part of their treatment."

While efficacy needs to be confirmed in a larger trial, "there's also a big safety difference and a difference in burden in terms of daily versus monthly therapy," he added, pointing to adverse events in most immunotherapy patients with other routes of administration and anaphylaxis in 10-15% of trial participants in some studies.

Immunotherapy shots offer an advantage of fewer office visits than the typically once-every-2-week schedule for oral immunotherapy up-dosing and also not requiring kids to consume peanut products daily, commented Jay Lieberman, MD, of the University of Tennessee Health Science Center in Memphis. With peanut protein, though, "you can't do it the same way we do allergy shots to cat or oak tree pollen, because it is too dangerous. It caused too many reactions," he said.

PVX108 comprises seven short peptides representing immunodominant T-cell epitopes of major peanut allergens rather than intact peanut proteins that interact with the immune system and can lead to reactions. "This is designed to get around that problem by formulating fragments of peanut proteins that are too small to interact with IgE [immunoglobulin E] and the allergic components of the immune system and instead interact directly with T cells, which are thought to be kind of the driving force behind the allergy," Vickery said.

"We have made some progress in being able to treat peanut allergy with oral immunotherapy and now FDA-approved omalizumab [Xolair] as the two most commonly used options," Vickery said in an interview monitored by media relations for drug developer Aravax. "But there are millions of patients out there with peanut allergy, and most of them are not being treated due to limitations in care and also limitations in access to these treatments and because of limitations in the treatments themselves."

"The scientific community believes that there is plenty of room for new forms of immunotherapy to be developed," he added, "because we don't think of peanut allergy as a one-size-fits-all condition where one treatment will solve the problem."

While the only FDA-approved peanut oral immunotherapy product recently left the market as clinicians rely on off-the-shelf commercial products, Lieberman agreed that PVX108 could find a place: "Bringing an [oral immunotherapy] FDA-approved thing to the market when people are already just using PB2 powder [commercially available peanut flour], that was the problem."

The trial included 71 peanut allergy patients ages 4 to 11 years at 14 trial sites in the U.S. and Australia in the primary efficacy and safety cohort. They were randomized to double-blind treatment with 5-nmol or 50-nmol PVX108 or placebo given monthly by intradermal administration over 12 months. At the end of that period, a double-blind placebo-controlled food challenge was done following the PRACTALL guidelines.

After 6 months off treatment, a follow-up food challenge was conducted at month 18. It showed evidence of maintenance or improvement in clinical effects compared with month 12, indicating disease-modifying potential, Vickery said, although this needs further confirmation.

The optimal length of treatment isn't clear yet, but immunotherapy shots for other allergens typically take 3 to 5 years of treatment, Vickery noted. "So it's likely that longer-term treatment might be necessary or even might be more optimal."

#5597. Trials Raise Questions About Perioperative Immunotherapy in Bladder Cancer

— Experts weigh negative KEYNOTE-866 and ENERGIZE findings against positive NIAGARA trial

In this exclusive roundtable video from MedPage Today, three expert leaders in the field of bladder cancer discuss the latest research presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) congress.

Moderator Matthew Galsky, MD, of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City, is joined by David Aggen, MD, PhD, of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York City, and Stephanie Berg, DO, of the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston.

In this second of four episodes, they examine the disappointing results from the KEYNOTE-866 and ENERGIZE trials, how those findings compare with the positive NIAGARA trial, and what they mean for perioperative treatment decisions in muscle-invasive bladder cancer.

Click here to watch all episodes of this roundtable series.

Following is a transcript of their remarks:

Galsky: Okay, so let's talk a little bit about the next set of studies. And we saw two studies at ESMO, really along the same theme, and that is should we add immune checkpoint blockade to cisplatin-based therapy for cisplatin-eligible patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer? We saw the results from KEYNOTE-866 and the ENERGIZE study, and I might add the long-awaited results from both of those studies. Previously, we saw the results of a similarly designed study called NIAGARA, which showed an improvement in essentially every endpoint, path CR [pathologic complete response] rate, event-free survival [EFS], and overall survival [OS].

But these studies were disappointing. There were some improvements in path CR rate versus the control arm. However, there was not an improvement in the time-to-event outcomes. And that raises some questions about cisplatin-based chemotherapy plus immune checkpoint blockade in the perioperative setting.

And now we have data with these different regimens that are mixing and matching components, so it's harder to say that it's just the class of IO [immunotherapy], PD-1 or PD-L1 blockade, or it's harder to say that it's the duration of treatment because duration of treatments were pretty similar. So, Dr. Berg, what do you make of these studies?

Berg: I agree. I kind of forgot they were around until when they were presented at ESMO. And I think ENERGIZE was really interesting because I didn't really know a lot about that compound. But in the end, they both were kind of negative and really aren't going to change practice in my mind.

But I think it was something where we saw, like you mentioned, some path CR gains, but it's also with the design of the studies and what's going to actually happen in current practice compared to what we were just discussing within ADC [antibody-drug conjugate] and IO. I'm not sure they're not going to really change practice, but it was something that, again, they were finally out and we are definitely abandoning cisplatin chemo.

Galsky: So these studies might not change practice themselves, as you point out, but there is another study that showed benefit with this type of approach, which is NIAGARA. And that really makes one wonder if all three studies were presented at the same time, whether or not the general interpretation of the studies would be different than having the positive study come out first and well before the others.

So, Dr. Aggen, what do these studies tell you in terms of how to interpret NIAGARA in retrospect?

Aggen: I think you can't compare because these trials sort of happen in different eras. Perhaps in the control arm of the more contemporary studies like ENERGIZE, there was more use of adjuvant IO that may have narrowed the difference. It's also quite striking in ENERGIZE, it enrolled a very high percentage of patients who had clinical T2 disease. And so maybe it was a slightly lower-risk population as well.

I think the question though is sort of obsolete given the striking results from KEYNOTE-905, KEYNOTE-B15, and now VOLGA that say that you should probably be giving ADC-IO to patients. I think that there may be a small subgroup with either variant histologies or other tumor features that needs durvalumab [Imfinzi] in combination with cisplatin. We don't really have the granularity of who that is.

And so at the moment I still think ADC-IO is our backbone of perioperative therapy. It is an interesting academic question though that you have two phase III trials with chemo-IO that show perhaps higher path CR rates than NIAGARA, but not the same benefit in terms of EFS and OS. And I don't think we're going to get crystal answers as to why those differences exist.

Galsky: So, Dr. Berg, Monday morning, any patient walking in the door who is going to be an appropriate candidate for cisplatin-based chemotherapy plus immune checkpoint blockade versus EV [enfortumab vedotin (Padcev)] plus immune checkpoint blockade?

Berg: I do agree with Dr. Aggen. I think the non-bladder or non-urothelial histology, perhaps even upper tract urethra, since they weren't enrolled on these studies, you would really discuss about cisplatin perioperative therapy. Even though those other studies too with variant histology, we normally go right to cystectomy.

But again, we can consider a perioperative therapy for them and I think it's still appropriate and active in those subsets, but I think more is going to come out with ADC and the non-urothelial histology. So there's some work being done in that center, but I think that's what I would use right now. I would still consider it pretty appropriate.

#5596. Einstein's equations reveal how gravity could break, reconnect, and release energy

More than 100 years after Albert Einstein developed his theory of gravity, physicists have uncovered a surprising possibility hidden within his equations. Their work suggests that gravitational fields can undergo a process in which their underlying structures break and reconnect, allowing energy to flow from gravity into matter.

The phenomenon, known as "gravitational reconnection," bears an unexpected resemblance to a process responsible for some of the Sun's most powerful eruptions. Researchers believe this connection could provide new insights into how gravity behaves under extreme conditions, including during collisions between black holes.

The discovery comes from Luca Comisso, an associate research scientist in Columbia University's Departments of Astronomy and Physics and the Columbia Astrophysics Laboratory, and Felipe A. Asenjo of Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez in Chile. By examining Einstein's equations from a different mathematical perspective, they identified a remarkable similarity between gravity and the behavior of electrically charged gases known as plasmas.

Their approach could help scientists uncover fundamental rules governing the behavior of gravitational fields. Such insights are especially valuable in regions where gravity severely distorts space-time, making even the most powerful computer simulations difficult to interpret.

How Gravity Could Behave Like a Solar Flare

The key to understanding this discovery lies in a well-known phenomenon called magnetic reconnection. Magnetic fields are often illustrated using curved lines, such as the patterns formed by iron filings around a magnet or the enormous magnetic loops extending above the Sun's surface.

In a plasma, which consists of electrically charged particles, these magnetic field lines can be pulled, twisted, and stretched. Under certain conditions, they undergo a sudden change in their connections, releasing stored magnetic energy into the surrounding particles. This process powers solar flares and ranks among the most important mechanisms for releasing energy throughout the universe.

"Magnetic reconnection is when these field lines, in some specific configuration, break and reattach in a different configuration," Comisso said. "When they break and reconnect, they release energy."

The resulting energy transfer can produce extraordinarily powerful events. As Comisso explained, "It takes energy from the magnetic field and gives it to the particles in the plasma, producing explosions, energetic events."

The researchers found that gravitational fields may undergo an analogous transformation. However, gravity operates within Einstein's four-dimensional space-time, which includes three dimensions of space and one dimension of time. This makes its underlying mathematical structure different from that of an ordinary magnetic field.

Gravitational Reconnection and the Fabric of Space-Time

"Because space-time is four-dimensional rather than three-dimensional, gravity involves something like field 'sheets' rather than field lines," explained Comisso. "Adding one dimension to a line gives you a plane. You can think of it as putting many lines together to form a 'sheet.'"

In this mathematical description, gravity is represented by sheets rather than individual field lines. Just as magnetic field lines can change their connections and release energy, these gravitational sheets can also rearrange their connections under the appropriate conditions.

Importantly, the sheets are mathematical representations, not physical surfaces that literally tear apart. Their reconnection describes a way for the gravitational field to transfer energy into matter.

The researchers arrived at this result by exploring properties of Einstein's equations that are not obvious in their usual mathematical form. Their work builds on an earlier investigation that revealed previously unrecognized restrictions on how space-time can bend, stretch, and change over time.

The new study, titled "Reconnection of Gravitational Fields," was published in Physical Review D, a journal of the American Physical Society. It extends findings from an earlier study published in Physical Review Letters by Comisso, Asenjo, and Maricarmen A. Winkler.

That earlier work identified mathematical constraints that determine which changes in the geometry of space-time are possible. Although these restrictions are built into Einstein's theory, they had not previously been recognized in this form.

"Einstein's equations contain constraints on how space-time can evolve that are not immediately apparent," said Asenjo. "By revealing these hidden new properties, we can begin to understand the fundamental rules governing how this gravitational reconnection process behaves."

In their latest research, Comisso and Asenjo investigated what happens when the ideal conditions that normally preserve connections within gravitational field structures no longer hold. They found that those connections can change, producing the phenomenon they call gravitational reconnection.

"Some implications are hidden in the equations, and they are not straightforward to capture just by looking at them," Comisso said. "You need to rewrite them in a different way, and then you can exploit that behavior."

Why Plasma Physics Offers New Clues About Gravity

The breakthrough depends on a different mathematical formulation of Einstein's equations developed by physicists in recent years. Although this formulation uses different variables, it is mathematically equivalent to the original equations and describes the same underlying physics.

What makes it particularly useful is its resemblance to equations used to study plasmas. These electrically charged gases make up the Sun, are used in nuclear fusion experiments, and occupy much of the space between stars.

Comisso has devoted his career to understanding plasma behavior. When he and his colleagues recognized the mathematical similarities between plasma physics and gravity, they realized that methods developed to study magnetic fields could also reveal previously overlooked properties of gravitational fields.

This approach allows physicists to identify patterns and restrictions governing space-time without necessarily solving every part of Einstein's equations.

"It helps us predict some patterns of the space-time," Comisso said. "Even without doing the full calculation, we know that space-time needs to behave in a certain way, that it needs to satisfy those constraints."

Rather than relying entirely on complex numerical calculations, researchers can use these underlying rules to determine which behaviors are physically possible. This could provide a valuable new perspective on gravitational events that are exceptionally difficult to model.

What Gravitational Reconnection Could Mean for Black Holes

One of the most promising applications involves black hole collisions. When two black holes approach and merge, their immense gravitational fields produce extreme distortions in space-time.

To understand these events, astrophysicists typically rely on massive supercomputer simulations. Researchers specify the initial conditions, calculate how the system changes over time, and examine the resulting behavior.

These simulations help scientists predict the gravitational waves generated by merging black holes. Gravitational waves are ripples in space-time that can be detected by instruments such as the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO), which is designed to measure the extraordinarily small distortions produced by powerful cosmic events.

The newly identified rules governing gravitational fields could complement these simulations by revealing patterns that might otherwise be difficult to recognize. They may also help researchers better understand how energy is transferred during some of the universe's most extreme gravitational interactions.

For now, gravitational reconnection remains a theoretical finding. Scientists have not yet established how the process operates in actual astrophysical environments or whether its effects can be observed.

The next step is to investigate gravitational reconnection in specific situations, particularly when black holes merge. Comisso hopes this research will eventually make it possible to estimate how much energy such events release and determine whether gravitational reconnection produces recognizable signatures in gravitational wave signals.

If those predictions can be developed and tested, the approach could offer a powerful new way to investigate the behavior of gravity under extreme conditions, revealing more of the physics concealed within Einstein's century-old equations.

The research received support from the National Science Foundation and NASA.

#5595. Are There Any V12 Engines That Could Be Called 'Dependable?'

A V12 engine under the bonnet is a symbol of automotive decadence, telling the world that you've made it and who cares about fuel consumption. Sure, there are plenty of engines that deliver as much performance, but few that exude extravagance and luxury in quite the same way. Still, can V12s be dependable? You might assume not, given their specialized nature and low-volume production.

V12s are installed in high-end sedans and limousines, in mid-engined supercars, and in a handful of opulent SUVs and 4x4s. But they're not that numerous in the grand scheme of production vehicles.

One of the first uses of the V12 came in 1913, when, in the UK, Louis Coatalen, the chief engineer of Sunbeam Motor Car Company, stuffed a new type of aircraft engine called the Mohawk into one of the company's race cars. Subsequently, "Toodles V" was born: a machine which, after a few hiccups, went on to set eight world speed-over-distance records at Brooklands racetrack.

After Toodles and before WWII, V12s grew in popularity for their smoothness and power, with the North American auto industry providing the bulk of them, even during the Great Depression of 1929: think Packard Twin Six, the Auburn 12, the Cadillac V-12, and the Lincoln series K.

But when Lincoln ceased production of the V12 in 1948, that was that for American V12s. No car company has made one in the U.S. since, and production was mainly left to Europe. Ferrari made its legendary "Colombo" V12, Lamborghini's 1963 V12 would eventually underpin the gorgeous Miura, and even Jaguar brought a 5.3-liter V12 engine to the E-Type in 1971.

There are still a few V12s in production today that you can buy with a new-car warranty, which are likely reliable, but what about those of yesteryear? Here's a look at the most dependable.

If you're after a V12 that's about as widespread and dependable as can be, then the Mercedes M120 is the one to seek out. Mercedes had been working on the idea of a passenger car with a V12 since the 1950s (and considered putting one in its 600 Pullman limo), but it was beaten to the punch by BMW's adoption of the 5.0-liter V12 in 1987's E32 750i. Mercedes didn't get its M120 V12 to market until 1991 in the W140-series S-Class. The 600 badge was given to the W140-series S-Class, the related CL coupe, and the R129 Mercedes SL due to the engine's displacement.

The M120 was a considerably more advanced engine than BMW's V12. It featured an aluminum-alloy block, a forged crankshaft, and LH-Jetronic fuel injection, along with dual throttle bodies, mass airflow sensors, and ECUs. Producing 402 horsepower and 428 pounds-feet of torque, the M120 had enough grunt to push the heavy 600 SE and SEL models from 0 to 60 mph in around six seconds.

What makes the M120 so desirable today, though, is its dependability. There are a few known weak points, such as oil leaks around the valve covers, the front timing covers, the lower oil pan, and the front crank seal, along with worn engine mounts. But aside from these relatively minor issues, this V12 is known for its reliability and solidity. Furthermore, owners of such high-end Mercs are likely to have kept up with their maintenance.

One final seal of approval comes in the form of the M120's subsequent use in the middle of the Pagani Zonda, a supercar classic we'll always love: a 7.3-liter development of the V12 powered various iterations, culminating in a near-800-hp final edition.

Japan is a country that has not wholeheartedly embraced the V12 engine. In fact, it has made but one road-going engine of this configuration in history, although it turns out to be one of the most reliable V12s you could imagine. It's called the 1GZ-FE, a naturally aspirated 5.0-liter lump with variable valve timing, two ECUs, and enough redundancy built in that it can run on one bank of six cylinders if necessary. The engine powered the second-generation Toyota Century.

A big plus point of the 1GZ is that it's not what you'd call a stressed V12. In its original 1997 incarnation for the Century model, the Japanese "gentleman's agreement" put in place to prevent a horsepower war meant that Toyota claimed a peak power output of just 276 horsepower, with torque rated at up to 355 pounds-feet. It was never going to be one of the most powerful JDM engines ever made, even if its horsepower was higher than the domestic advertising suggested.

If that's not a big enough perk, know that like so many Toyota engines, the 1GZ-FE would accommodate a heck of a lot of tuning. In fact, the notorious Smokey Nagata – founder of Top Secret and the man who pushed a Supra to 194 mph on a British motorway in 1998 – later built another Supra with a Century's V12 in it. Only that was adorned with a pair of HKS GT2540 turbos, liberating 930 hp and a top speed of over 220 mph.

When the engine was launched, Toyota published an engineering paper stating, amongst other things, that the 1GZ-FE was more reliable than its competitors, and though the sample size is small, it has been proven to be a dependable V12, with nothing other than age-related failures of minor parts generally reported.

The original BMW V12, the M70, started an entire line of engines that went into the 7 Series as well as the 8 Series. BMW's M70 successor, the M73, was employed by Rolls-Royce starting in 1998 with the Silver Seraph. Rolls began using a V12 in its Phantom III (1936-1939), but after trying that 7.3-liter monster out for size, it eventually dedicated itself to inline-6 and V8 engines. Rolls-Royce did not use a V12 again until the 1998 Silver Seraph.

Perhaps the most famous application of a BMW V12 was the S70/2, designed by Paul Rosche, which was the incredible engine that powered the legendary McLaren F1 with 627 horsepower. Though maintenance costs are high, the engine itself is robust.

Both Ferrari and Lamborghini's V12s are highly tuned, and of course, they're installed in the sorts of cars that command huge fees on the used market. Nonetheless, the 5.5-liter engine in the Ferrari 456 GT, for example, is supposed to be fairly dependable, as long as it is subjected to regular (and expensive) maintenance.

Aston Martin has been making production V12s since the DB7 Vantage of 1999, and while these "AML" units were not just two Ford Duratec V6s welded together, there was plenty of Ford-derived DNA in the British engine courtesy of Ford's advanced powertrain division. It's generally dependable, so long as owners keep up with maintenance. Oil starvation to the crankshaft is one of the more common issues.

Finally, Jaguar had a good array of V12s in such cars as the E-Type and XJ models. While the mechanicals are reasonably durable, these engines are frequently let down by their electrics.

HLTH 2026: Suki unveils agentic OS to automate complex healthcare workflows" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Ambient clinical intelligence platform Suki announced Monday the launch of an agentic operating system designed to connect fragmented healthcare technology.

The operating system—dubbed Suki OS—is built on three core pillars, the company says: a partner ecosystem, unified artificial intelligence agents and a performance guarantee. It plans to expand the capabilities beyond its Suki for Clinicians platform over time.

Suki is introducing two initial AI agent initiatives as part of its goal to reduce administrative work.

Suki Prior Authorization will streamline the process by identifying requirements and gathering supporting clinical documentation. Its Clinical Documentation Improvement (CDI) Agent will focus on identifying documentation gaps, improving accuracy and supporting downstream coding and revenue cycle workflows.

Additional agents are planned across clinical, operational and financial workflows as part of the company’s broader strategy to develop agents that can execute complex workflows with human oversight.

Suki’s Partner Ecosystem is comprised of its Insight Partners, which integrate intelligence with Suki patient context, and Platform Partners, which let health tech companies embed Suki’s AI directly into their products.

The Suki Guarantee offers eligible customers up to a 100% refund if agreed-upon performance targets aren't met, the company says.

Suki CEO and Founder Punit Soni told Fierce Healthcare that healthcare has an "execution problem" rather than an AI shortage.

"We've spent years building technology that can understand clinical conversations, but understanding is only the beginning," Soni said. "The real opportunity is to turn that intelligence into action, connecting the systems, people and workflows that make healthcare run."

That’s the motivation behind Suki OS, according to Soni.

"Nearly a decade ago, we pioneered ambient AI, and today, our technology is trusted by more than 450 healthcare organizations, with independently validated clinical and financial outcomes," Soni said. "We've built deep clinical intelligence, integrations across EHRs, and an expansive partner ecosystem. That foundation uniquely positions Suki to move beyond documentation and help automate the complex work that surrounds patient care."

Soni said that the next generation of AI tools have to "do more than save time" as health systems face mounting financial pressures and workforce constraints. "It has to deliver meaningful clinical and financial outcomes," he said.

Soni continued, "Ultimately, the measure of AI's success won't be how many agents we build. It will be how much complexity we remove from healthcare, how much time we give back to clinicians and their patients, and how much measurable financial value we create for the organizations delivering care."

In October, the company secured $90 million in series E funding to accelerate its growth and continue expanding its AI capabilities.

The company has raised more than $250 million to date, executives say. Patient encounters supported by its tools grew more than 190% year over year in 2026, with revenue doubling in 2025 and on track for similar growth this year.

#5592. Slate Sells 'Screenless GPS' For Its Trucks, Which Is Just A Map

Slate, maker of the barebones $26,400 electric truck that I desperately want to see succeed despite my worries about its competition, is all about simplicity. Simple truck, simple purchase price, simple construction, simple accessories. So what happens when buyers want something more complex — something like GPS, which requires satellite connections, maps, screens, and code? Well, the company does it the old fashioned way by stamping its brand on a Rand McNally Road Atlas and selling it as "Screenless GPS."

The automaker is selling these atlases for $30, and on the website it's currently marked as sold out. The product description reads, "This is the original navigation system — no signal required. Spiral bound, large print, and ready for wherever your Slate takes you. Covers the US, Canada, and Mexico. Limited edition." This particular book is the 2027 Rand McNally EasyFinder Road Atlas, and it includes "7 curated Rand McNally road trips."

Rand McNally, for the younger readers out there, makes books of maps that it calls its road atlases. I grew up with a road atlas wedged between the driver's seat and center console of my mom's car, and I certainly remember thumbing through its pages while bored — behavior my mom encouraged, so I'd know how to read a map by the time I started driving myself. It's certainly a skill the average Slate buyer has, and maybe the folks that appreciate a simple truck will likewise appreciate a simple way to navigate it around.

Paper maps have had a bit of a renaissance as we all get ever more tired of our constantly-increasing screentime. Backcountry Discovery Routes has worked with Butler Maps for years to create paper maps of its BDR routes for those looking to go screenless on the trails, and it seems Slate is hoping to bring the same enthusiasm to road maps with its Rand McNally tie-in. I'm just hoping the promotion Slate is doing for its map, like the Instagram post above, is all tongue in cheek. If the company really means "analog pinch to zoom" is a feature, it comes off a bit I HATE WIFE AND PHOEN.

For most of us, a phone mount suction-cupped to the windshield will make a better navigation solution than a Rand McNally shoved next to the center console. For Slate's target market, buyers who actively miss simpler, older cars and want a return to that kind of design, the bent and worn pages of a worn Road Atlas may provide a bit of the nostalgia they're looking for in an all-electric truck. After all, they probably had one in their old Ranger all those years ago.

#5591. A simple supplement may help clear brain fog after cancer

For some breast cancer survivors, the effects of treatment can linger long after their cancer care ends. Memory lapses, difficulty concentrating, and persistent exhaustion can interfere with everyday life, sometimes for years. Now, researchers at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center have found promising early evidence that a supplement containing a naturally occurring molecule could help relieve these symptoms.

The molecule, called oxaloacetate, is already present in the human body and plays an important role in how cells generate energy. In a small clinical trial, breast cancer survivors who took the supplement for eight weeks reported noticeable improvements in thinking, memory, concentration, and fatigue.

The results, published in JCO Oncology Advances, also showed improvements on cognitive tests measuring how quickly participants processed information and performed tasks requiring planning, attention, and mental flexibility. Although larger studies are needed to confirm the findings, the results suggest a potentially new way to address a problem that has long been difficult to treat.

"Cancer-related cognitive impairment can persist long after treatment ends and can have a significant impact on a person's daily life, yet we still have very few effective treatments for it," said Dr. Patricia Ganz, the study's first author and a distinguished professor of medicine at UCLA's David Geffen School of Medicine and UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.

Why Brain Fog Can Persist After Cancer Treatment

Cognitive difficulties are a lasting concern for many people who survive breast cancer. Researchers estimate that roughly 15% to 25% experience ongoing problems with memory, concentration, or other thinking abilities after their diagnosis and treatment. These symptoms are often described as "chemo brain" or "brain fog."

Despite the name, chemotherapy is not necessarily the only cause. Scientists increasingly recognize that cancer-related cognitive impairment can develop through several overlapping processes. The cancer itself, chemotherapy, endocrine therapy, inflammation, hormonal changes, and other biological and behavioral influences may all contribute.

Because the causes are complicated and effective treatments remain limited, researchers are investigating ways to address the underlying changes that may disrupt normal brain function.

One area of interest involves the relationship between inflammation, brain chemistry, and energy production. Inflammation linked to cancer and its treatments may interfere with glutamate signaling, an important part of communication between nerve cells. It may also disturb the processes that allow brain cells to produce and use energy efficiently. Together, these disruptions could contribute to difficulties with thinking and persistent mental exhaustion.

Oxaloacetate attracted the UCLA team's attention because it participates in both cellular energy production and the regulation of glutamate. The researchers wanted to learn whether providing additional oxaloacetate through a supplement might reduce the cognitive symptoms and fatigue experienced by cancer survivors.

Testing Oxaloacetate for Brain Fog and Fatigue

To investigate, the researchers carried out a phase II clinical trial involving 18 women who had been diagnosed with early-stage breast cancer between one and five years earlier. All participants were experiencing substantial cognitive difficulties when they entered the study.

The women were approximately 50 years old on average. Most had undergone chemotherapy, and nearly 90% were still receiving endocrine therapy during the trial.

Each participant was instructed to take 500 milligrams of oxaloacetate twice a day for eight weeks. The researchers tracked changes in cognitive symptoms using questionnaires completed by the participants, along with standardized tests designed to evaluate memory, attention, processing speed, and executive function. Executive function includes the mental abilities needed to organize activities, maintain focus, make plans, and manage tasks.

The study also examined fatigue, sleep, anxiety, depression, physical health, and mental well-being. Throughout the treatment period, the team monitored participants for possible side effects.

Brain Fog Scores Improved After Eight Weeks

Of the 18 women enrolled, 16 completed the full eight weeks of supplementation. Every participant who finished the treatment reported significant improvement in her cognitive symptoms.

The changes were particularly striking on the study's main measure of perceived cognitive impairment. Before treatment, the participants had an average score of 29.1. After eight weeks, that average had climbed to 55.5, placing the group in the range considered normal rather than impaired.

Signs of improvement were already apparent after four weeks, and the benefits reported by participants generally became more pronounced as treatment continued.

The results extended beyond memory and concentration. Participants reported significantly less fatigue, including the mental exhaustion that can make everyday activities difficult. They also described meaningful improvements in their ability to function physically.

Standardized cognitive testing provided additional encouraging evidence. Researchers observed improvements in processing speed and executive function, suggesting that some aspects of thinking performance may have improved alongside the participants' perceptions of their symptoms.

However, the scientists emphasized that these results remain preliminary because the trial included so few participants.

Promising Results, but More Research Is Needed

Oxaloacetate was generally well tolerated during the eight-week study. The most frequently reported side effects involved the digestive system, including indigestion, bloating, constipation, diarrhea, and nausea.

Two women stopped taking the supplement because of gastrointestinal symptoms. No serious adverse events were recorded.

Despite the encouraging improvements, the researchers cautioned against drawing firm conclusions about the supplement's effectiveness. The trial was small and did not include a placebo group or another comparison group. Without that comparison, it is not possible to determine whether oxaloacetate itself caused the improvements.

"These early findings give us a strong reason to continue studying oxaloacetate as a potential approach for managing cognitive problems after breast cancer treatment," Ganz said.

Larger Clinical Trial Will Test the Supplement's Benefits

To build on these initial findings, the UCLA team has been preparing a randomized, placebo-controlled phase II clinical trial involving breast cancer survivors with cancer-related cognitive impairment. The study was expected to begin enrolling participants in late 2026.

By comparing oxaloacetate with a placebo, the researchers hope to establish whether the supplement produces measurable benefits beyond those that might occur without active treatment.

The investigators are also conducting preclinical research in mice to better understand how oxaloacetate affects the body and brain. These experiments include a placebo-controlled study examining whether the molecule produces similar improvements (improved fatigue and physical function) in animals.

The research received partial financial support from the Breast Cancer Research Foundation and the National Cancer Institute.

In addition to Ganz, the study's authors were Kathleen Van Dyk, PhD, Catherine M. Crespi, PhD, Laura Petersen, MS, Mina Sedrak, MD, MS, and Julienne Bower, PhD, all affiliated with UCLA.

#5590. Measles update: US loses measles elimination status; more deaths reported

Measles update: US loses measles elimination status; more deaths reported" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The United States has lost its measles elimination status, and has now exceeded 5,400 cases and 10 total measles-associated deaths in 2026.

The status determination from the Pan American Health Organization, which is part of the World Health Organization, was made late last week and first reported by the Wall Street Journal before being confirmed by other outlets. (Editor's note: The public health body made its official announcement on Nov. 17)

The U.S. had notched elimination status, reflecting no continuous spread of the disease for at least 12 months, in 2000. Regaining it similarly requires the country to stop continuous spread for 12 months. PAHO recommends countries that have lost elimination status submit and enact a corrective action plan that includes immunization and surveillance.

The decision landed shortly after the country hit 5,412 confirmed measles cases, per a Nov. 13 update from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The federal public health body also lists 591 hospitalizations (11% rate) and six deaths—though it has been hesitant to outright confirm states' reports of measles-associated deaths, of which there have now been 10.

Health groups and public health professionals have pointed to lagging vaccination rates and checked endorsement of routine childhood vaccines from current leadership at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, namely Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., as fueling the country's outbreaks.

The Wisconsin Department of Health Services on Thursday reported its first measles-outbreak associated death since 1990.

The deceased was an infant whose case was among many in the southwestern part of the state, for whom the coroner listed measles as immediate cause of death. As of Nov. 3, the department has reported 431 cases across 13 counties in 2026, the highest number of cases in over 35 years. All but three of those are among individuals who were not vaccinated, and nine have involved hospitalizations.

"Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease," Kirsten Johnson, secretary of the Wisconsin Department of Health Services, said in the announcement. "Measles can cause serious illness and death, and it is important for all Wisconsinites to evaluate their risk and take steps to protect themselves and their family."

As of Oct. 29, the Centers for Disease Control reports 4,852 confirmed cases of measles this year across the country, far outpacing 2025's total of 2,289. Of these, 511 have been hospitalized (versus 244 in 2025) and three deaths have been recognized—though health officials in Pennsylvania alone said they have confirmed five measles-associated deaths. The CDC has said its death count may change after it completes work to develop a new standardized case definition for "deaths due to measles."

The New York State Department of Health on Monday afternoon reported its first measles-associated death in 30 years.

The state has counted 210 total cases this year as of Nov. 3. The reported death was a child in the northern Lewis County, according to the department. No information was given about the child's specific illness or the role measles infection may have played in their death.

Sixteen confirmed cases of measles have been reported in Lewis County as of Tuesday, the department said. Many of New York's cases are located among upstate counties, and just eight are in New York City, according to the department.

In a statement, New York Governor Kathy Hochul—who on Oct. 5 declared a Disaster Emergency in response to rising measles case rates—expressed her sympathies to the child's family and told residents that "vaccination remains our best protection against this dangerous disease."

"This is New York’s first measles-related death in 30 years, a devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses," the statement reads, echoing criticisms of federal health leadership voiced by Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro regarding measles-associated deaths in his own state.

As of Oct. 29, the Centers for Disease Control reports 4,852 confirmed cases of measles this year across the country, far outpacing 2025's total of 2,289. Of these, 511 have been hospitalized (versus 244 in 2025) and three deaths have been recognized—though health officials in Pennsylvania alone said they have confirmed five measles-associated deaths. The CDC has said its death count may change after it completes work to develop a new standardized case definition for "deaths due to measles."

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services told Fierce Healthcare that it had deployed epidemiologists and other experts to New York after receiving a formal request for support. The support is currently scheduled to run through Nov. 13, and includes on-the-ground "surveillance, data analysis, strategic planning and other outbreak response support," they said.

Of the roughly $100 million in additional measles and vaccine-preventable diseases funding the department has provided via the CDC since August, nearly $2.4 million has gone directly to New York State and $2.1 million to New York City, they said.

"Secretary Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz continue to make clear that the MMR vaccine is the most effective way to prevent measles," they added.

The U.S. is in the midst of its worst measles outbreak in decades, with more than 4,000 cases reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention as of early October and a sixth measles-associated death disclosed by local Pennsylvania officials on Monday.

The vaccine-preventable disease was declared eliminated in the U.S. back in 2000—meaning that there was no endemic spread of the disease—but has resurfaced in force during recent years as declining childhood vaccination rates have pushed most states below the 95% coverage bar for school-age herd immunity.

The CDC had counted 2,289 cases across the entirety of 2025, which had been the country’s highest total since 1990, and several public health officials have warned for months that number would likely be surpassed based on the scale and frequency of early-year cases.

Measles-associated deaths have also accompanied the higher case counts, though just how many is a subject of dispute. While three deaths were confirmed in all of 2025, this year logged its first in late August with Pennsylvania, which hosts more than a quarter of the total cases, now reporting six measles-associated deaths as of Oct. 13. The CDC, however, lists two deaths alongside a note that its count is subject to change, and has promised more broadly to develop a new, standardized case definition to be used across all reporting states.

That discrepancy is an example of friction between federal health leadership and the broader public health community that experts say has contributed to this year’s outbreaks.

Pennsylvania’s initial death announcements in August were contested by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who accused Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro of withholding sufficient information for the CDC to confirm the deaths and using his press conference announcing them as “gaslighting the public” for political purposes.

During an ensuing social media feud, the governor and the secretary described a heated phone call in which Shapiro (at the time) rejected federal assistance and accused Kennedy of fueling the outbreaks with only lukewarm endorsement of the MMR vaccine and a broader concurrent campaign to scale back other routine childhood vaccinations.

Numerous state public health officials and experts have lobbed similar criticisms of Kennedy, who is affiliated with anti-vaccine groups, and federal health agencies under his purview.

The CDC, for its part, has reportedly infused at least $100 million of extra public health funding to states for immunization programs and surveillance, and leading officials including Kennedy and new CDC Director Erica Schwartz, M.D., have described the MMR vaccine as safe and effective when asked directly. Still, the agency has not launched the type of broader vaccine messaging and awareness campaigns that it would have in years past, critics are quick to note.

Pennsylvania isn’t alone in raising alarms over rising measles cases. New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a State Disaster Emergency in early October, the first such declaration in recent years.
