#5575. A 24-hour fast triggers a surprising repair response in the gut

A 24-hour fast may help prepare the intestines to recover from radiation damage, but scientists have discovered that a particular gut bacterium plays a crucial role in making this possible. New preclinical research from The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center reveals how fasting and beneficial microbes work together to activate the body's natural tissue repair mechanisms.

The findings could eventually lead to new ways to protect healthy tissue during cancer treatment. By improving the intestine's ability to recover from radiation exposure, researchers hope to reduce serious side effects and potentially make radiation therapy safer and more effective.

Published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the study was co-led by Helen Piwnica-Worms, Ph.D., professor of Experimental Radiation Oncology, and Kunal Rai, Ph.D., professor of Genomic Medicine.

"Fasting helps prepare intestinal cells to respond more quickly and effectively after injury, almost like training the cells with an emergency preparedness plan," Piwnica-Worms said. "This study helps explain how that plan is organized and identifies a key bacterium involved in coordinating the response."

Why Radiation Therapy Can Damage the Intestines

Radiation therapy is widely used to treat cancers in the abdomen, including pancreatic, colorectal, and gynecologic cancers. Although radiation can destroy cancer cells, it can also harm nearby healthy tissue. The small intestine is particularly vulnerable because its delicate lining is highly sensitive to radiation exposure.

When this protective lining becomes damaged, patients may experience nausea, diarrhea, and infections. Severe injuries can cause life-threatening complications. These risks can also restrict the amount of radiation doctors can safely administer, potentially limiting treatment options.

Previous preclinical research from the Piwnica-Worms Laboratory showed that fasting before radiation exposure helped the intestines recover afterward. However, researchers had not fully determined why going without food produced this protective effect.

The latest study provides an important piece of that puzzle by identifying a specific gut bacterium and explaining how it helps intestinal cells prepare for injury.

Researchers found that 24 hours of fasting increased the abundance of a beneficial bacterium called Akkermansia muciniphila, also known as AKK, in the small intestine. This microbe produces a substance called propionate, which helps trigger changes inside intestinal cells that make them better prepared to regenerate following radiation damage.

Propionate works alongside other metabolic changes caused by fasting to modify proteins known as histones. These proteins serve as structures around which DNA is packaged inside cells. Small chemical markers added to histones can influence which genes become active without changing the underlying DNA sequence.

These modifications make portions of DNA more accessible, allowing cells to activate genes involved in tissue regeneration. During fasting, a population of intestinal cells carrying these repair programs becomes more abundant.

In effect, fasting helps prepare these cells with the biological instructions they will need if an injury occurs. When the intestines are subsequently exposed to radiation, the prepared cells can expand and help rebuild the damaged intestinal lining.

One Gut Bacterium Proves Essential for Recovery

To determine how important AKK was to this process, the researchers selectively removed the bacterium. Without it, fasting no longer produced the same regenerative benefits.

Even more revealing, the protective response returned only when the bacterium was restored in combination with fasting. This demonstrated that neither component alone was sufficient to reproduce the full effect observed in the study.

The results suggest that fasting does more than temporarily change the gut's metabolism. Together with AKK, it alters the activity of intestinal cells before radiation exposure, placing them in a state that supports more efficient recovery after damage occurs.

By uncovering this connection between nutrition, gut bacteria, and cellular regeneration, the researchers have identified a potential new way to strengthen the body's response to tissue injury. The discovery could be especially valuable for protecting healthy organs during cancer treatment.

Could Gut Bacteria Make Cancer Treatment Safer?

Although the results are promising, the research remains preclinical. Additional studies will be needed to determine whether the same protective mechanism operates in humans and whether it can safely improve outcomes for patients receiving radiation therapy.

One possibility is that the newly discovered pathway could be used to help other healthy tissues recover from cancer treatment. Researchers are particularly interested in tissues with rapidly dividing cells, including bone marrow, which can also suffer treatment-related damage.

If further investigations support the findings, clinical trials could eventually explore whether activating this repair mechanism benefits patients undergoing abdominal radiation therapy.

Importantly, the discovery may also provide ways to achieve these effects without requiring patients to fast. Treatments involving beneficial bacteria or the molecules they produce could potentially stimulate similar repair processes while avoiding the practical difficulties of food restriction during cancer care.

"Fasting is not always practical for cancer patients, and this work supports several other potential ways to enhance recovery after treatment," Rai said. "Whether through dietary interventions, targeted microbes or their metabolites, the goal is to help repair healthy tissue more effectively while patients receive the cancer therapies they need."

The research was funded by the National Cancer Institute (NCI) within the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the Cancer Prevention and Research Institute of Texas (CPRIT).

#5574. Most nonprofit hospitals' tax breaks outpaced their community spending in 2023: Lown Institute

Most nonprofit hospitals' tax breaks outpaced their community spending in 2023: Lown Institute" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Just over half of the country’s nonprofit hospitals have charity care and community benefit investments that fall short of their tax savings, according to the latest of the Lown Institute’s analyses on more than 3,000 hospitals’ tax filings.

In 2023, the most recent year in which Internal Revenue Service Form 990s were available for review, the think tank identified $38.8 billion of industry-wide tax exemptions, or $12.8 million per hospital and 3.8% of total expenses on average. About $37.1 billion was collectively spent by the same hospitals on various community benefits, as reported in the IRS forms matched to other filings such as Medicare cost reports.

While the total exemption handily outpaces the benefits investments by Lown’s measure, the group underscored that these "fair share” deficits or surpluses also vary widely between facilities, and that some of the industry’s biggest names are on the wrong side of the divide.

Here, Mayo Clinic Hospital led the pack with a $366 million deficit, according to Lown’s analysis, followed by Tisch Hospital (-$294 million deficit), Stanford Hospital (-$255 million deficit), New York-Presbyterian Hospital (-$248 million deficit) and Massachusetts General Hospital (-$219 million deficit).

"Some of America's wealthiest hospitals fall hundreds of millions short of giving back what they receive from their communities, leaving those with fewer resources to pick up the slack," Vikas Saini, M.D., president of the Lown Institute, said in a release on the new analysis, released Tuesday.

Among those leading the latter group were North Shore University Hospital ($167 fair share surplus), Rochester General Hospital ($146 million surplus) and Englewood Hospital ($142 million surplus). Lown’s analysis includes a searchable hospital-by-hospital breakdown of the tax exemptions and community investment totals.

When splitting the 52% of deficit hospitals apart from the surplus hospitals, the former group logged about $15.5 billion above their reported community benefits—a deficit Lown said could wipe the medical debt of 12 million Americans. Fair share surplus hospitals outpaced their exemptions by $13.8 billion.

Total tax exemptions were also “very unevenly distributed” among the hospitals, Lown said. The 30 hospitals, or about 1% of all hospitals, with the largest tax exemptions collectively avoided $6.8 billion, or about 18% of total exemptions. The 607 hospitals, or about 20%, accounted for three-quarters of the country’s hospital tax exemptions.

Lown’s measure of nonprofit hospitals’ tax breaks includes exemptions from federal and state corporate income taxes, state and local sales taxes, property taxes, tax-exempt bonds, tax-exempt charitable donations and federal unemployment tax exemptions. Not included are other benefits provided to many nonprofits, like Medicaid disproportionate share payments, 340B discounts or profits from indirect tax arbitrage.

Its tally of community benefit includes spending on patient financial assistance, subsidized care, payments to other nonprofits to improve health or various community health or social determinants of health investments.

Of note, it excludes Medicaid shortfall—the difference between hospitals’ costs and revenues when treating Medicaid patients—and spending on professional education and research. The hospital industry typically points to these billions of dollars of exclusions when discussing their tax breaks, with Medicaid shortfall alone accounting for nearly half of their preferred community benefit spending totals. Lown noted in its methodology that these accounting losses are often offset by other discounts and supplemental benefits and don’t always have a direct impact on community health, among other objections.

Lown said the disparities between hospitals and the outsized benefits being delivered by some are a call to amend, not eliminate, nonprofit status exemptions. The think tank accompanied its analysis with calls to increase reporting transparency and set spending targets for hospitals tied to variables such as size, exemption value, financial health and prior spending.

“Tax exemptions aren't a gift—they're an expectation, and regulators need to make sure all hospitals hold up their end of the bargain," Saini said.

Lown acknowledged the impending financial pressure hospitals will face with upcoming H.R. 1 policy changes and said such changes should be accompanied by “short-term” financial protections.

Still, the group isn’t alone in drawing scrutiny to the tax breaks. Lawmakers and policy advisors have pointed to, and questioned the justification for, nonprofits’ exemptions when questioning health system leaders on collections policies or high prices.

Academics and researchers have also called for greater transparency or other overhauls of how community benefits are reported or calculated. Of note, a research article published earlier this month in Health Affairs reviewing hospital filings between 2013 and 2022 outlined a disconnect between different hospitals’ listed charity care eligibility thresholds and their relative spending, which more closely aligned with community need than their stated policy.

#5573. Alibaba launches Qwen4-Max with training, attention optimizations

Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. today introduced Qwen4-Max, its newest and most capable large language model.

The algorithm not only generates higher-quality output than its predecessor but also costs less. Those improvements are the result of a new architecture, Qwen4, that made the LLM’s training run more efficient. Additionally, Alibaba has equipped the model with an upgraded attention mechanism.

Qwen4-Max’s backbone, the part of an LLM that functions as its main processing engine, comprises 2.4 trillion parameters. The model activates only 71 billion at any given time. The backbone is supported by 328 billion so-called N-gram parameters, which function as a kind of cache. They save the results of oft-repeated calculations and thereby remove the need to compute them from scratch every time.

An LLM’s artificial neurons are organized into sets known as layers. When the model learns something new during training, a piece of data called a gradient travels through the layers and refines their output. The gradient moves through them one by one starting from the last layer, which finalizes and displays prompt responses.

Qwen4-Max includes a feature that enables the gradient to skip some layers. That feature, or residual, is effectively a shortcut inside the LLM. Its purpose is to reduce errors during the training workflow, which in turn lowers costs and improves output quality.

Residuals can also be found in many other LLMs. Historically, the mechanism was implemented as a single gradient transportation channel. Qwen4-Max’s implementation of the technology features four channels. Moreover, those channels have a “gate” that can adjust the movement of gradients to further improve the training process.

Qwen4-Max’s attention mechanism, a module that helps it understand user prompts, features two key customizations. The first is a technology called Gated DeltaNet that lowers the amount of hardware needed to process large prompts. The second optimization, QSA, skips pieces of data that the LLM doesn’t need to answer a prompt. That arrangement further lowers infrastructure costs.

Alibaba compared Qwen4-Max with its predecessor, Qwen3.8-Max, using an internal benchmark that includes knowledge work tasks. The former model achieved a higher score and used up to 35% fewer tokens to complete tasks. Those savings grew to 49% when the models were tested using the Terminal-Bench 4.0 suite of coding challenges.

Qwen4-Max is available through Alibaba’s cloud platform. The company plans to open-source a collection of smaller models based on the same technologies further down the line. It’s also open-sourcing Qwen-Live-Delivery-Plugin, an extension that makes Qwen4-Max better at performing time-consuming tasks.

When an LLM is assigned a long-horizon project, users often have to wait until the model completes its work before they can review the results. Alibaba’s plugin shortens the wait. It enables Qwen4-Max to quickly deliver an initial draft and then iteratively add improvements. Users can give the model feedback along the way to refine its work.

#5572. HHS finalizes updates to HIPAA privacy rule to ease patient access to health information

HHS finalizes updates to HIPAA privacy rule to ease patient access to health information" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The final rule, issued by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office for Civil Rights (OCR), strengthens and clarifies the right of an individual to access their protected health information and reduces regulatory and administrative burdens, the agency said.

The proposed rule was issued more than five years ago, in January 2021. An unpublished version of the final rule is available here.

Under the final rule, healthcare organizations must respond faster to patient requests for copies of their health records. HHS said covered entities will have no more than 15 calendar days to respond to a request, reduced from the current 30-day period. Organizations are allowed one extension of no more than 30 calendar days, HHS said in the final rule.

The rule also establishes that patients can access their protected health information through personal health apps when the covered entity has the technical capacity to deliver the records in that form and format.

The rule also expands circumstances when patients must receive copies of their health records for free, requires advance notice of fees and modifies identity verification requirements.

To make it easier for healthcare organizations to share data for care coordination, the final rule clarifies that health plans may use and disclose protected health information for care coordination and case management for individuals. The rule also expressly permits covered entities to disclose PHI to social services agencies, community-based organizations and similar third parties for care coordination and case management for individuals.

“Americans should never have to fight for access to their own health records,” said HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr in a statement. “Under President Trump’s leadership, we are putting patients in control, requiring faster access to their information, and cutting red tape that gets in the way of coordinated care. This rule modernizes HIPAA to serve patients and help providers spend more time delivering care and less time navigating bureaucracy.”

Provisions in the final rule will become effective 60 days after publication in the Federal Register, and compliance will be required 180 days after that date, according to HHS in a fact sheet.

Gleason said there are three main components of the rule: the designation of a "personal health app," identity verification and speed. "It should be almost instantaneous with electronic data, and it also says that this information is free to the patient," she said.

“This final rule provides Americans with faster and easier access to their health information, which is critical to them being able to take control of their own health and health care,” said Office for Civil Rights Director Paula M. Stannard in a statement. “Consistent with the Trump Administration’s deregulatory goals, the rule also reduces regulatory burdens on health care providers and other regulated entities and decreases costs for the health care system

#5571. 314 Action Celebrates Its Victories in Getting Docs, Other Clinicians Elected

— "Things went even better than expected," said Shaughnessy Naughton, the group's founder

The midterm results earlier this month included the election of several physicians and other healthcare professionals to federal and statewide seats, especially on the Democratic side. MedPage Today Washington Editor Joyce Frieden spoke with Shaughnessy Naughton, founder and president of 314 Action, about the organization's role in helping to get some of these clinicians -- as well as scientists -- elected to office. The conversation, which was conducted over the phone with a public relations person present, has been edited for length and clarity.

How did your organization do in terms of seeing its chosen candidates elected?

Things went even better than expected. We are the only organization to elect Democratic scientists and doctors to all levels of government -- 14 members to the House, including 10 who took seats from Republicans -- two new doctors to the Senate, which hasn't had Democratic doctors serving in close to 60 years; and a Democratic doctor as governor in Ohio, the first woman doctor-governor in the country.

There's a couple of arms to that answer. First, we recruited and invested early in quality candidates. Additionally, this was a healthcare election and our candidates leaned into their backgrounds as doctors and as problem-solvers to present a clear contrast with their opponents that have overseen, particularly in the federal races, the slashing of Medicaid, the elimination of the [Affordable Care Act Enhanced Premium Tax Credit], the assault on rural health, and on and on.

Then you couple that with [HHS Secretary] Robert F. Kennedy Jr. -- the vaccine delusionist -- overseeing HHS during one health crisis after another, leading to preventable deaths from measles and preventable diseases. So I think all of that compounded to really create a lane that voters saw as a viable and important alternative to what they currently had.

Annie Andrews, MD, [D-S.C. senator-elect] is at the top of that list. South Carolina hasn't elected a Democrat statewide, I think, in over 20 years. It is very hard to change people's voting patterns, but it does speak to the strength of her message and her candidacy that she was able to not only get elected, but she brought along a congressional race in South Carolina -- one that flipped to Democrat -- and 10 statehouse seats. Wow!

We are really looking forward to what she can accomplish in the Senate. I was having coffee this morning with a senator who had just met her at orientation this week, and he said he told her to "Lean in and make sure your voice is being heard because we really need you right now." I think that that is true coming from the senator's mouth, but I think it's also true coming from the voters' mouth.

You mentioned the vaccine issue and the Affordable Care Act tax credits. What other healthcare issues are you hoping to see acted on in the new Congress?

We were promised [by the current administration and Congress] to see a reduction in healthcare costs, and we've seen the exact opposite. Premiums continue to skyrocket. Out-of-pocket costs and deductibles just keep going up, and there doesn't seem to be much relief on prescription drug prices either.

This is at a time when we're having record numbers of foodborne illness outbreaks and measles deaths and spread. The threshold for herd immunity is 95% for measles, and most kindergarteners' classes are below that at this point. So it really does call to have strong health leaders leading with facts and evidence and their values to protect Americans' health and make healthcare more affordable.

We are looking for action on healthcare affordability and accessibility, and holding the administration accountable for what, to say the least, have been questionable choices such as the approval of candy-flavored vapes, so we do expect that Congress should be able to deliver on both.

Even though they don't have enough votes to override a presidential veto?

What happens remains to be seen. The moves from the administration do not [suggest] that they want to work with Democrats, but the remaining Republicans in the House still have elections in 2 years, and the American people spoke loud and clear that they want relief from high prices across the board.

Can you explain more about your organization's role? I understand you spent more than $30 million this cycle. Do you recruit as well as contribute financially?

Yes, we are involved in recruiting. One of the things we're seeing bearing fruit is an investment at the state and local level. One of the people we endorsed in the 2018 cycle was [microbiologist] Jasmine Clark, PhD. She ran in a Republican district in the Georgia statehouse and flipped the seat. This year she stepped up to run for a congressional seat, and won.

We work with campaigns, helping them put together their campaign strategy, a financing plan, and consulting teams. We find staff and work at the grassroots level with them. Often our campaign staff will be in the district with them when they launch, and our communications staff works with them on media training.

We have individual donors; this cycle we had 150,000 individual contributors. Their first donation average is $10; the lifetime average is $17. People usually donate three times a year and many have been donating to us for 3, 4, or 5 years. We do a lot of grassroots fundraising, and we also have been the beneficiary of [former New York City Mayor] Michael Bloomberg's generosity this cycle, which makes a lot of sense because he is someone invested in public health and public health education.

We have candidates fill out a questionnaire, which is on our website. And we are already thinking about 2028 -- even 2027 has some local elections [of interest]. We need to play everywhere. When you run credible candidates, they can resonate and make a difference and get elected.

What is your background and how did you end up starting 314 Action?

I was a chemist and worked in breast cancer research and drug discovery, and I worked on creating an antibiotic to combat superbugs. In 2014, I became concerned by the antiscience rhetoric coming out of so many politicians, so I decided to run for Congress in Bucks County, Pennsylvania, where I'm from. But I didn't have 314 Action and was locked out of the [standard] donor network, so I started cold-calling chemists and making my case and building out a network from there.

Ultimately, I didn't win, but I learned a lot in the process and part of what I learned is that it's very hard to break into politics when you don't have that traditional political background. And so I founded 314 Action to break down those barriers, to recruit, train, and elect people with scientific backgrounds, with the thinking that there isn't an issue that doesn't benefit by having data-driven analytical thinkers actually at the governing table.

#5570. For decades, we were told to avoid full-fat dairy. New research says otherwise

For years, people have been encouraged to choose low-fat or fat-free dairy products to protect their hearts and manage their weight. But growing scientific evidence suggests that full-fat dairy may not carry the health risks many have come to expect.

A new Canadian study led by University of Toronto professor Harvey Anderson adds to that evidence. Researchers found that adults who consumed three servings of full-fat dairy each day for 12 weeks did not experience harmful changes in body weight, body composition, energy metabolism, or blood cholesterol levels compared with participants following a diet containing little dairy.

Even more surprisingly, participants who consumed more dairy showed improvements in blood pressure and obtained greater amounts of several important nutrients.

The findings, published in The Journal of Nutrition, raise new questions about longstanding dietary recommendations and suggest that the health effects of dairy may be more complicated than its saturated fat content alone would indicate.

For decades, nutrition guidelines in Canada and many other countries have recommended choosing low-fat or fat-free milk, yogurt, and other dairy products. The main concern has been saturated fat, which can raise levels of LDL cholesterol in the blood.

Often called "bad" cholesterol, LDL can contribute to fatty deposits in the arteries. Over time, this buildup can increase the risk of heart attacks, strokes, and other cardiovascular problems.

Because full-fat dairy contains more saturated fat than reduced-fat alternatives, health authorities have traditionally encouraged people to limit their intake.

However, research examining what happens when people actually consume full-fat dairy has produced a more complicated picture.

Anderson, a professor of nutritional sciences at the University of Toronto's Temerty Faculty of Medicine, points out that numerous studies involving humans have failed to find a clear association between full-fat dairy consumption and poor health outcomes.

Other research has even identified potential protective effects. That includes a recent study led by Temerty Medicine professor Kozeta Milliku, which found an association between whole-fat milk consumption and a lower risk of childhood obesity.

These findings have prompted scientists to investigate whether dairy foods behave differently in the body than their individual nutrients might suggest.

What Happened When Adults Ate Full-Fat Dairy Every Day?

To explore the question, Anderson and his colleagues conducted a 12-week study involving 74 adults with overweight or obesity.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of three dietary approaches. The first group followed a calorie-restricted diet containing little dairy. The second consumed three daily servings of dairy while maintaining an energy-neutral diet, meaning their calorie intake was intended to match the energy their bodies used. The third also consumed three servings of dairy each day but otherwise ate without specific calorie restrictions.

All participants received guidance based on Canada's food guide, and the researchers supplied full-fat dairy products during the study.

At the end of 12 weeks, the team compared several measures of metabolic health, including body weight, body composition, and cholesterol levels.

The results challenged expectations. Participants who consumed three servings of dairy daily did not show meaningful differences in weight gain, body composition, or blood cholesterol compared with those who ate little dairy.

The higher-dairy groups also experienced improvements in blood pressure and consumed more calcium, protein, and vitamin D. These nutrients play essential roles in maintaining healthy bones, supporting muscle function, and regulating numerous processes throughout the body.

"Those that had three servings of dairy didn't have adverse levels of blood cholesterol or lipids or evidence of insulin resistance," says Anderson.

Blood lipids are fats and fat-like substances circulating in the bloodstream, including cholesterol and triglycerides. Insulin resistance occurs when the body's cells become less responsive to insulin, making it harder to regulate blood sugar and increasing the risk of type 2 diabetes.

Although the results are encouraging, the study was relatively small and lasted only three months. Longer and larger studies are needed to determine whether the findings translate into lasting health benefits or changes in cardiovascular disease risk.

Why might full-fat dairy have different health effects than researchers would predict from its saturated fat content?

One possible explanation is the dairy matrix hypothesis, an idea that emphasizes how the physical structure of food influences the way the body processes its nutrients.

Rather than treating milk, cheese, or yogurt as simple collections of fat, protein, vitamins, and minerals, this theory considers how those components interact within the food itself.

"With dairy products, it's got two proteins -- casein and whey -- that are bound together with fat and with nutrients mixed in," says Anderson.

Casein and whey are the two major types of protein found in milk. Both provide amino acids that the body uses to build and maintain tissues, but they are digested and absorbed at different rates.

According to Anderson, the complex arrangement of proteins, fats, and other nutrients in dairy products can help regulate how quickly those nutrients are released during digestion.

This means the body's response to eating a whole dairy food may differ from its response to consuming an equivalent amount of saturated fat on its own.

The broader implication is that a food's health effects cannot always be predicted by examining a single ingredient. Its structure, nutritional composition, and interactions among nutrients may all matter.

Why the Findings Could Be Important for Older Adults

The researchers believe these results could be particularly relevant for older people, who often need to obtain sufficient protein and essential nutrients while consuming fewer calories.

As people age, their overall energy requirements frequently decrease. However, maintaining muscle mass, bone strength, and other important bodily functions still requires adequate nutrition.

That can make it difficult to meet nutritional needs, particularly for people with smaller appetites.

Anderson explains that dairy products offer a familiar, convenient source of concentrated nutrition. They provide protein, calcium, and other nutrients in foods that many older adults already enjoy and regularly consume.

The new findings suggest that including full-fat dairy in a balanced diet may help people meet these nutritional requirements without necessarily worsening cholesterol levels or markers associated with diabetes risk.

However, the study did not directly establish whether long-term consumption prevents or increases diabetes, heart disease, or other chronic conditions.

Rethinking Nutrition Advice Beyond Individual Nutrients

Beyond the debate over dairy fat, the research highlights a broader challenge in nutrition science: judging the health effects of entire foods rather than focusing exclusively on individual nutrients.

Traditional dietary advice has often emphasized reducing specific components, such as saturated fat. Although these recommendations are grounded in evidence about cardiovascular risk, researchers increasingly recognize that different foods containing the same nutrients may not have identical effects on health.

The University of Toronto findings contribute to this discussion by showing that full-fat dairy can be incorporated into certain diets without the unfavorable short-term metabolic changes that might be expected from its saturated fat content.

That does not mean saturated fat is harmless or that everyone should switch to full-fat dairy. Instead, it suggests that the overall food, its nutritional structure, and the broader dietary pattern deserve consideration.

For people trying to navigate changing nutrition recommendations and conflicting health messages, Anderson favors a practical approach rather than complicated dietary rules.

"Keep it simple, eat a variety of foods and not too much of anything."

This research was supported by Dairy Research Cluster 3 under the Canadian Agricultural Partnership AgriScience Program, and the Mitacs Accelerate program.

#5569. HLTH 2026: GLP-1 costs remain a challenge. A new CVS study aims to identify the right price

HLTH 2026: GLP-1 costs remain a challenge. A new CVS study aims to identify the right price" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Cost and access to GLP-1s remains a challenge, but the benefits of these drugs aren't in doubt.

A new study from CVS Health aims to quantify at what price a GLP-1 drug has generated enough savings elsewhere through improved clinical outcomes. The healthcare giant used anonymized claims data from Aetna members in fully insured plans and found savings from reduced hospital and medical spending, as well as improved health outcomes.

But those benefits weren't enough to offset the increased pharmaceutical spending at the current price point, the study found.

The study tracked a mix of members who took GLP-1s from 2023 to 2025, so some patients had three years of follow-up care and management.

Amy Compton-Phillips, M.D., chief medical officer at CVS, told Fierce Healthcare that part of the challenge in this equation is that these drugs gained steam as a treatment for obesity at a high price. And while those costs have come down, the reductions haven't yet been enough to offset the expenditures.

Another challenge for employers in particular—where GLP-1 coverage has been most in flux—is turnover, she said. While GLP-1s do drive significant improvements, an employer may not reap the benefit of the reduced cost if an employee moves to a different company before those are realized, even though they paid for the medication initially.

The study sought to identify a price point where those savings would be felt and landed at $350 per month over a three-year period. Achieving that, Compton-Phillips said, would likely lure employers into embracing broader GLP-1 coverage.

"For them, it might be really worthwhile to say, 'Hey, at this price point, I can afford to cover this for my employees, knowing that in the near term the savings will pay for my investment,'" she said.

The study found obesity rates declining after a 2022 peak, as well as a reduction of between 34% and 42% in hospitalizations over three years. Patients also had 14% lower odds of a serious cardiac event.

For patients who remained on the drugs for three years, their total medical spending decreased by $9,400, but associated pharmacy spending increased in tandem by $13,300, the study found.

Clinical improvements also fell off when patients were not able to remain adherent to the medication over several years, highlighting the importance of a wraparound approach that supports broader care management rather than simply prescribing a patient a GLP-1.

Compton-Phillips said CVS' own weight management program brings nutrition, peer coaching and other supports into the fold, in addition to the prescription. This is especially critical, she said, as evidence suggests weight gain is common after a patient stops taking their GLP-1, making behavior change key.

"At the moment, there's not great evidence that if you come off the drugs, you will maintain the weight loss," she said.

The CVS researchers said that the ultimate goal of the study was not to demand that all GLP-1 prescriptions repay their own costs, but to ensure that drug costs align with patient benefits and the broader cost of access. By lowering the net price of these products, more people can access them, the study concludes.

"These drugs make people's lives better, and I want to give them out," Compton-Phillips said. Doing so becomes a challenge, though, "at the price they are today," she said.

#5568. FDA Adds Another Player in ALK-Positive Lung Cancer

— Among the indications, neladalkib approved in second-line after alectinib

The FDA granted accelerated approval to the third-generation ALK inhibitor neladalkib (Nelkarmi) for previously treated advanced ALK-positive non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), making it the seventh approved agent in a crowded therapeutic field.

The approval limits use to patients with unresectable locally advanced or metastatic ALK-positive NSCLC previously treated with alectinib (Alecensa) or at least two prior ALK tyrosine kinase inhibitors and platinum-based chemotherapy.

Support for the conditional approval came from 222 patients in the phase I/II single-arm ALKOVE-1 trial.

In the cohort of 67 patients who had only received alectinib in the metastatic setting, neladalkib induced responses in 49%, with a duration of response (DOR) of at least 6 months in 76% of the responding patients. For the cohort of 155 patients previously treated with two or more ALK inhibitors and platinum-based chemotherapy, 32% responded, with a DOR of at least 6 months for 69% of the responders. The proportion of responders with DORs of at least 12 months was 52% and 51% for the two cohorts, respectively.

"Patients with ALK-positive lung cancer are often treated with multiple targeted therapies over many years," said investigator Alice Shaw, MD, PhD, of Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston, in a press release from drugmaker GSK. "Advances in treatment have brought us closer to the goal of managing ALK-positive lung cancer as a chronic condition, but balancing disease control and long-term tolerability remains a significant challenge. The approval of neladalkib provides an important new treatment option for patients."

An analysis reported at the 2026 American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) meeting showed a response rate of 26% among patients with exposure to lorlatinib (Lorbrena), the only other approved third-generation ALK inhibitor, versus 46% in patients not previously treated with lorlatinib. DORs of at least 6 or 12 months in the lorlatinib-treated subgroup occurred in 68% and 54% of responders.

In the full cohort of patients presented at the meeting (median three prior lines of therapy), landmark analyses of progression-free survival (PFS) showed a 6-month PFS of 50%, 12-month PFS of 33%, and 18-month PFS of 28% for patients treated with neladalkib. Median PFS was 5.7 months, increasing to 14.5 months in patients not previously treated with lorlatinib. Additionally, a third of patients with brain metastases had objective responses with neladalkib.

At the ASCO meeting, invited discussant Angel Qin, MD, of the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor, said the ALKOVE-1 results suggest neladalkib has potential as an option in the post-lorlatinib setting, albeit with relatively modest activity, and a manageable side-effect profile.

The most common adverse events (AEs) were elevated liver enzymes, which occurred in almost half of patients and was grade ≥3 severity in 15-20% of patients. Other AEs occurring in at least 20% of patients were musculoskeletal pain, constipation, dysgeusia, peripheral neuropathy, edema, and fatigue. Prescribing information for neladalkib includes warnings and precautions for hepatotoxicity, renal toxicity, ocular toxicity, creatine phosphokinase elevation, and embryo-fetal toxicity.

The ongoing phase III ALKAZAR trial of neladalkib in the first-line setting may provide more information about the drug's potential as upfront therapy in advanced ALK-positive NSCLC. A preliminary analysis from ALKOVE-1 at ASCO showed an objective response rate of 86% for patients with no prior ALK-targeted therapy.

#5567. When your gut bacteria run out of fiber, they may start eating your gut lining

Eating more plants is widely associated with better health, but scientists are still uncovering exactly why. New research suggests that fiber is only part of the story. Certain plant proteins that resist digestion may also play a surprisingly important role in shaping gut bacteria and determining whether they produce beneficial or potentially harmful substances.

Plant-based diets support digestive health, immune function, metabolism, and cardiovascular health. One reason is that they help maintain a diverse community of microorganisms in the intestines, collectively known as the gut microbiome. Many of these bacteria are beneficial, helping break down food components that the human digestive system cannot process on its own.

Fiber is particularly important because it provides food for gut microbes. Plants also contain phytochemicals, natural substances that often give fruits and vegetables their vibrant colors and help protect them from environmental threats. These compounds can also contribute to human health. Yet researchers have only begun to understand the complicated chemical interactions that occur when gut bacteria digest plant foods.

Two studies led by Jenna AbuSalim and Joshua Rabinowitz, director of the Princeton Branch of the Ludwig Institute for Cancer Research, provide important new insights. One, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, shows how plant fiber and certain proteins influence gut bacteria to favor the production of beneficial compounds over potentially harmful ones. The other, published in Nature Metabolism in June, challenges the longstanding belief that many important chemical compounds circulating in the body originate exclusively from intestinal microbes.

"There's growing interest across medical disciplines in manipulating the human microbiome or using its metabolic products themselves for therapy," said Rabinowitz. "Diet holds great promise for controlling the microbiome and its outputs. But to devise effective therapeutic interventions, we need to understand what aspects of the diet control which microbial outputs."

How Plant Foods Change the Chemicals Your Gut Produces

In the PNAS study, researchers examined a group of substances called phenol metabolites. Metabolites are chemicals formed when the body or microorganisms break down and process nutrients. Some are essential for normal biological functions, while others can contribute to health problems when they accumulate.

The phenol metabolites investigated by the team are produced when gut bacteria process two amino acids, tyrosine and phenylalanine. Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins, but the compounds they ultimately produce can have very different effects on health.

Two metabolites derived from phenylalanine, phenylpropionate and hippuric acid, are associated with healthy body weight and better gut health. In contrast, two compounds derived from tyrosine, p-cresol sulfate and phenol sulfate, have been linked to worse outcomes in cancer patients and harmful effects throughout the body in people with kidney disease.

The researchers wanted to understand whether different components of plant foods could influence which of these substances gut microbes produce.

"Our studies showed that both the fiber and indigestible proteins from plants -- which we call 'proteins imitating fiber,' or Prif -- shift the balance of phenol metabolites from the harmful kind made from tyrosine to the healthful variety derived from phenylalanine," said AbuSalim.

An Overlooked Plant Protein Works Alongside Fiber

Although the health benefits of dietary fiber have been studied extensively, scientists have paid much less attention to plant proteins that pass through the digestive system without being fully broken down.

The researchers found that these indigestible proteins, which they call Prif, can reach the gut microbiome and serve as material for bacterial metabolism. In doing so, they influence which microbes thrive and which chemical compounds are produced.

Importantly, these proteins do not work in isolation. They cooperate with plant fiber to change how gut bacteria process nutrients, shifting their activity toward the production of beneficial phenol metabolites.

This discovery suggests that the nutritional value of plant foods may depend on more than their familiar concentrations of fiber, vitamins, and minerals. The amount and type of protein that escapes digestion could also help determine how food influences the gut microbiome.

When Gut Bacteria Run Low on Fiber, They May Feed on Your Gut's Protective Mucus

One of the most intriguing findings concerns where gut bacteria obtain the raw materials used to produce harmful metabolites.

To investigate, the researchers labeled proteins with stable (non-radioactive) isotopes, allowing them to track exactly where the proteins traveled and how they were processed in the digestive systems of mice. This technique works by giving molecules a detectable chemical signature without making them radioactive.

The experiments revealed an important difference between the sources of beneficial and harmful phenols.

The potentially harmful phenols came from gut bacteria breaking down proteins belonging to the host, including proteins found in the mucus layer that coats the intestines. This protective mucus helps separate intestinal microbes from the cells lining the gut and forms part of the body's natural defenses.

Meanwhile, the beneficial phenols were produced almost entirely from indigestible proteins supplied by food.

Fiber helped suppress the bacterial breakdown of the gut's protective mucus, reducing the production of harmful phenols. The indigestible plant proteins (Prif), in turn, supplied more dietary protein to gut bacteria, encouraging them to produce beneficial compounds instead.

Together, the findings reveal two complementary ways plant foods can influence intestinal chemistry. Fiber helps discourage bacteria from consuming proteins in the gut's protective mucus, while Prif provides an alternative source of nutrients that supports the production of healthier metabolites.

"We think Prifs represent an emerging class of dietary nutrients that shape the composition of the gut microbiome and could have a far-reaching influence on metabolic health," said AbuSalim.

The implications could eventually extend to nutrition labels and dietary recommendations.

"Food packaging may eventually list Prif right below fiber," said Rabinowitz.

A Second Discovery Challenges What Scientists Thought About Gut Bacteria

The companion study in Nature Metabolism addressed another important question: Are gut bacteria really responsible for producing all the metabolites traditionally attributed to them?

Along with phenol metabolites, the researchers examined indole metabolites, which are formed from tryptophan, another amino acid found in dietary proteins.

These substances have attracted considerable scientific interest because they participate in biological processes linked to inflammation, immune activity, and disease. Researchers have investigated their involvement in inflammatory bowel disease, neurodegenerative disorders, and cancer. Some indole metabolites have also been found to influence the spread of cancer and the immune system's ability to attack tumors.

Scientists have generally assumed that gut bacteria are the source of these compounds. That belief has encouraged efforts to develop probiotics and dietary interventions that increase the production of potentially beneficial indole metabolites.

However, this approach depends on an important assumption: that intestinal microbes are responsible for producing most or all of the compounds researchers want to influence.

If the body's own cells make substantial amounts of these metabolites, changing the microbiome may not be the most effective way to control their levels.

Your Body Can Make Compounds Once Attributed to Gut Microbes

To investigate, the research team used isotope tracing in mice, rats, and human cells to follow how different metabolites were produced.

The results challenged conventional thinking. Mammalian cells were capable of generating numerous phenol and indole metabolites independently of intestinal bacteria.

Among these were indole-3-lactate and indole-3-acetate, two biologically important compounds previously considered products of microbial metabolism.

The researchers also examined what happened when antibiotics disrupted the intestinal microbiome. If certain metabolites depended entirely on gut bacteria, their concentrations would be expected to decline sharply when those bacteria were depleted.

But many metabolites remained at substantial levels in the blood of antibiotic-treated mice. A similar pattern appeared in samples from patients receiving antibiotics, including people undergoing cancer treatment.

Other compounds behaved differently. Levels of indole-3-propionate and p-cresol sulfate, which are produced exclusively by microbes, declined following antibiotic treatment.

These results provided further evidence that some metabolites depend on intestinal bacteria, while others can also be manufactured by the body's own metabolic processes.

The distinction matters because it could change how researchers develop treatments intended to increase beneficial metabolites or reduce harmful ones.

What These Discoveries Mean for Nutrition and Future Treatments

Together, the two studies offer a more detailed understanding of how diet, gut microbes, and the body's own metabolism interact.

The first identifies an overlooked category of plant proteins that works with fiber to influence bacterial activity, potentially helping shift the balance away from harmful metabolic products. The second demonstrates that the body itself can produce many compounds once believed to originate exclusively from gut bacteria.

Both findings have implications for research into metabolic disease, digestive health, cancer, and other conditions involving the microbiome.

They also suggest that attempts to manipulate gut chemistry through diet, probiotics, or other therapies will need to account for both microbial activity and the body's own metabolic capabilities.

Much of the experimental evidence comes from animals and laboratory studies, so additional research will be needed to determine how these mechanisms influence long-term health outcomes in people.

Nevertheless, a better understanding of the relationship between different food components and microbial metabolism could eventually make dietary advice more precise and help researchers identify new therapeutic strategies.

"Beyond that," said Rabinowitz, "a clearer picture of how different foods interact with the microbiome to modulate the production of bacterial metabolites will help sharpen the guidance nutritionists and doctors can give to people for disease prevention and therapy."

These studies were funded by the Ludwig Institute for Cancer Research, the National Institutes of Health, the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, the Princeton Alliance for Collaborative Research and Innovation, Princeton University.

Aside from his post as Director of the Princeton Branch of the Ludwig Institute for Cancer Research, Joshua Rabinowitz is Professor in the Department of Chemistry & Lewis-Sigler Institute for Integrative Genomics and a member of the Rutgers Cancer Institute.

#5566. Humana launches national provider Gold Card program

Humana launches national provider Gold Card program" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Humana is continuing its push to reform prior authorization with the launch of a national provider gold card program.

The program will go into effect on Dec. 1, the company announced Tuesday. It will focus initially on MRI, CT and MRA imaging as well as physical and occupational therapy. Through the program, eligible providers will no longer need to secure a prior authorization approval and can instead use a streamlined process.

Humana estimates that about 50,000 providers will qualify for the program. Eligible providers must be able to demonstrate a proven track record of high-quality care and patient outcomes.

Traci Granston, M.D., vice president of clinical innovation and trend at Humana, told Fierce Healthcare in an exclusive interview that prior authorization and other utilization management approaches are key in ensuring that patients receive the appropriate care.

However, lengthy decision times and other barriers can create a painful friction. So for providers that consistently demonstrate that they are aligned with clinical guidelines, the gold cards can remove that guardrail.

"If they're following those guidelines and providing appropriate care, prior auths don't really serve a purpose for them," Granston said.

The insurer conducted a pilot earlier this year with about 400 provider organizations and approximately 8,000 clinicians. Through that process, the team conducted interviews with clinicians and office staff who shared their desire for fewer administrative burdens and a simpler experience.

Those insights shaped the broader launch, Humana said, and the insurer intends to continue to iterate and evolve the gold card program over time, including by adding new service lines. It's not uncommon for a program to roll out that aims to support providers, but their voice is less often at the table in shaping what the experience looks like to ensure that their pain points are being addressed.

Granston said that the team is examining more time-sensitive services that could fit within the program, for example.

"For our top-performing providers, we would like to essentially get out of the way and let them continue to care for our members," she said.

The gold card program builds on Humana's existing work to reform prior authorization, including a streamlined approval process for electronic submissions that took effect in January of this year. Under this initiative, Humana responds within one business day in 95% of electronic prior authorization cases.

The insurer also announced earlier this month that it would join forces with athenahealth to accelerate the use of electronic prior authorization. Through the partnership, more of the process is embedded directly in the provider's workflow, streamlining the experience for them at the point of care.

Granston said that the goal is to make it easier to surface the data necessary to make an approval and enable that to occur in real time. This also means that fewer people have to be dedicated to the work of submissions and approval.

"When the information exists, you don't really need all these people to be touching it," she said.

#5565. Erectile Dysfunction Drug Shows Mixed Results in Alzheimer's

— AR1001 missed the primary endpoint in one population, but slowed decline in another

Mirodenafil (known as AR1001), an oral phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor approved in South Korea to treat erectile dysfunction, showed mixed results in people with early Alzheimer's disease in the phase III POLARIS-AD trial.

The treatment missed the primary endpoint in one prespecified group but showed positive results in another, reported Sharon Sha, MD, MS, of Stanford University in Palo Alto, California, at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer's Disease conference in Boston.

In the overall study population, AR1001 showed a nonsignificant difference of -0.11 points versus placebo in Clinical Dementia Rating-Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) scores at 52 weeks (P=0.4015). CDR-SB scores measure cognitive and functional impairment and can range from 0 to 18.

In a population of monotherapy patients -- those not on an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor or memantine at baseline -- AR1001 demonstrated a significant 52-week treatment difference of -0.44 points versus placebo (P=0.0266), representing a 31% slowing of decline.

Secondary endpoints of cognitive and functional measures trended in favor of AR1001 in both populations, with a nominally significant difference in Mini-Mental State Examination scores emerging in the monotherapy population.

The most frequent adverse events were diarrhea, falls, and dizziness. Adverse events led to discontinuation in 5.2% of patients in the AR1001 group and 1.7% in the placebo group.

Serious adverse events were similar in the AR1001 group (10.0%) and the placebo group (9.8%). Four deaths occurred in the AR1001 group (acute myeloid leukemia, cerebrovascular accident, suicide, and ruptured cerebral aneurysm) and three deaths occurred in the placebo group.

The CDR-SB data and safety profile are encouraging, Sha noted. "POLARIS-AD made its primary efficacy endpoint in the prespecified monotherapy population," she said. "The secondary endpoints had trends in favor of AR1001."

AR1001 is a brain-penetrant phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor that enhances cyclic guanosine monophosphate (GMP) signaling. In preclinical Alzheimer's models, the treatment improved cognitive performance and reduced amyloid and tau burdens.

"AR1001 takes a novel approach, relaxing blood vessels to increase blood flow to the brain," noted Richard Oakley, PhD, of the Alzheimer's Society in England, who wasn't involved in the study.

"AR1001 is from the same family of medicines as Viagra [sildenafil], but it is being developed specifically for Alzheimer's disease. People should not take Viagra to try to treat Alzheimer's," Oakley said in a statement. "We look forward to seeing the full results from this trial and how this drug progresses."

In 2024, a study of 270,000 men in the U.K. linked erectile dysfunction drugs with a reduced risk of Alzheimer's disease. Those findings conflicted with data from the NIH DREAM initiative, but supported an earlier study of Medicare beneficiaries that suggested that sildenafil users were less likely to develop Alzheimer's than non-users.

The POLARIS-AD trial included 1,535 amyloid-positive Alzheimer's patients with mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia in the overall population; the monotherapy subgroup had 604 patients. The average patient age in the study was 73, and just over half were women. Participants were randomized to receive AR1001 30 mg or placebo once daily for 52 weeks.

The primary endpoint was the 52-week change in CDR-SB score in the overall and monotherapy populations. The primary efficacy objective required a significant treatment difference compared with placebo at week 52 in at least one population under the prespecified multiplicity procedure. The prespecified plan was suggested by AR1001's phase II findings, Sha pointed out.

Biomarker tests showed that AR1001 increased cyclic GMP levels in cerebrospinal fluid compared with placebo at week 52 in both the overall (P<0.0001) and monotherapy populations (P=0.0058), supporting target engagement, Sha said.

The presentation included no data about sex differences in treatment effects and Sha said the company has not yet run those analyses. "These results are hot off the press as of Friday," she noted, adding that "continuing analysis is happening, and the open-label extension is ongoing."
